title: Tighten p95 regression thresholds for Runtime LTS gates + document waiver workflow
body:
Tighten p95 regression thresholds for Runtime LTS gates + document waiver workflow

Context: As part of standing up Runtime LTS, we’re using perf-canary to gate patch releases with a small set of canonical workloads. During the 1.18 LTS pilot we saw a few cases where p95 latency regressed in ways that were operationally meaningful (tail spikes / backpressure) but didn’t trip the existing thresholds because they were tuned for mainline signal rather than “slower-change” LTS expectations.

This PR tightens p95 regression thresholds for the LTS gate and adds explicit documentation for the exception/waiver flow that Release Managers can use when benchmarks are noisy (runner contention, transient GPU clocking variance) or when a known/acceptable tradeoff is made (e.g., deliberate throughput vs tail trade).

What changed (high level): 1) LTS-specific thresholds: reduce allowed p95 latency regression from 5% -> 3% on the canonical LTS benchmark set; keep p50 at 2% (unchanged) and tighten throughput regression from -4% -> -3% for the same set. 2) Add a minimum sample-count rule for p95 comparisons (avoid false positives on short runs): require >= 20k tokens per scenario before gating is evaluated; otherwise mark as “insufficient data” and require rerun. 3) Add a documented waiver workflow: a single, auditable “perf-waiver” artifact linked in the PR / release issue, requiring approvals from Perf Owner + SRE + Release Eng lead, with time-bounded validity (per patch only) and mandatory rerun on dedicated runners if the initial run was on shared capacity.

Why: LTS customers are more sensitive to tail latency regressions because they tend to run closer to reserved capacity and use stricter SLOs; we want the default gate to be conservative. The waiver process is to keep us pragmatic when the measurement system is noisy—without silently weakening gates.

Risk: Tightening gates will increase failures/flake until we reduce runner contention (tracked in INT-3368). This PR mitigates with (a) sample-count rule, (b) rerun guidance, and (c) explicit waiver process rather than ad-hoc “LGTM, ship it” decisions.

Rollout: Enabled only for LTS release-branch workflows (release/* and runtime-*-lts) and leaves main branch thresholds unchanged.

Test plan: ran CI unit tests; validated config parsing; dry-ran the LTS workflow against an existing baseline artifact; verified the waiver template renders and is attached to the GitHub Action summary.

Refs: ENG-4825 (Integrate perf-canary gates into LTS release), ENG-4821 (Runtime LTS initiative), INT-3368 (benchmark runner capacity).
Marcus Reed (Perf test suite owner): The 3% p95 limit feels right for LTS, but we should be explicit about what metric we compare (p95 end-to-end vs model-only). Can you clarify in docs? Also, sample count: is 20k tokens enough for the long-context scenario?

Jonas Weber (author): Good call. The gate compares end-to-end request latency p95 as emitted by the benchmark harness (includes queueing + runtime). I’ll add a note in docs/lts/gates.md. Re: 20k tokens—this is per scenario per variant; for long-context we typically hit ~60–120k tokens/run, so we should be safe. The rule is mainly preventing short “smoke” runs from tripping p95.

Claire Dubois (Benchmark methodology): +1 to explicit metric definition. I’m slightly worried about flake on shared runners with 3%. Can the waiver doc require rerun on dedicated runner capacity before waiver is granted?

Jonas Weber (author): Yes—updated waiver doc: if the run was on shared capacity or if the variance indicator > 1.5%, rerun on dedicated runner is mandatory before waiver can be approved.

Allison Grant (Observability/perf signals): Waiver workflow needs an audit trail for release managers. Can we make the action upload a waiver form (even if empty) so the release PR has a consistent artifact name?

Jonas Weber (author): Implemented: the action always publishes a “perf-waiver.md” artifact stub. If waiver requested, it must be filled and re-uploaded (or attached in the release PR) with approvals.

Connor O'Brien (Release Eng lead): Please align terminology with runtime LTS runbook: “waiver” vs “exception”. We’ve been using “waiver” in runbooks. Also, ensure this only applies to LTS release workflows.

Jonas Weber (author): Renamed docs and action summary to “waiver”. Confirmed the workflow applies lts_profile only for release/* and *-lts branches. Mainline continues to use default_profile.

Marcus Reed: Docs update looks good. One more request: add a reminder that repeated waivers for the same scenario should open an infra ticket (runner contention) or a runtime ticket (real regression). Not a blocker but useful.

Jonas Weber (author): Added a “When waivers repeat” section linking to INT-3368 and suggesting filing a runtime perf regression ticket if the same benchmark regresses twice.

Approvals: Marcus Reed approved; Claire Dubois approved; Allison Grant approved; Connor O'Brien approved.
LTS perf gates now enforce stricter p95 latency and throughput regression thresholds.
Release managers have a documented, auditable waiver workflow for noisy benchmark results.
Added minimum sample-count requirements to reduce false-positive p95 regressions.

title: Add trigger endpoint for Optimize quality gating (config diff + baseline)
body:
Add trigger endpoint for Optimize quality gating (config diff + baseline)

Context: Optimize needs a first-class way to run offline evals against a proposed serving config change (batching/caching/quantization profile) before allowing apply/rollout. This PR adds a new API endpoint and job plumbing in eval-harness to accept a config diff + baseline reference, execute the requested gate tier against selected prompt sets, and return structured metrics plus artifact pointers suitable for Console/Optimize consumption. Endpoint: POST /api/v1/gates/trigger (auth: service-to-service token; scoped to optimize-gating). Request (JSON): gate_tier ("smoke"|"full"), model_id, baseline (baseline_model_version + baseline_runtime_config_ref), proposed (runtime_config_diff, optional proposed_model_version), prompt_sets (ids), sample_count (optional; defaults per tier), run_metadata (route_id, account_id, region, commit_sha, idempotency_key). Validation: limits request payload size, rejects unknown diff keys, enforces that baseline ref is immutable (no "latest"), and checks prompt set ids exist and are enabled for gating. Execution: enqueues a GateRun job to the existing eval runner queue, pins model + runtime settings for the duration of the run, and writes an immutable run record with normalized inputs for audit/debug. Response: 202 Accepted with gate_run_id + status_url + estimated_duration_s; once complete, GET /api/v1/gates/runs/{id} returns status, summary metrics (per prompt set and overall), and artifact pointers (artifact_store_uri + optional signed_url when allowed), including: raw per-example outputs, rubric/score breakdowns, and a compact "comparison.json" (baseline vs proposed deltas). Artifacts: stored under artifact_store_uri prefix gates/{gate_run_id}/..., with retention aligned to existing eval artifact policy; Optimize can deep-link using gate_run_id. Observability: emits gate_trigger_requests_total and gate_run_enqueue_latency_ms (tags: gate_tier, model_id, region, caller=optimize) and attaches trace/span attributes for correlation from Optimize -> eval-harness. Tests: adds contract tests for request validation + schema stability, a fake runner integration test that asserts correct pinning of baseline/proposed configs, and golden JSON snapshots for the run detail response. Notes: This PR does not implement flake scoring/rerun aggregation (tracked in pr-418); response schema includes an optional flake_score field but it is not populated yet. Rollout: endpoint is behind feature flag OPTIMIZE_GATING_TRIGGER_API and requires allowlisted client identity; we can safely deploy without enabling any callers.
Jonas Weber: Can we ensure baseline is immutable? We should reject 'latest' and require an explicit version/ref so Optimize can't accidentally compare against a moving target.
Olivia Grant (author): Added baseline_runtime_config_ref validation + explicit version requirement; request now rejects 'latest' and any ref without a content hash.
Selene Huang: Please include per-prompt-set summary in the run detail response; Optimize needs to surface which suite failed, not just overall.
Olivia Grant (author): Updated response schema to include prompt_set_results[] with aggregate metrics + artifact pointer per suite; added snapshot tests.
Connor O'Brien: CI note—these tests will be run in CPU-only jobs. Make sure the fake runner path is deterministic and doesn't require GPU.
Olivia Grant (author): Switched integration test to FakeExecutor; runner job only asserts config pinning + manifest write, no model execution.
Ethan Park: Any reason this isn't idempotent? Optimize will retry on 5xx; we should support idempotency_key to avoid duplicate runs.
Olivia Grant (author): Added idempotency_key to request; service now dedupes within 24h on (caller, idempotency_key) and returns existing gate_run_id.
Jonas Weber: Approving with the caveat that flake_score is optional and must remain nullable until pr-418 lands.
Selene Huang: LGTM after the per-suite summary; thanks.

title: Add `restore apply` workflow with preflight checks and post-restore validation report
body:
Add `restore apply` workflow with preflight checks and post-restore validation report

Implements the end-to-end restore path for Redwood Private in the installer CLI. This adds a new `restore apply` command that: (1) performs strict preflight checks (cluster connectivity, namespace/CRD readiness, version compatibility, storage backend access, and integrity checks on the backup artifact), (2) restores control-plane state in a deterministic order (cluster prerequisites, control-plane chart values/config, DB restore, then service rollout), and (3) runs post-restore health checks and emits a validation report that Support/SRE can use for escalation. The goal is to make restores repeatable, safer to run under time pressure, and easier to debug when something goes wrong. Restore ordering is intentionally conservative to avoid the on-prem issues we saw in SUP-18477 (missing CRDs/incorrect bootstrap order). Security note: we do not restore secret material from backups; we restore secret references and validate that required KMS/external secret providers are reachable. The report includes sanitized environment details (versions, timestamps, artifact IDs), step-by-step results, and pointers to relevant logs. Usage examples: `private-installer restore apply --artifact s3://<bucket>/backups/<id> --namespace redwood-private --report /tmp/restore-report.json` and `private-installer restore apply --artifact ./backup.tgz.enc --offline --validate-only`.
- Private installer: introduce `restore apply` with deterministic ordering, guardrails, and a support-ready validation report. - Adds optional `--validate-only` mode and clearer failure categorization (preflight/artifact/restore/validation).
Ethan Park: The ordering looks good, but we need a hard stop if CRDs aren’t present. We cannot attempt to apply the control-plane chart before CRDs exist (this is what bit us on-prem). Also please ensure we fail fast with an actionable message (which CRD group/version is missing). Benji Okafor: Agreed—added a CRD preflight step that checks the required GVKs and prints the exact missing resources. Also added `--skip-crd-check` (hidden) for internal dev only; default is strict. Sean Gallagher: Can we make sure the report is something Support can ask customers to upload without leaking secrets? Also: step timings and error categories are key. Benji Okafor: Implemented redaction for env vars/flags that may contain tokens; report includes timings per step and `error_category` (preflight | artifact | restore | validation). Added `--report-redact-level=strict` defaulting to strict. Hanae Suzuki: Please confirm we never write decrypted artifact contents to disk in a temp dir by default. On air-gapped/offline this becomes a footgun. Also how do we handle KMS unavailability during restore? Benji Okafor: Updated decrypt path to stream to the restore consumer; temp files are only used if `--workdir` is set explicitly. For KMS: preflight checks reachability and key access; if KMS is down we fail before touching cluster state. Connor O'Brien: This should produce a stable artifact ID and include installer version/backup format version in the report. Also ensure exit codes are consistent for automation. Benji Okafor: Added `artifact_id`, `backup_format_version`, `installer_version`, and standardized exit codes (2=preflight, 3=artifact, 4=restore, 5=validation). Fatima Noor: On-prem edge case: missing CRDs after a cluster rebuild is common; the runbook expects the installer to provide a clear remediation step. Benji Okafor: Added remediation hints to the CRD check output and linked to the internal runbook section in the CLI message. Final review: Ethan approved after CRD check and exit code cleanup; Sean approved after report redaction review; Hanae approved after streaming decrypt change.

title: introduce-ci-dependency-coordinator-and-fastpath-lint-lane
body:
introduce-ci-dependency-coordinator-and-fastpath-lint-lane

Motivation: CI feedback latency has been increasing as dependency upgrades, monorepo-wide lint runs, and full integration tests run for small focused changes. This PR introduces a lightweight 'dependency-coordinator' job that centralizes dependency-bump orchestration and a fastpath lint lane to give engineers quick feedback for localized edits. Goals: 1) reduce developer wall-time for common changes, 2) make dependency upgrades non-blocking by separating coordination and artifact creation, 3) improve signal-to-noise for lint failures by scoping fast failures to touched packages and running the full lint in a slower gated lane, and 4) tighten action pinning for release hooks.

What this PR does: - Add a new CI job workflow: .github/workflows/ci-dep-coordinator.yml that runs weekly and on demand to batch compatible dependency upgrades, create curated PRs, and publish a coordination manifest picked up by downstream CI lanes. The coordinator does not merge but posts a Linear ticket suggestion and a release-note draft. - Introduce fastpath lint lane: .github/workflows/lint-fastpath.yml which runs for changes limited by path filters (packages/*, sdk/*, docs/*). It runs eslint/ruff/format-checks and a lightweight type-checker. - Update existing lint workflow to run as lint-full.yml (nightly and pre-merge for high-risk PRs) that includes exhaustive checks and cross-package rules. - Change release automation: release-annotator action pinned to a specific sha with an updater that reads the coordination manifest to reduce false-positive release notes generated during batched upgrades. - Add caching/warmers: small prebuild job to fetch prebuilt toolchain artifacts and restore node/python caches earlier in the pipeline to reduce redundant installs for shard jobs. - Add documentation: docs/ci/README.md with contributor-facing guidance on when the coordinator will create PRs and how to opt out for single-package hotfixes. - Pin a handful of actions (setup-node, actions/cache, release-annotator) to SHAs and update lockfiles for the hermetic builder image.

Important notes: - No runtime code changes to product binaries. All edits are CI and tooling only. - The coordinator introduces a curated manifest under .ci/dep-coordinator/manifest.json; downstream jobs read it through a single artifact download step to minimize repeated network calls. - This PR intentionally narrows the fastpath lint to produce earlier, high-value feedback; teams touching multiple packages will still get the full lint. - There was one flaky integration test during validation; tests were rerun and all checks passed prior to merge.
add: initial ci-dep-coordinator workflow + manifest writer
feat(lint): add lint-fastpath workflow with path filters and cache warming
chore(ci): pin release-annotator and setup-node actions to SHAs
docs: add docs/ci/README.md explaining coordinator behavior
ci: add prebuild cache-warmer job and update workflow dispatch inputs
Arjun: Can the coordinator produce per-package PRs instead of a single batched PR? Answer: design intentionally produces a curated batched PR with optional per-package splits; added opt-out flag to manifest.
Sofia: Suggest adding a TTL to the manifest artifact to avoid stale automation picks. Action: added a timestamp and expiry field and updated downstream download step to validate freshness.
Devon: CI image bump looks risky for on-prem private installs. Response: hermetic-builder bump limited to toolchain images used by CI only; documented change and added rollback switch.
Arjun: +1 after addressing manifest expiry and adding README guidance.
Sofia: approved
Devon: approved
- Add dependency coordinator to batch safe dependency upgrades and surface suggested Linear tickets.
- Introduce lint-fastpath lane for quick per-package lint feedback.
- Pin critical GitHub actions to SHAs and add cache warmers to reduce CI wall-time.

title: Add tiered batching profile schema (fast/standard/cost-efficient) with validation + backcompat
body:
Add tiered batching profile schema (fast/standard/cost-efficient) with validation + backcompat

Summary: This PR introduces the config schema and validation needed to ship tiered batching defaults (fast / standard / cost-efficient) while keeping backwards compatibility with existing per-route batching knobs. This is plumbing-only: it defines how tiers and optional per-tier profile overrides are expressed, validated, and surfaced to runtime config resolution. It does not change scheduler heuristics or default knob values; those land in follow-up PRs. Context: As part of workload-aware batching defaults, we need a stable, customer-facing tier concept that can be selected at the route/model policy level and overridden by enterprise/Dedicated configs. We also need to ensure customers with existing manual batching settings do not break, and that invalid or partially-specified configs fail fast with actionable error messages. What’s included: (1) New schema types: - Adds a new enum `BatchingSloTier` with values: `FAST`, `STANDARD`, `COST_EFFICIENT`. - Adds `batching.tier` to `RoutePolicy` (optional). If unset, the effective tier is `STANDARD` (subject to higher-precedence overrides in later work). - Adds `batching.profiles` (optional) for per-tier explicit knob overrides. This is intended primarily for internal benchmarking and Dedicated overrides; public docs will steer customers to tier selection rather than manual knob tuning. (2) Validation + guardrails: - Enforces that per-tier profiles, when present, include required knobs as an all-or-nothing set (prevents partial overrides that can create surprising behavior). - Validates numeric ranges for knob fields (e.g., wait budgets >= 0, token limits > 0) and cross-field constraints (e.g., `max_batch_tokens` >= `max_prefill_tokens_per_request` when both present). - Rejects unknown tier strings with explicit error output listing allowed values. (3) Backwards-compatible defaults / migration path: - Preserves the legacy batching config surface (`max_batch_tokens`, `max_wait_ms`, etc.) for existing customers and internal configs. - Adds a compatibility layer: if legacy knobs are present and `batching.tier` is not set, config resolution treats it as `tier=STANDARD` with an implicit `profiles[STANDARD]` override populated from legacy values (so existing behavior is maintained and the new tier field can be introduced gradually). - If both `batching.tier` and legacy knobs are set, validation fails with a clear message to avoid ambiguous precedence (the explicit guidance is: pick tier OR legacy knobs, not both). (4) Config introspection: - Extends `configctl validate` output to include a normalized view of effective tier + effective profile (for debugging config rollouts and Dedicated deployments). - Adds structured error codes for common validation failures (to support Console UX and customer-facing errors later). Files/areas touched (high level): - `control-plane/config/schema/route_policy.proto` (adds tier and profile fields) - `control-plane/config/validation/batching.go` (validation + compatibility rules) - `control-plane/config/normalize/route_policy_normalize.go` (legacy -> tiered normalized representation) - `tools/configctl/validate_cmd.go` (debug output improvements) - `docs/internal/config-schema.md` (internal-only note; public docs are separate) Example config (normalized): route_policies: - name: chat-default model: llama-3.1-70b batching: tier: FAST profiles: FAST: max_wait_ms: 1 max_batch_tokens: 4096 STANDARD: max_wait_ms: 4 max_batch_tokens: 8192 COST_EFFICIENT: max_wait_ms: 10 max_batch_tokens: 16384 Notes: Values above are illustrative only; final recommended defaults per tier/model/hardware are owned by perf/benchmarking work and will land separately. Testing: - Unit tests for schema validation (valid tiers, invalid tiers, missing required fields, range checks). - Golden tests for normalization output (legacy knobs -> normalized tiered profile). - Ran `configctl validate` against production-like snapshots from Hosted + Dedicated staging (no changes required; legacy configs continue to validate). Rollout plan: - Safe to merge behind existing behavior since tier is optional and legacy configs are untouched. - Follow-ups will: (a) wire tier selection to runtime config consumption, (b) add reason codes/telemetry, (c) add feature flagging and rollout controls. Checklist: - [x] Backwards compatibility confirmed with staging config snapshots - [x] Validation errors are actionable (include field path + suggestion) - [x] Added unit/golden tests - [x] No runtime behavior change in this PR Related: - Linear: ENG-18422 - Project: Workload-aware batching defaults (tiered SLO profiles) Review notes / conversation (abridged): Priya Natarajan: Please ensure we don’t end up with three different places to set batching (legacy knobs, tier, per-tier profiles) without clear mutual exclusivity. Ethan Park: Agreed. Added explicit validation to fail if `tier` is set alongside legacy knobs; also updated normalize logic to only synthesize a `STANDARD` profile when tier is unset. Jordan Lee: Can we avoid `COST_EFFICIENT` vs `COST_EFFICIENT` naming drift across components? Also prefer stable casing in JSON. Ethan Park: Implemented strict enum mapping with JSON strings `fast|standard|cost_efficient` and canonicalized output in `configctl`. Added tests to ensure round-trip stability. Sean Gallagher: Please add guardrails for negative/zero limits; also want error codes for alerting/triage. Ethan Park: Added range checks + `CFG_BATCHING_*` error codes surfaced by `configctl validate` and control plane logs. Approvals: - Priya Natarajan (approved) - Jordan Lee (approved) - Sean Gallagher (approved) CI: build-and-test (pass), configctl-golden (pass), lint (pass). Merge: Squash merged into `main`.

title: Demo: pin model versions per route + controlled fallback by family/region
body:
Demo: pin model versions per route + controlled fallback by family/region

Context: The demo tenant has been brittle when the model catalog changes (new default revisions, deprecations, regional capacity reshuffles). This PR makes demo behavior deterministic by (1) pinning demo routes to known-good model versions and (2) introducing a controlled fallback policy that stays within a narrow compatibility envelope (same model family + compatible profile) and within an explicit region preference list.

What changed (high level): Adds a demo-only route config schema for model pinning; introduces a SafeFallbackPolicy implementation used only when `tenant_class=demo` (or when a route has `demo_mode=true`); adds a compatibility matcher (family, major version, context window, tool-calling capability flags, output format support) to avoid surprising capability changes; wires routing to emit fallback reason codes and chosen target metadata; and adds unit + integration tests covering both the happy path and failure modes.

Pinning behavior: Demo routes can now set `pinned_model` (family + exact revision), `pinned_profile` (e.g., fp16/int8 preset), and `pinned_region`. If the pinned target is healthy and has capacity, routing is deterministic. If it is not routable (catalog missing, capacity constrained, health degraded), routing consults the fallback policy described below.

Fallback behavior (controlled): Fallback is only allowed when ALL of the following hold: (a) the request is in the demo tenant (or demo-marked route), (b) the pinned target is not routable, (c) there is at least one allow-listed candidate defined for the route, and (d) the candidate is compatible per matcher. Candidates are sorted by region preference and then by explicit priority. We intentionally do NOT fall back across model families or across major revisions, and we do NOT fall back to any model not explicitly allow-listed.

Allow-list structure: Each demo route may define `fallback_candidates` with entries like `{ model_revision, region, profile, priority }`. This list is intentionally verbose so Sales Eng can point to a concrete, auditable policy during demos (and we can keep it stable across time).

Safety rails: The policy refuses to run outside demo context. Additionally, when in demo context, if no compatible allow-listed candidates exist, we fail fast with a clear error: `DEMO_PINNED_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE_NO_SAFE_FALLBACK` (instead of silently routing to a random default).

Observability: Adds routing counters/tags: `demo_fallback_attempted`, `demo_fallback_selected`, and `demo_fallback_reason` (enum: `catalog_missing`, `capacity`, `health`, `policy_disallowed`, `no_compatible_candidate`). Also logs a structured routing event with `pinned_target`, `selected_target`, and `compatibility_summary` to support post-demo debugging.

Files / areas changed: Routing layer: `services/router/*` (policy selection + matcher); Control plane config validation: `services/control-plane/demo/*`; Model catalog interface: `pkg/modelcatalog/*` (exposes revision capability flags needed by matcher); Telemetry: `pkg/telemetry/routing/*`; Demo seed config: `config/demo/demo_routes.yaml` and `config/demo/demo_fallback_allowlist.yaml`; Tests: `services/router/tests/test_demo_pinning_and_fallback.py` and `services/router/tests/test_compatibility_matcher.py` plus a small golden test for config parsing.

Testing: Unit tests cover: pinned target success; pinned target missing from catalog -> safe fallback; pinned target capacity constrained -> safe fallback; incompatible candidate rejected (context window mismatch, tool-calling mismatch); disallowed fallback outside demo context; error message correctness; and telemetry tags. Integration tests run a fake catalog with multiple revisions across two regions and assert deterministic selection order. CI: `router-unit`, `control-plane-lint`, `config-schema`, and `integration-smoke` all passing.

Rollout plan: This is gated to demo tenants only via `tenant_class=demo` (from org metadata) and a route flag. No behavior change for customer tenants. After merge, we will update the demo tenant seed job to write pinned routes + allow-lists (tracked in ENG-4833 follow-ups) and update the SE runbook to include a quick “pin validation” healthcheck step.

Rollback plan: Revert this PR or flip `demo.safe_fallback.enabled=false` in demo environment config to restore prior behavior (default routing). If reverting, also remove the new demo config files from the seed job to avoid validation failures.

Notes for Sales/SE: The pin + allow-list files are meant to be stable and version-controlled; please do not edit them ad-hoc during a live demo. If a pinned model needs to change, update the allow-list and the pinned revision together and run the demo tenant reset workflow.

Review discussion (highlights): Ravi Menon asked to make compatibility matching strict by default and to document why we reject cross-family fallback; implemented and added reason codes. Sean Gallagher requested telemetry + an explicit fail-fast error when no safe fallback exists (instead of best-effort routing); added and covered by tests. Ethan Park requested guardrails preventing accidental enablement in non-demo orgs; added `tenant_class` gating and config validation error messages. Chloe Martin requested that Console can surface the pinned vs selected target for screenshots; added structured log fields (Console wiring in separate PR). Markus Klein asked for a deterministic region preference order for live demos; added `region_preference` list at route level and test coverage. Naomi Feldman asked for assurance we do not broaden data access by falling back to other regions unexpectedly; clarified that region fallback is explicit per route and defaults to pinned region only unless allow-listed.

Merge: Squash merged into `main`.

Follow-ups: Update demo tenant seed definitions to include pinned routes + allow-lists for all known-good scenarios (PM-197/ENG-4833); add a demo healthcheck endpoint check to validate pinned revisions exist and are routable (ENG-4862); add Console UI for “Pinned vs Served model” in routing trace view (internal ticket to be filed by Dylan/Chloe).
Demo tenant routes can now pin an explicit model version (and quantization/profile) and only fall back to an allow-listed set of compatible variants.
Adds demo-specific fallback telemetry (reason codes) to make regressions diagnosable during live demos.

title: Audit: standardize request_id/trace_id propagation and include correlation fields on emitted events
body:
Audit: standardize request_id/trace_id propagation and include correlation fields on emitted events

Context: As part of the audit logging standardization work (schema v1 + sensitive action coverage), we need correlation identifiers to be present on every audit event so customers and internal responders can pivot from an API/Console action to the corresponding traces, logs, and downstream service calls. Today we have a mix of x-request-id, requestId, and trace-only correlation depending on service, and some async flows drop context entirely.

What this PR does: (1) Standardizes request_id propagation via x-request-id across internal HTTP hops, and ensures it is echoed back on gateway responses. (2) Standardizes trace_id extraction from W3C traceparent when present (OpenTelemetry), and ensures we always have a stable trace_id in request context when a span exists. (3) Updates the audit event builder so request_id and trace_id are set from context (best-effort) across all producers using the shared library.

Key behaviors / rules: - request_id: treated as a correlation token (not an auth token). We accept an inbound x-request-id only if it matches a conservative allowlist (length + charset). Otherwise we generate a new id and record a debug log. We always forward exactly one x-request-id downstream. - trace_id: derived from the active OTel span when present; otherwise left unset (schema allows null/omitted) to avoid creating fake trace IDs. - async/background jobs: when a job is enqueued from an HTTP request, we attach request_id and traceparent to the job payload headers so workers can restore correlation.

Scope: This PR touches the API gateway middleware, the control plane HTTP middleware used by tenant/config/policy/RBAC services, and the shared audit emitter library. Console UI / admin_action_id work is intentionally not included here (tracked separately), but this unblocks most of the cross-service correlation for sensitive actions.

Testing: Added unit tests for header parsing / sanitization, and integration tests that assert emitted audit events include request_id and trace_id when requests have trace context. Also validated locally against the audit exporter dev sink (events show consistent request_id across gateway -> control-plane).

Rollout/compat: No schema changes. Existing producers that don’t use the shared builder are unchanged (still tracked as gaps in ENG-4833). Exporter will see new fields populated more frequently; customers can safely ignore if not needed.

Follow-ups: - Apply the same middleware to remaining services that bypass the shared HTTP stack (runtime admin plane, some legacy internal tools). - Add enforcement (CI lint) to fail builds when sensitive-action code paths emit audit events without request_id (ENG-4831/PR-22071). - Add admin_action_id propagation for Console-triggered workflows (ENG-4830 follow-up + Console workstream).
Allison Grant (review): Can we be explicit about which inbound headers we trust? Specifically, do we accept any x-request-id from customers, and could it blow up cardinality if someone sends a huge random string?
Caleb Johnson (author): Good call. Added sanitization: max length 64, [A-Za-z0-9-_], otherwise we generate a new one. Also added a metric counter audit_correlation.request_id_sanitized_total to track occurrences.
Sean Gallagher (review): For incident response, echoing x-request-id back to clients is helpful. Confirming we do it at the edge only and don’t accidentally override internal ids?
Caleb Johnson (author): Yes. Gateway is the canonical generator/normalizer. Downstream services only read from incoming context; they don’t regenerate unless the header is missing entirely (internal calls). Gateway always includes the header in response.
Hanae Suzuki (review): Any chance trace_id could contain sensitive data or become a stable identifier across tenants?
Caleb Johnson (author): trace_id is produced by OTel (random 16-byte) and not derived from tenant/user data. We’re not logging user identifiers into it. Also kept it best-effort (unset if no active span) to avoid inventing IDs.
Nadia Rahman (review): For async jobs, are we copying traceparent verbatim? Some producers might not have trace context (e.g., cron).
Caleb Johnson (author): We only attach traceparent if present; workers restore span context when available. For cron/background-only, request_id is generated per job run; trace_id remains unset unless the worker creates a span.
Ethan Park (review): Small nit: The control-plane middleware currently prefers x-request-id over a legacy header requestId. Should we keep legacy for a bit?
Caleb Johnson (author): Agreed. Added temporary fallback: requestId -> x-request-id with a deprecation log (once per process) so we can find remaining callers. Will remove after we update the last internal clients.
Logan Wright (review): Please add one integration assertion that the same request_id shows up across gateway event + downstream RBAC event in the same flow (helps coverage dashboard join logic).
Caleb Johnson (author): Added integration test: create API key via gateway -> control-plane; asserts both events share request_id, and trace_id is non-empty when traceparent is provided.
Marcus Lin (comment): Not a blocker, but what’s our stance on UUID vs ULID for request_id for sorting in SIEMs?
Caleb Johnson (author): Left as UUIDv4 for now to avoid changing existing assumptions; we can switch to ULID/UUIDv7 later as a separate change once exporter + docs are updated. This PR focuses on propagation and consistency.

title: docs: document tool-calling compatibility differences (payload + streaming)
body:
docs: document tool-calling compatibility differences (payload + streaming)

## Summary
Adds explicit compatibility notes for tool calling when using Redwood via the OpenAI-compatible surface area. This is primarily a docs change, but it closes the gap that caused a few recent “copy/paste” examples (in Redwood docs + community snippets) to imply behaviors that the compat layer either doesn’t support or intentionally normalizes.

## Motivation
We saw repeated confusion around:
- Payload shape differences (e.g., `function_call` vs `tool_calls`, presence/absence of `id`, what’s required in tool result messages)
- Streaming behavior during tool calls (partial arguments, ordering, when `finish_reason` arrives)
- Expectations around “parallel tool calls” and mixing assistant text + tool calls in the same streamed turn

These misunderstandings showed up in support tickets (SUP-18421, SUP-18452) and in the DevEx parity audit work (ENG-4821). This PR documents the reality so that Redwood examples/docs can safely link to a canonical compat note and avoid overpromising.

## What’s included
- New page: `docs/compat/tool-calling.md`
  - Side-by-side examples of request/response payloads
  - Streaming transcripts showing partial tool args and final assembly expectations
  - Explicit “Not supported / differs from OpenAI” callouts
- Updates to `README.md` and `docs/compat/streaming.md` to link to the new tool-calling page
- Adds a small “Known pitfalls” section tailored to compat users (partial args, JSON parse, tool result role)

## Key compatibility notes captured
- **Tool call representation:** The compat layer accepts OpenAI-style `tools` and returns `tool_calls` on assistant messages; legacy `function_call` is not documented and should not be used in new examples.
- **Tool call IDs:** `tool_call_id` is required for tool result messages; some models omit/rename fields in intermediate streaming chunks, so examples must assemble the final `tool_call_id` and `arguments` from deltas before invoking tools.
- **Streaming partial args:** `arguments` may be streamed as partial JSON fragments; clients must not `json.loads()`/`JSON.parse()` until the tool call is complete.
- **Parallel tool calls:** Multiple tool calls can appear in one assistant turn, but ordering/streaming interleaving is model-dependent. Examples should treat tool calls as an array and iterate deterministically after finalization.
- **Mixing content + tool calls:** Do not assume assistant `content` will be present alongside `tool_calls` in the same message. Some backends emit empty content when tool calls are present.
- **Finish reasons:** `finish_reason` may arrive only on the final chunk; streaming consumers should not rely on early `finish_reason` to decide that tool args are complete.

## Why this lives in redwood-openai-compat
We want a single source of truth for compat-specific constraints, so the main docs/SDK repos can link out instead of duplicating nuanced edge cases (which then diverge). This also makes it easier to keep up with changes in the compat adapter.

## Testing
- `pnpm lint` (docs)
- `pnpm test` (link checker)
- Manual verification of code blocks against the current compat adapter behavior using the internal “golden transcript” fixture referenced in ENG-4822

## Follow-ups
- Update redwood-docs tool-calling guide to include a short compat callout + link to this page (tracked in ENG-4826)
- Ensure SDK examples that mention OpenAI compat default to the “assemble deltas, then parse” pattern

Checklist:
- [x] Docs have explicit “differs from OpenAI” callouts
- [x] Streaming example avoids parsing partial JSON
- [x] Links validated (no redirects introduced)
- [x] PM terminology matches PM-412 signoff (uses “structured output” vs “JSON mode” consistently where referenced)

Brian Murphy (review): The callout about `function_call` is good, but be explicit that we don’t guarantee accepting legacy `function_call` requests through compat. People will copy/paste. Also, in the tool result example, please show the `tool` role message with `tool_call_id` (not a made-up `tool_result` role).

Ibrahim Khan (author): Good catch. Updated language to “not supported / not documented” and changed the tool result snippet to use `role: "tool"` + `tool_call_id`.

Wei Chen (review): Can we add one line that warns against assuming content+tool_calls co-exist? This is a frequent docs comment.

Ibrahim Khan (author): Added a dedicated bullet + updated the streaming transcript to show empty `content` while tool calls are being emitted.

Dana Lo (review): In the TypeScript ecosystem, folks parse `arguments` per chunk. Please add a short snippet that shows buffering/assembling. Doesn’t need to be language-specific, but a pseudocode block helps.

Ibrahim Khan (author): Added “assembly pseudocode” section and linked the canonical event nomenclature doc (internal) for future alignment.

Brian Murphy (final): Approving. This should reduce the number of ‘tool args truncated mid-stream’ tickets we’ve been seeing.

title: Add Splunk HEC export target (batching, retry/backoff, delivery metrics)
body:
Add Splunk HEC export target (batching, retry/backoff, delivery metrics)

## Summary
Adds a first-class Splunk HEC export target to audit-log-exporter. The target supports (1) bounded batching to control request volume and Splunk HEC payload size, (2) retry w/ exponential backoff + jitter for transient failures, and (3) explicit delivery visibility via metrics and structured logs.

This is part of the audit logging standardization effort to ensure customers can reliably export normalized audit events into common SIEMs. Splunk HEC is a frequent enterprise requirement (see SUP-18477) and has been a blocker for at least two Private-deployment evaluations.

## Motivation / context
- Customers want to ingest audit logs into Splunk with predictable field semantics and stable delivery.
- Our current exporter supports HTTP generic sinks, but Splunk HEC has specific behavior and recommended payload structure (event wrapping, source/sourcetype, token auth, and status codes that require careful retry handling).
- We also need exporter-side metrics to troubleshoot "events missing" vs "events delayed" vs "events duplicated" reports.

## Design notes
### Delivery semantics
- Exporter remains at-least-once for supported sinks. Splunk HEC requests are retried on transient errors and select 5xx/429 responses.
- We do NOT attempt exactly-once. Deduplication is supported via stable `event_id` and consistent batching behavior; customers should dedupe on `event_id` downstream (aligns with SUP-18510 guidance).

### Splunk HEC payload format
We use the standard HEC /services/collector endpoint with JSON events in the form:
- `event`: the original audit event JSON (already normalized upstream)
- `time`: derived from audit event `timestamp` (unix seconds, float)
- Optional metadata fields: `host`, `source`, `sourcetype`, `index`

We intentionally do not flatten the audit event or remap top-level keys here; normalization happens earlier (tracked in ENG-4827). This PR focuses on transport + operational correctness.

### Batching
- Configurable max events per batch and max bytes per batch.
- Flush triggers: size threshold, byte threshold, or max flush interval.
- Conservative defaults tuned for Splunk HEC typical limits (keeps payloads < ~900KB by default).

### Retry / backoff
- Exponential backoff with jitter.
- Retries on: network errors, 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504.
- No retry on: 400/401/403/404 (treat as configuration/auth issue), unless explicitly forced by `retry_on_4xx` (default false).
- Backpressure: the exporter queue will grow up to `queue.max_size`. Once full, we drop with explicit counters and structured error logs (same pattern as other sinks).

### Failure visibility metrics
Added metrics (Prometheus) under the existing exporter namespace:
- `audit_exporter_sink_requests_total{sink="splunk_hec",status="success|error",code="..."}`
- `audit_exporter_sink_request_duration_seconds_bucket{sink="splunk_hec"}`
- `audit_exporter_sink_events_sent_total{sink="splunk_hec"}`
- `audit_exporter_sink_events_failed_total{sink="splunk_hec",reason="..."}`
- `audit_exporter_sink_batch_size_events{sink="splunk_hec"}` (histogram)
- `audit_exporter_queue_dropped_events_total{sink="splunk_hec"}`

Also added structured logs with stable fields: `sink`, `endpoint`, `hec_ack`, `attempt`, `backoff_ms`, `batch_events`, `batch_bytes`, `http_status`.

## Configuration
New sink type: `splunk_hec`

Example:
- `sinks:
    - type: splunk_hec
      name: splunk-prod
      endpoint: https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector
      token_env: SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN
      index: redwood_audit
      sourcetype: redwood:audit:v1
      source: redwood-audit-exporter
      host: ${HOSTNAME}
      batch:
        max_events: 500
        max_bytes: 900000
        flush_interval_ms: 1000
      retry:
        max_attempts: 8
        base_backoff_ms: 200
        max_backoff_ms: 10000
        retry_on_4xx: false
      tls:
        ca_bundle_path: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt
        insecure_skip_verify: false`

Notes:
- `token_env` is required; we do not allow a raw token literal in config to reduce accidental secrets exposure.
- Endpoint must be HTTPS by default; HTTP is allowed only if `allow_insecure_http=true` (intended for lab environments).

## Tests
- Unit tests:
  - payload wrapping and time parsing from RFC3339 timestamp
  - batching thresholds (events + bytes) and flush interval
  - retry classification matrix for status codes and network errors
  - token lookup and redaction in logs
- Integration-ish tests (mock server):
  - simulates 503->success with retry
  - simulates 401 and asserts no retry + surfaced config error
  - validates metrics emission and counters increment as expected

## Changed areas
- `src/sinks/splunk_hec.rs`: new sink implementation
- `src/config/sinks.rs`: config schema and validation
- `src/metrics.rs`: sink metrics additions
- `src/retry.rs`: shared helper updated to support per-sink override of retry-on-4xx
- `docs/sinks/splunk-hec.md`: setup + troubleshooting guide
- `examples/private/splunk-hec-values.yaml`: example Helm values (Private)

## Security considerations
- HEC token is treated as a secret: never logged; config printing and error messages redact it.
- We do not log raw event payloads on errors. Error logs include event counts and event_id sampling limited to 5 IDs per batch (behind debug level), to avoid accidental PII expansion.

## Rollout plan
- Phase 1: enable in staging for Hosted exporter and validate metrics + retry behavior under induced 503s.
- Phase 2: ship behind feature flag `exporter.sinks.splunk_hec.enabled` for Private charts.
- Phase 3: document customer guidance (PM-939) and share config snippets with Solutions Engineering.

## Reviewer notes / discussion highlights
- Allison requested we avoid high-cardinality labels. We removed `endpoint` as a metrics label (kept it only in logs).
- Sean asked for explicit dropped-event counters and a clear failure mode when queue is full; added `audit_exporter_queue_dropped_events_total` and a WARN summary every 60s during sustained drops.
- Hanae requested stricter TLS defaults; HTTP now requires `allow_insecure_http=true` and emits a startup WARN with a link to docs.

## Commits
1) config: add splunk_hec sink type and validation
2) sinks: implement Splunk HEC client + payload wrapper
3) retry: backoff + retry classification for HEC
4) metrics/logging: add sink counters, histograms, and structured logs
5) tests: unit + mock-server retries and auth failure behavior
6) docs/examples: Splunk setup, Private values example

## CI
- build: pass
- unit tests: pass
- lint/format: pass
- security scans (secrets + dependency audit): pass

Merged via squash as: "Add Splunk HEC export target (batching, retry/backoff, delivery metrics)"
Audit Log Exporter: Added Splunk HEC export target with configurable batching, retry/backoff, and delivery visibility metrics. Includes example configs for Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments.

title: Add latency-per-dollar metric + normalization rules (with unit tests)
body:
Add latency-per-dollar metric + normalization rules (with unit tests)

Summary: This PR adds a first-class derived metric `latency_per_dollar` to the benchmark pipeline, along with explicit normalization rules so results are comparable across runs that differ in token shapes (prefill/decode mix, output length) and delivery mode (streaming vs non-streaming). It also adds unit tests and schema/export updates so the metric is available to downstream consumers (web ingestion, report charts). Motivation / context: For the public benchmark report we need a single headline metric that combines latency and cost while still being defensible. Raw latency is not comparable across token shapes, and cost per token alone hides latency differences. `latency_per_dollar` is intended to be used alongside supporting metrics (p50/p95, throughput, $/1M tokens), but it must be computed in a consistent, reviewable way. Metric definition: We define request cost in USD based on observed run cost attribution (runner_cost_usd) normalized by total tokens served (input+output) within the run: cost_per_token_usd = runner_cost_usd / total_tokens_observed. We define a canonical request shape (see normalization) with fixed prefill_tokens and decode_tokens. For a given run we compute a normalized per-request cost for the canonical shape: canonical_request_cost_usd = cost_per_token_usd * (canonical_prefill_tokens + canonical_decode_tokens). We define normalized latency for that canonical shape using measured per-stage slopes derived from the run (prefill latency component + per-token decode slope). Finally: latency_per_dollar_ms_per_usd = normalized_latency_ms / canonical_request_cost_usd. Lower is better (less time per dollar) and this makes the tradeoff explicit. Normalization rules (v1): Canonical shape is specified per workload family in config (default: prefill=1024, decode=256 for prod-mix v3 unless overridden by the suite). We estimate prefill latency component as p50_prefill_ms from the instrumentation when available; otherwise we approximate with (p50_e2e_ms - decode_tokens * p50_decode_ms_per_token). Decode slope is computed as median(decode_ms / generated_tokens) across samples with generated_tokens > 0. Normalized latency is: normalized_latency_ms = prefill_component_ms + decode_slope_ms_per_token * canonical_decode_tokens. Note: we intentionally do not normalize concurrency; concurrency remains part of the benchmark definition, and the cost attribution already reflects concurrency/queueing. Streaming handling: For streaming responses, we treat e2e latency as time-to-last-token (TTLT) and ignore TTFT for the primary latency/$ metric. We still export TTFT separately for supporting charts. Rationale: latency/$ is intended to reflect full completion time for a request at the canonical shape. If a run only has TTFT (rare), we skip latency/$ and mark derived metric as null with a reason tag in logs. Retries / failed attempts: We exclude failed attempts from latency distribution aggregation (unchanged behavior), but cost attribution uses runner-level cost, which implicitly includes compute spent on retries/failures. This is intentional for economics realism. To avoid pathological skew, we add a stability guard in derivation: if retry_rate > 2% for a run, we compute latency/$ but emit a warning in the run summary and include retry_rate in the exported artifact. (The stability gate PR will enforce reruns separately; this PR only surfaces the data.) Schema + exports: Bumped result schema to v7 to add fields: derived.latency_per_dollar_ms_per_usd (number | null), derived.normalized_latency_ms (number | null), derived.canonical_shape (string), derived.derivation_notes (string). Updated JSON exporter to include derived.* in the top-level result blob so the web ingestion pipeline can read it without recomputing. Tests: Added unit tests covering: (1) deterministic normalization for variable output lengths, (2) streaming TTLT vs TTFT behavior, (3) cost attribution edge case: missing runner_cost_usd => derived metric null, (4) retries: retry_rate warning path does not change computed metric, (5) floating point tolerance for slope estimation (previously flaky). Notes / follow-ups: This PR does not change benchmark runner behavior, only aggregation/derivation. The canonical shape defaults are configurable; we should align final canonical shapes with the public methodology doc before freezing v1 of the report. Related: ENG-18477 (artifact export pipeline) will consume these fields; ENG-18521 (stability gates) will enforce rerun thresholds where retry_rate / variance is high.
Claire Dubois (review): Can you clarify why we’re using TTLT for streaming vs TTFT? A lot of customers care about “first token” latency. Also: is the canonical shape documented anywhere outside code?
Nadia Rahman (author): Agree TTFT matters; I kept it out of the primary latency/$ metric because it’s not comparable across models that differ in generation cadence (and TTFT can look great while total completion time is poor). We still export TTFT so the report can show both. I added a README section + config comment for canonical shape; we’ll also mirror this in the methodology doc once locked.
Rina Kobayashi (review): The cost_per_token_usd = runner_cost_usd / total_tokens_observed assumes tokens_observed includes all attempts, including failed retries. Does our token counter include failed attempts consistently? If not, we could under/over-estimate cost per token.
Nadia Rahman (author): Good catch. Token counters in this pipeline only count successful completions; failed attempts don’t contribute tokens, so retries will increase runner_cost_usd without increasing tokens => cost_per_token_usd increases, which is directionally correct (you pay more per delivered token). I added an explicit comment + a unit test for retry_rate > 0 to make sure we don’t accidentally drop runner_cost_usd in that path.
Jonas Weber (review): Normalization: you’re estimating prefill_component_ms using p50_prefill_ms “when available”. What’s the expected coverage? Also, please make sure we don’t silently compute nonsense when generated_tokens=0 (e.g., empty output).
Nadia Rahman (author): Coverage: current runner emits prefill_ms on ~95% of suites; older artifacts won’t have it, so we fallback. For generated_tokens=0 we now skip those samples for slope estimation and return derived metric null if we can’t compute a slope with >= N samples (N=30). Added tests for the empty-output case.
Mei Lin (review): CI flaked on golden-export-snapshots due to float diffs. Can we round derived numbers at export, or use tolerant comparison?
Nadia Rahman (author): I updated the snapshot matcher to use a tolerance for derived.* fields (1e-6 relative). Keeping full precision in JSON helps debug and avoids “quantization by export”.
Jonas Weber (approval): Looks good with the added null/guard behavior and the documentation. Please ensure the methodology team signs off on canonical shapes before we publish.
Rina Kobayashi (approval): Approved. The retry/cost behavior is now explicit and test-covered.

title: Add retention verification + compliance pack generation dashboards/alerts
body:
Add retention verification + compliance pack generation dashboards/alerts

Summary: This PR adds the first version of the retention/compliance dashboards and alerting rules needed for the “Retention controls + compliance reporting pack” program. It introduces (1) Retention Enforcement Verification dashboards (TTL lag, purge throughput/failures, backlog) and (2) Compliance Report Pack Generation SLIs (success rate + latency) with corresponding alerts. It also updates the repo README to document metric prerequisites and rollout guidance.

Context / why: We’ve had multiple incidents/tickets where enforcement was “working” but not observable at the right level (e.g., policy applied but TTL lag growing in a single region; purge jobs silently throttling after maintenance). Security/GRC also needs a customer-ready way to evidence enforcement (at least internally) and to demonstrate the compliance pack generator’s reliability as we start using it for enterprise security reviews.

What’s included:
- Dashboards:
  - “Retention Controls: Verification (Overview)”
    - TTL lag (p50/p90/p99) by store + region
    - Purge throughput (rows deleted / min) and runtime
    - Purge failures (rate + top error reasons when exported)
    - Backlog / lag trend line for the last 7d
  - “Retention Controls: Purge Jobs (Deep Dive)”
    - Per-job panels (request-logs, audit-logs, traces, metrics, artifacts where applicable)
    - Retry volume + idempotent re-run indicators (based on job outcome labels)
  - “Compliance Pack: Generation SLI/SLO”
    - SLI: report_pack_generation_success_rate (derived)
    - Latency: report_pack_generation_duration_seconds (p50/p90/p99)
    - Queue/backlog (if enabled) and saturation signals
- Alerts (Prometheus rules):
  - RetentionTTLTooHigh (warning/page)
    - Warning: ttl_lag_seconds{store=~"request_logs|audit_logs"} p99 > 6h for 30m
    - Page: p99 > 24h for 15m (per region) OR backlog increasing for 60m
  - RetentionPurgeFailuresHigh (page)
    - purge_failures_total increase > 10 in 15m per job_type/region
  - RetentionPurgeNoProgress (warning)
    - purge_rows_deleted_total no increase for 2h while ttl_lag_seconds p90 > 2h
  - CompliancePackGenerationSLOViolation (warning/page)
    - Warning: success rate < 99.5% over 1h
    - Page: success rate < 98% over 30m OR p90 duration > 15m over 1h
- README updates:
  - Documents required metrics + labels (store, region, job_type, tenant_tier)
  - Notes on cardinality: alerts intentionally avoid tenant_id; dashboards allow optional filtering but default views are store/region only
  - Rollout instructions: enable dashboards first, then alerts at warning-only for 1 week before paging

Metric dependencies (expected to exist from the product/runtime PRs):
- ttl_lag_seconds{store,region}
- purge_rows_deleted_total{store,region,job_type}
- purge_failures_total{store,region,job_type,reason?}
- purge_job_duration_seconds{store,region,job_type}
- report_pack_generation_duration_seconds{region,outcome}
- report_pack_generation_total{region,outcome}

Implementation notes:
- Alert thresholds were chosen to match SRE guidance in the retention purge runbook: lag > 24h is a customer-impacting condition (policy drift / failure to meet retention), while shorter lags are warning signals that typically correlate with DB throttling or a stuck worker.
- We added a small “debug” row in the deep-dive dashboard for correlating lag spikes to purge job runtime, failures, and DB maintenance windows (annotation placeholder; actual annotation source is separate).
- Dashboards follow the existing Jsonnet conventions in this repo; panel UIDs are stable and include ‘retention-*’ prefixes for easy lookup.

Testing:
- Rendered dashboards locally (make dashboards) and validated against a staging Prometheus snapshot.
- promtool rule checks pass.
- Verified that rule expressions don’t use tenant_id and don’t blow up cardinality with region x store x job_type only.

Rollout plan:
- Ship dashboards immediately (safe).
- Enable alerts in warning-only in staging for 1 week; then promote to production warning-only for 1 week; then turn on paging routes.

References:
- Linear: ENG-18452 (verification dashboards/alerts), PM-842 (initiative), ENG-18441 (report pack generator)
- Related product metrics PRs: redwood/pr-28540-add-retention-verification-metrics, audit-log-exporter/pr-612-add-time-windowed-exports-and-filters

Screenshots: Added to the README section “Retention & Compliance Dashboards” (rendered preview images) and attached in the PR for review.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): The dashboard looks good, but we should avoid any alert dimensions that could explode cardinality. Please confirm no tenant_id usage anywhere in rule expressions. Also, can we add a “no progress” alert? That would have caught the post-maintenance backlog we saw last week.

Allison Grant (author): Confirmed: no tenant_id in any rule. Dashboards have tenant_tier as an optional filter but rules are strictly store/region/job_type. Added RetentionPurgeNoProgress (warning) based on ‘rows deleted’ not increasing while lag is elevated.

Logan Wright (Telemetry): For ttl_lag_seconds, some stores won’t emit p99 depending on scrape interval; please use histogram_quantile on the bucket metric where available, or fall back to max over time. Right now it looks like you’re assuming precomputed p99.

Allison Grant: Good catch. Updated rules to use histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le,store,region)(rate(ttl_lag_seconds_bucket[5m]))) where the bucket exists; added a compatibility path guarded by recording rules in lib/metrics/retention.libsonnet. README updated to note both options.

Nadia Rahman (Observability): Can we standardize the panel naming to match the rest of the pack (“Overview / Deep Dive / SLO”) and add tags so they show up in search?

Allison Grant: Renamed dashboards and added tags: [retention, compliance, security, verification].

Kevin Osei (Retention/Audit exports): For compliance pack, I’d like an explicit panel for ‘percent generated within 15m’ since that’s what we’ll be quoting to GRC. Also, please keep the alert window >= 30m to avoid paging during deploys.

Allison Grant: Added “<=15m” SLI panel and kept paging criteria at 30m/1h windows.

Sean Gallagher: Approved once you flip the initial paging severity to warning-only (we’ll route to #oncall-retention for the first week).

Allison Grant: Done. Paging labels are present but default route config is warning-only; README includes staged enablement steps.

Approvals:
- Sean Gallagher: Approved
- Logan Wright: Approved
- Nadia Rahman: Approved
Observability-pack now includes Grafana dashboards and Prometheus alert rules for retention enforcement verification and compliance report pack generation SLIs; README documents prerequisites and rollout guidance.

title: Kernel auto-selection v2: add model allowlist/denylist rules + hot reload for rollout control
body:
Kernel auto-selection v2: add model allowlist/denylist rules + hot reload for rollout control

Context
Kernel auto-selection v2 is landing behind gates for Runtime 1.21. For staged rollout (Hosted first, then Dedicated pools) we need a fast, explainable control surface to enable/disable v2 at a per-model granularity, with the ability to react to incidents/customer escalations without restarting the runtime. This PR adds model allowlist/denylist rules, evaluation precedence, and hot reload behavior for those rules.

What this PR does
1) Allowlist/Denylist evaluation
- Adds a new rule set: ModelRolloutRules { allow: [Rule], deny: [Rule] } consumed by the v2 selector entrypoint.
- Rule matching supports: exact model id (including pinned rev), family wildcard, and optional environment/region scoping.
- Precedence (explicit + deterministic):
  (a) deny match -> v2 disabled
  (b) allow match -> v2 enabled
  (c) otherwise -> fall back to global feature gate (existing)
- The selector records the rollout decision reason and exposes it to telemetry/logging (without increasing per-request cardinality).

2) Hot reload (no restart)
- Wires rules into runtime config loader and existing config watcher.
- Reload is atomic: config is parsed/validated, then swapped; on parse/validation failure we retain the last-known-good rules and emit an error + metric.
- Includes monotonic config version handling (ignore out-of-order updates) to reduce flapping when the control plane retries.

3) Safety checks (fail closed + guardrails)
- Validation on load:
  - Disallow ambiguous rules (e.g., the same exact target in both allow and deny).
  - Disallow rules that would match everything unless explicitly marked as a wildcard rule (prevents accidental global enable).
  - Require normalized model identifiers (canonicalization uses existing model registry normalization; rejects unknown/empty ids).
  - Enforce max rule count to keep evaluation bounded and to protect against config explosion (default 500, overridable for Private with a hard cap).
- Runtime behavior: if rule evaluation errors (should be unreachable post-validation), v2 defaults to disabled for that request (consistent with correctness-first posture).

4) Metrics + logs
- Metrics added (names subject to final prefix alignment; see below):
  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_rule_eval_total{outcome="allow|deny|fallback|error", scope="global|region|env"} (no model label)
  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_config_load_total{result="success|failure|ignored_stale"}
  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_rules_count (gauge)
  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_config_version (gauge)
- Structured log event emitted on config load + on rule evaluation only when debug logging is enabled (not default), including a stable rule_id hash to support incident triage without high-cardinality model labels.

Rule syntax (examples)

title: Add safe timeout/retry defaults + circuit breaker for Redwood API calls (incl. streaming)
body:
Add safe timeout/retry defaults + circuit breaker for Redwood API calls (incl. streaming)

## Summary
This PR implements production-minded networking defaults for the Python RAG/agent quickstart scaffold:
- **Timeout defaults** for connect/read/overall request time
- **Retries with exponential backoff + jitter**, honoring `Retry-After` when present
- **Lightweight in-process circuit breaker** to avoid thundering herds during upstream instability
- **Streaming-specific policy** (SSE/chunked responses): retry only if the connection drops *before first token*; otherwise surface partial output and emit actionable logs/metrics

Motivation: internal beta users and early adopters hit a mix of streaming disconnects behind proxies (SUP-29410), 429s from bursty defaults, and "hung" requests due to missing read timeouts. We want templates to be resilient by default without being aggressive (avoid retrying non-idempotent work or multiplying token spend).

## Design notes
### Timeouts
Defaults (can be overridden via env):
- `RW_HTTP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S=3.0`
- `RW_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT_S=30.0` (time between bytes/chunks)
- `RW_HTTP_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_S=120.0`

Rationale:
- Connect timeout should fail fast in misconfigured networks.
- Read timeout for streaming is "between chunks" to detect dead connections without prematurely killing long generations.
- Total timeout prevents hanging requests when upstream/proxies keep sockets open.

### Retries
Retries are enabled by default for **transient failures** only:
- HTTP: `429`, `502`, `503`, `504`
- Network: connect resets, DNS failures, timeouts

Not retried:
- `401/403` (auth), `400/422` (bad request / schema), `404` (misconfig), `409` (conflict)

Defaults:
- `RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3` (non-streaming)
- `RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS_STREAMING=1` (only pre-first-byte)
- backoff: exponential with full jitter; base 0.5s, cap 8s; respects `Retry-After` if provided

### Circuit breaker
A minimal per-host circuit breaker is introduced to prevent overload loops when Redwood or an intermediate proxy is failing:
- Opens after `RW_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=5` consecutive failures
- Remains open for `RW_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_OPEN_WINDOW_S=30`
- Half-open allows a single trial request; success closes, failure re-opens

Important: this is intentionally simple and in-process (template-safe). For multi-replica deployments we still recommend an L7 proxy / service mesh policy, but templates should degrade gracefully locally and in single-instance deployments.

### Streaming reconnect strategy
We cannot safely "resume" a generation mid-stream without explicit server support. Retrying after partial tokens risks duplicate output and unexpected token spend.
Policy implemented:
- If stream disconnects **before first token**: retry once (counts as a normal retry attempt)
- If disconnects **after some tokens**: do not retry; return partial output with a user-facing message and log an error with `stream_state=partial`

## What changed
- Added `networking.py` helper that wraps the Redwood client request path with:
  - standardized timeout config
  - retry policy
  - circuit breaker
  - streaming guardrails
- Updated template entrypoints to use the shared networking helper.
- Added unit tests for retry classification, `Retry-After` handling, and circuit breaker transitions.
- Updated README troubleshooting and "Safe defaults" sections with rationale + override env vars.

## Testing
- `pytest -q` (unit)
- Added a small "simulated flaky stream" test using a local stub server to validate pre-first-byte retry only.
- Manual sanity:
  - run app behind a local reverse proxy w/ idle timeouts
  - verify logs include retry attempt counts and final classification

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- TS template parity once the TS scaffold lands (Dana already tracking).
- Add explicit docs guidance on proxies that reject unknown headers; separate PR will make telemetry headers opt-in.

Co-authored-by: Sabrina James <sabrina.james@redwoodinference.com>
- Templates now use standardized timeouts, retries (w/ backoff + jitter), and a lightweight circuit breaker for Redwood API calls.
- Streaming requests get a conservative reconnect policy (retry only before first byte/token) to avoid duplicate generations.
- README includes rationale + env var overrides and guidance for proxies/429s.
Ibrahim Khan: Please make sure we do NOT retry on 401/403, and that 429 respects Retry-After if present. Also, can we cap total retry sleep so users don't think the app is frozen?
Monica Patel: Updated classification to explicitly exclude 401/403 and to honor Retry-After. Added cap via `RW_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_S` (default 8s) and ensured we log `retry_sleep_s` per attempt.
Christine Wong: Circuit breaker should be per-host and thread-safe. Also, be careful with streaming retries after partial output—I'd rather we never retry after the first token.
Monica Patel: Circuit breaker now keys on `base_url` and uses a lock. Streaming policy updated: retry only before first byte/token; after partial, return partial and log `stream_state=partial` with a remediation hint.
Brian Murphy: Please avoid retrying on 400/422. Also can we include the Redwood request id in the error logs so support can correlate?
Monica Patel: Confirmed 400/422 are non-retriable. Added log field `redwood_request_id` when present in response headers (best-effort). Follow-up PR will standardize propagation across templates once SDK helpers land.
Christine Wong (follow-up): Add a short README note explaining why we don't "resume" streaming.
Monica Patel: Added a paragraph under Troubleshooting > Streaming disconnects with the rationale and recommended proxy settings.

title: Document Dedicated Burst: behavior, limits, denial reasons, and client retry guidance
body:
Document Dedicated Burst: behavior, limits, denial reasons, and client retry guidance

Summary: This PR adds customer-facing documentation for the new Dedicated “Burst Capacity” option: what it is (borrowing temporary capacity from Redwood-managed burst pools), how limits/guardrails work, how to configure it (what’s controlled by Redwood vs what customers can tune), and what clients should do when burst is denied. Motivation: During beta we saw repeated support questions around (a) why burst was denied even when baseline looked “underused”, (b) what HTTP status / reason codes mean, and (c) how retries can accidentally amplify load or trigger double-counting concerns. This doc set aims to make behavior predictable and reduce time-to-resolution for incidents. Scope: Documented (1) baseline vs burst semantics, (2) per-tenant caps (max burst ratio, absolute cap), cooldown windows, and fleet safety caps at a high level, (3) denial reasons and what the platform does (fallback vs immediate backpressure), and (4) recommended client retry patterns with Retry-After handling + jitter and idempotency guidance. Non-goals: This does not document internal pool sizing policy, exact threshold numbers (these are contract/config dependent), or any cross-region bursting (not supported in initial GA). Notable behavior notes included in docs: Burst is best-effort and admission-controlled; baseline Dedicated capacity is not reduced by enabling burst. Burst is constrained to the same region and hardware class as the Dedicated baseline. When burst is denied, the platform returns a deterministic denial reason code and (when applicable) a Retry-After value; clients should not spin in tight loops. When the fleet safety circuit breaker is active, burst admissions may be broadly denied to protect non-burst SLOs. Customer guidance highlights: Prefer app-level smoothing (queues) for batch jobs; avoid synchronized retries across workers; use exponential backoff with full jitter; honor Retry-After; set an overall deadline; and ensure request idempotency keys are stable across retries. Checklists: Docs reviewed by Product + SRE; includes Support-facing “how to explain denials” section; includes example curl/SDK snippets; links to dashboards and runbook placeholders for CS enablement. Screenshots: None added in this PR (Console UI landing in a separate change); docs reference the Console location and API fields customers should expect to see. Testing: Docs build + link check in CI; manual preview in staging docs environment.

title: Add trafficctl emergency GSLB weight setter for api.redwoodinference.com
body:
Add trafficctl emergency GSLB weight setter for api.redwoodinference.com

### Context
During game day and recent regional brownouts, the fastest safe mitigation is to shift Hosted API traffic between regions without waiting for Terraform applies. We currently do this via manual console operations, which is error-prone.

### What this PR does
- Introduces `trafficctl`, an audited CLI wrapper around our GSLB provider API
- Adds commands to:
  - read current targets + weights
  - set weights for api.redwoodinference.com
  - set record TTL (temporary)
- Enforces RBAC via the `infra-traffic-admin` role
- Writes an audit log event for every invocation (who, what record, old/new weights)

### Usage
```
trafficctl gslb get --record api.redwoodinference.com
trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 60
trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=0,us-west-2-gw=100
trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 300
```

### Rollback
- Disable the `trafficctl` GitHub Actions release workflow and revert to manual console operations
- No data-plane changes are required to roll back this PR
