title: Fix double-counting on stream retry/fallback for Hosted API metering
body:
Fix double-counting on stream retry/fallback for Hosted API metering

Context: We’ve seen invoice disputes and internal drift checks flag double-counted billed_tokens when the server performs a retry/fallback during streaming responses (e.g., upstream timeout mid-stream, router switches to a compatible model/region, or control plane triggers a hedged request). The customer sees one response stream, but we were emitting usage events for both the initial attempt and the retried attempt, and the ledger aggregation was summing both. This PR fixes the retry/fallback accounting path for streaming so that billed token meters reflect the final successful attempt only.

Root cause: In streaming mode, we incrementally populated a per-attempt UsageAccumulator and emitted a usage_event on stream termination for each attempt (including attempts that were superseded). When a retry/fallback occurred after partial chunks, the original attempt emitted a terminal usage_event with partial token counts; the retried attempt emitted its own terminal usage_event; downstream billing ledger summed both because both had unique event_ids and the aggregator did not have a stable “superseded by” key.

Fix (high level): (1) Introduce a stable request-scoped usage_dedupe_key derived from (account_id, api_key_id, idempotency_key||request_id, billing_period_day, meter_version). (2) Emit attempt-scoped usage events with attempt_seq and a new terminal_reason enum. (3) Update ledger aggregation to bill only the max attempt_seq per usage_dedupe_key where terminal_reason == SUCCESS, and to ignore attempts where terminal_reason in {SUPERSEDED, RETRY_ABORTED}. (4) For the streaming handler, ensure we mark the prior attempt as SUPERSEDED before starting the retry path, and we do not emit a SUCCESS terminal event for any attempt that did not complete.

Details:
- New fields on usage events:
  - usage_dedupe_key: stable across retries/fallbacks for the logical request
  - attempt_seq: monotonic int starting at 0
  - terminal_reason: SUCCESS | ERROR | SUPERSEDED | RETRY_ABORTED | CLIENT_DISCONNECT
  - superseded_by_attempt_seq: populated on SUPERSEDED events
- Streaming retry semantics: When router triggers retry/fallback after partial streaming, we immediately close the old accumulator with terminal_reason=SUPERSEDED (not SUCCESS) and start a new accumulator for attempt_seq+1. Only the attempt that reaches stream completion and returns a final usage summary is eligible for billing.
- Metrics/observability: Added counters for retry_double_count_prevented_total and usage_events_superseded_total, plus a gauge for per-route superseded rate to help tune alerting. Added structured log fields for usage_dedupe_key and attempt_seq in the streaming gateway.

Tests:
- Unit tests in metering: simulate (a) stream completes without retry; (b) retry after N chunks; (c) fallback to different model mid-stream; (d) client disconnect then server retry does not run; verify billed tokens count equals final successful attempt only and that superseded attempts are excluded.
- Integration test: added a harness that forces an upstream timeout on first attempt and verifies the exported usage API returns a single billed record for the request (with billed_tokens matching the final attempt).
- Regression: added a fixture for OpenAI-compatible streaming endpoint where retries previously double-counted due to different request_id normalization.

Rollout notes:
- This change is behind feature flag billing.metering_stream_retry_dedupe_v1 (default off). Plan: enable in staging for 48h, then canary 5% of hosted traffic (US-East + two high-volume accounts), then ramp to 50% and 100% if drift checks remain within thresholds.
- Shadow-billing: for the canary phase, ledger will compute both old and new billable usage in parallel (annotated in the recon export) to quantify deltas; Finance/RevRec sign-off required before 100% rollout.
- Backfill: no backfill in this PR. If shadow-billing indicates material historical impact, we’ll follow the RevRec playbook for corrective credits rather than retroactive invoice edits.

Customer impact: Fixes an overbilling bug in specific streaming retry/fallback scenarios (primarily server-side retries). In most cases, customers should see billed token counts decrease slightly for affected days; usage API exports will show clearer attempt attribution fields once the related API surface PR lands.

Checklist:
- [x] Added unit coverage for streaming retry + fallback paths
- [x] Added integration coverage for forced retry in staging
- [x] Added metrics + logs for superseded attempts
- [x] Rollout plan documented + flag added
- [x] Linked to support escalation SUP-28463 and Linear ENG-4430

Notes for reviewers: Please focus on (a) dedupe key stability across OpenAI-compatible endpoints, (b) ensuring we never bill SUPERSEDED attempts, and (c) any edge cases where SUCCESS could be emitted after partial stream termination.
Logan Wright (review): The dedupe_key derivation uses request_id for non-idempotent requests — do we normalize OpenAI-compat request IDs the same way as native endpoints? Author (Cole): Good catch. I added normalization to strip the gateway-generated suffix and included a regression test for /v1/chat/completions streaming. Nadia Rahman (review): Can we guarantee terminal_reason cannot be SUCCESS for the superseded attempt if the client disconnects? Also please document semantics of CLIENT_DISCONNECT vs SUPERSEDED. Author: Updated the state machine so SUCCESS is only emitted from the finalization path that sees a completed stream; client disconnect now emits CLIENT_DISCONNECT and short-circuits retries. Added inline docs and tests. Aisha Bello (review): Please add a metric we can alert on for high superseded rates per route/model; also add log fields so SRE can join events. Author: Added usage_events_superseded_total with route+model labels (bounded), and structured log fields usage_dedupe_key/attempt_seq. Connor O'Brien (review): Rollout plan needs an explicit canary and revert procedure. Author: Expanded rollout section with percentages, regions, and revert steps (flag off, keep shadow-billing for 24h). Monica Patel (review): Ensure SDK retries using idempotency_key don’t change dedupe semantics. Author: Dedupe prefers idempotency_key when present; added a test that simulates client retry with same idempotency key and confirms single billable attempt. Final: Approved after changes; merged squash.
Fixes a bug where streaming retries/fallbacks could double-count billed tokens by ensuring only the final successful attempt is billable; adds retry attempt attribution fields and regression coverage; rolled out behind feature flag billing.metering_stream_retry_dedupe_v1 with shadow-billing support.

title: private-installer: add `backup create` command (manifest + encrypted artifact + verification output)
body:
private-installer: add `backup create` command (manifest + encrypted artifact + verification output)

This PR introduces an initial `backup create` workflow in the Redwood Private installer CLI to support Day-2 operations and DR readiness. The command produces (1) a human-readable manifest (JSON) describing what was captured and how it was encrypted, and (2) an encrypted artifact (tarball) containing the control-plane state snapshot files and selected deterministic configuration inputs. The goal of this PR is to ship the core mechanics (consistent snapshot + packaging + encryption + basic verification/logging) so Solutions/SRE teams can begin rehearsing restores in staging while we iterate on storage backends, scheduled jobs, and restore automation. Scope: control-plane backup only (no data-plane model cache / no customer prompt data). Secrets are not exported as raw secret material; we only record references (e.g., external KMS key ARNs, secret names) and require the target cluster to have access to the same secret sources at restore time. The artifact format is intentionally versioned (`format_version: 1`) and includes integrity checks (SHA256) for each included file and the encrypted blob. Encryption is implemented as AES-256-GCM with a randomly generated data key; for this PR, the data key is derived from a user-provided passphrase via scrypt and stored only in-memory during packaging (no plaintext key material written to disk). A follow-up will add a KMS provider interface for envelope encryption (see ENG-9823) and backup storage backends (S3/NFS) integration. Operator UX: `redwood-private backup create --output ./backups --cluster-context <ctx> [--include-etcd-snapshot=auto] [--quiesce-timeout=60s]` prints a summary, writes `manifest.json` and `backup-<cluster>-<ts>.tar.enc`, and optionally runs a post-backup verification step that re-reads the artifact header and validates checksums. Logging: adds structured log lines with `backup_id`, `duration_ms`, `bytes_written`, and `error_category` for future metrics wiring. Documentation: adds CLI help text and a short internal README section describing the artifact layout and the restore prerequisites. Known limitations (explicitly documented in help output): (a) does not back up Kubernetes resources/CRDs (Velero integration is tracked separately), (b) etcd snapshot capture is best-effort and gated behind `--include-etcd-snapshot` because some Private installs do not grant direct etcd access, (c) no remote upload; output is a local directory only, (d) no key rotation / KMS-based sealing yet. This aligns with ADR-027 direction (manifest + encrypted bundle + deterministic layout), but the key management details are expected to change once KMS provider lands; the format_version is reserved for that evolution.
Unit tests: `go test ./...` (added focused tests for manifest serialization, checksum generation, and decrypt+verify path using a fixed nonce in test-only helper). Manual: validated on staging cluster `stg-private-3` by running `redwood-private backup create --output /tmp/rw-backups --include-etcd-snapshot=off` and confirming (1) artifact + manifest written, (2) summary printed, (3) `--verify` reports PASS, (4) failure modes produce actionable error_category (permissions, missing kubecontext, insufficient disk).
Ethan Park: The include list mentions `routing-policies`. Where are those sourced from? We should be explicit that we’re backing up control-plane DB state + installer-known config, not live K8s objects. Also please add a format_version to the manifest so we can evolve encryption without breaking restores.
Benji Okafor (author): Routing policies are persisted in the config DB and surfaced via the control-plane API; this implementation snapshots the DB, and the manifest component list is descriptive (not a source-of-truth inventory). I added `format_version: 1` and clarified in help text that K8s resources are out of scope for this command.
Sean Gallagher: For on-call usability, we need deterministic filenames and a stable location for `latest`. Also, log output should include duration and bytes; future dashboards will rely on it. Can we also avoid printing anything that looks like key material?
Benji Okafor (author): Added deterministic filename template `backup-<cluster>-<timestamp>.tar.enc` and `manifest-<backup_id>.json`. I held off on a `latest` symlink because Windows/on-prem customers may not have it; instead we print the output paths and backup_id. Logging now includes `duration_ms`/`bytes_written` and we never log salt/nonce or passphrase-derived data.
Hanae Suzuki: Please double-check the crypto: AES-GCM nonce reuse would be catastrophic. Make sure nonce is random per artifact and not derived from timestamp. Also, can we add guardrails so the artifact never includes raw Kubernetes Secret values?
Benji Okafor (author): Nonce is generated from `crypto/rand` per artifact; tests use fixed nonce in a test-only helper. Added an explicit denylist in the planner: we will not read `Secret` data from the cluster; we only snapshot application datastores + config files and record secret *references* in the manifest when applicable.
Connor O'Brien: Packaging question: we’ll need this to work in air-gapped flows later. Please keep the output fully self-contained, and don’t add implicit network calls. Also, ensure we can verify integrity offline.
Benji Okafor (author): No network calls in this PR. Verification is offline: we hash files pre-encryption, hash the encrypted blob, and emit those in the manifest. `--verify` reads the artifact header and validates checksums without external dependencies.
Kira Thompson: The CLI help reads like a runbook; keep it concise but include prerequisites and a link to the Confluence runbook once it exists. Also, add an example command with `--quiesce-timeout` since that’s a common customer ask.
Benji Okafor (author): Updated help text to a concise prerequisites list + example commands, and added TODO link placeholder for Confluence page (will be replaced when docs land).
Private installer now supports `redwood-private backup create` to generate a versioned manifest and encrypted backup artifact suitable for staging DR rehearsals. No external storage backends or KMS envelope encryption in this release.

title: Add shadow billing compare mode (dual-run meters without impacting invoices)
body:
Add shadow billing compare mode (dual-run meters without impacting invoices)

Summary: Introduces a "shadow billing compare" mode that dual-runs meter calculations (old vs new) on the same usage inputs and persists both results for diffing, without affecting invoices or the customer-facing Usage API. This is intended to support safe metering changes (token counting, retries/idempotency fixes, embeddings batching, Dedicated GPU-seconds v2) by allowing Finance/RevRec and Eng to validate deltas before any meter output is used for ledger writes.

Context / Motivation: We’ve had multiple meter changes in-flight (retry double-counting, region dimension fixes, embeddings batch accounting, Dedicated GPU-seconds v2). Historically the only way to validate meter deltas was ad-hoc queries and backfills, which makes it easy to miss edge cases (late events, partial streaming chunks, fallback routing) and increases risk of invoice disputes. This PR adds a first-class mechanism to compute both versions on live traffic and quantify expected diffs by account/model/region/day, while keeping billing ledger writes pinned to the existing “active” meter version.

Design: 1) Meter versioning: Adds a MeterVersion enum and per-meter "active" vs "shadow" selection. The active version continues to drive billing_ledger writes; the shadow version is computed in parallel and written only to billing_shadow_results.
2) Dual-run execution path: In billcalc/usage-aggregator, after we build the canonical UsageSlice (account_id, workspace_id, api_route, model, region, timestamp_bucket, dimensions), we invoke both calculators behind a shared normalization layer to ensure identical inputs (including tokenization inputs, request-id grouping, and dedupe windowing).
3) Persistence + schema: Adds a new table billing_shadow_results (Snowflake) with: run_id, meter_name, active_version, shadow_version, key dimensions, active_value, shadow_value, delta_abs, delta_pct, computed_at, and a small set of “attribution hints” (retry_count, cache_hit_rate, late_event_ratio) used for triage.
4) Metrics + alerting hooks: Emits Prometheus counters/gauges for compare coverage (percent of slices dual-run), compute lag, and delta distributions. This is intentionally not paging on delta magnitude yet; alerting is added in a follow-up once we have baseline noise levels.
5) Feature flag + safety rails: Shadow mode is gated via control-plane config: billing.shadow_compare.enabled, billing.shadow_compare.meters=[...], and billing.shadow_compare.sample_rate. When enabled, the service will: (a) compute shadow only for sampled slices; (b) never write shadow values to billing_ledger; (c) never expose shadow values via /v1/usage exports; (d) annotate runs with config hash for auditability.

Operational workflow (intended): Enable shadow compare for a target meter + shadow version (e.g., hosted_tokens:v2) at low sample_rate in staging → verify invariants → enable in prod at ~1–5% for 3–7 days → Finance/Eng review delta report (by top accounts + aggregate) → if within expected bounds, proceed with meter activation change under PM-1872 change control.

Test plan: - Unit tests: Added tests for dual-run selection logic, schema mapping, delta calculation, and “never write to ledger” invariants.
- Integration tests: Staging job executes dual-run on recorded usage fixtures including retries + streaming partials. Validates stable keys and that idempotent replays don’t multiply shadow rows.
- Load/perf: Verified added compute overhead stays under 3% CPU at sample_rate=5% on canary; most overhead is tokenization, which is already cached per UsageSlice.

Risk / Rollout: - Default OFF in all envs. - When enabled, writes to a separate table with separate retention policy (30 days) and restricted access (Finance/RevRec + Telemetry on-call). - Backfill is intentionally out of scope for this PR; we only support forward compute on incoming slices.

Follow-ups (not in this PR): - Add dashboard panels in Console/Grafana to visualize deltas and top contributors. - Add a paging policy for sustained drift beyond threshold (once we characterize baseline noise). - Apply the same compare mode to Dedicated GPU-seconds v2 activation and embeddings batch meter fixes.

Notes for reviewers: Most of the surface area is plumbing + safety rails; the meter calculators themselves are unchanged. Please focus review on (1) ledger write invariants; (2) stable join keys between active and shadow; (3) sampling + idempotency interactions.
Nadia Rahman: Can you confirm the join key for active vs shadow rows is stable across backfills/replays? We’ve been burned by timestamp bucketing differences. Also, please ensure tokenization cache is keyed by the normalized prompt bytes, not request_id.
Connor O'Brien: Join key is (run_id, meter_name, account_id, workspace_id, bucket_start, model, region, route, dimension_hash). bucket_start comes from the canonical UsageSlice, so both calculators receive identical bucket_start. Replays: writer uses deterministic row_id = sha256(join_key) to upsert, so idempotent. Tokenization cache is keyed by normalized prompt bytes + model tokenizer version; request_id is not used.
Mei Lin: Finance will need to query this by account/day and get a "top deltas" view. Are we persisting both absolute and pct delta? Also please add an easy way to map run_id to the config used.
Connor O'Brien: Yes: delta_abs and delta_pct stored; also added config_hash + config_json to the run header table billing_shadow_runs (created in same migration). Queries can join on run_id to fetch config_json.
Cole Summers: Safety: I want a hard invariant that ledger writes cannot occur when compare mode is enabled and active_version != configured active. Right now it looks like a conditional in compute_meters. Can we add an assert/metric to detect accidental writes?
Connor O'Brien: Added an explicit guard in ledger_writer: if request_context.shadow_compare_enabled == true then we only accept active meter results (tagged is_active=true). Added a counter billing_shadow_compare_ledger_write_blocked which increments if any non-active attempt reaches the writer (should remain 0).
Logan Wright: Sampling semantics: are we sampling per request, per slice, or per account? We don’t want sampling to bias toward high-volume accounts only.
Connor O'Brien: Sampling is per UsageSlice (post-aggregation) using hash(account_id + bucket_start + meter_name) < threshold so it’s stable and evenly distributed. It will still overweight high-volume accounts in absolute row count, but coverage is stable per-account; we can also force-include accounts via billing.shadow_compare.force_accounts=[...].
Aisha Bello: Please add explicit SLO language in the runbook: compare lag and write failure behavior. Also confirm PII isn’t being written into the shadow tables.
Connor O'Brien: Updated runbook with expected lag (< 30m p95 from slice close) and failure mode (shadow failures do not block active billing). Tables include only ids/dimensions; no prompts/responses/token text is written.
billcalc: add MeterVersion + active/shadow configuration plumbing
billing: introduce billing_shadow_results table + writer
usage-aggregator: dual-run execution path w/ shared normalization
metrics: expose shadow-compare coverage/lag/delta histograms
tests: add invariants for "no ledger writes" + idempotent replays
docs: add runbook notes for enabling shadow compare in staging/prod
Internal: Added shadow billing compare mode to dual-run meter versions and persist diffs for validation prior to meter activation.
No customer-visible changes; billing ledger and Usage API remain driven by active meter version.

title: Add service-scoped KMS guardrails and audit ingestion harmonizer
body:
Add service-scoped KMS guardrails and audit ingestion harmonizer

Motivation: Customers operating multiple logical services under the same tenant require strict guarantees that service-A cannot request or unwrap keys bound to service-B. Incidents surfaced during an internal postmortem showed ambiguous key attribution for cross-service operator actions which complicates audits and violates customer isolation promises. This PR implements service-scoped KMS guardrails and a lightweight audit ingestion harmonizer to make audit events canonical and to prevent cross-service key usage by default.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a new enforcement middleware (kms/service-guard) that validates the requesting principal's service claim against the requested key's service binding. Introduces a new policy API to bind keys to a service identifier and to define an exception allowlist for operator flows. Adds an audit-ingestor microservice that normalizes incoming audit records, deduplicates identical events within a short window, enriches events with residency and key binding metadata, and forwards to the existing audit pipeline. Provides a backfill migration to tag historical events with best-effort service_kms_id and residency_claim (logged separately for traceability).

Design notes: - Service binding model: keys have an optional service_id tag set at creation time. When present, only principals with matching service_id or explicit allowlist entries may perform wrap/unwrap or key usage actions. The enforcement is opt-in for existing keys (to avoid breaking legacy customers); new keys have binding encouraged by CLI/console UX. - Failure modes: requests that violate binding fail early with 403 and an structured error code kms.service_bound. Operator-level exceptions can be granted via RBAC role "kms:service-bypass" which requires multi-approver escalation (see RBAC section). - Audit harmonization: the ingestor normalizes heterogenous audit sources (gateway, kms-proxy, operator-proxy) into a canonical event schema (timestamp, principal, service_id, kms_key_id, op, residency_claim, request_id, provenance_chain). It also deduplicates retry storms within a 30s window to reduce noise in retention stores. - Backward compatibility: enforcement for existing keys is behind a feature flag enforcement.kms.service_bind and rollout uses a canary cohort. The ingestor will accept both legacy and canonical payloads and will write a normalized event alongside the original raw event for troubleshooting.

Changed areas (representative): - core/kms/middleware/service_guard.go: new enforcement middleware and policy evaluator - api/kms/policy.go: API surface to bind keys and query service bindings - services/audit/ingestor/*: new service that normalizes, dedupes, enriches audit events and forwards to kafka/topic audit.normalized - infra/eks/manifests/audit-ingestor.yaml: k8s manifest and RBAC for the ingestor - tools/migrations/20241112_backfill_service_kms_tags.go: migration to tag historical events - docs/security/kms-service-binding.md: runbook and operator guidance - tests/e2e/kms_service_binding_test.go and unit tests across middleware/ingestor

Testing and verification: - Unit tests cover policy evaluation matrix, denial messages, and the fallback path for unbound keys. - Integration tests run a mini-ingestor and replayed audit payloads validating normalization and dedupe behavior. - E2E smoke includes creation of bound key, attempt to use key with non-matching service principal (expect 403), and operator unbind flow (requires role and audit note). - CI: lint, unit, integration, and e2e stages passed on the merge run (flaky test t-queue-429 retried once).

Migration and rollout plan: - Phase 1 (canary): enable audit-ingestor in staging and wire a 5% subset of production traffic for 48h. Run backfill in read-only mode to evaluate heuristics. - Phase 2 (soft enforcement): enable service_bind enforcement for newly-created keys and opt-in existing keys via console prompts. Run with monitoring dashboards for reject rate and false positives. - Phase 3 (enforce for cohort): enable enforcement for a subset of tenants that opted-in; continue backfill and provide operator tooling to request exception. - Phase 4 (global): flip enforcement.kms.service_bind and promote ingestor as primary audit-normalizer.

Rollout guards and SLOs: - Alert if reject rate for bound-key usage > 0.1% of normal traffic for 1h and if normalized audit ingest latency > 500ms p95. - Provide a rollback flag to disable enforcement cluster-wide within 15 minutes.

Security and compliance notes: - Audit events now include canonical residency_claim and service_kms_id; these fields are surfaced to Compliance exports. - RBAC: introduced new role kms:service-bypass that is gated by two approvers for granting via the console; role change events are captured by the ingestor. - KMS provider compatibility: enforcement checks are performed in the request flow and do not require KMS provider changes (we attach binding metadata at Redwood's metadata layer).

Related work and references: Linear ENG-8842 (design doc), SEC-1471 compliance review. Follow-ups: integrate key binding UI in Console (tracked in ENG-9129) and rotation flow to preserve bindings (ENG-9204).

Files changed summary: small code additions across middleware and a new service. No schema changes to core tenant records; audit store schema extended with optional fields (backfill added separately). Storage impact estimated ~1.2% increase in retention store per event due to added metadata.

Merge: squash and merge. This PR includes migration scripts and an operator playbook under docs.

Elliot Zhang: Can we ensure the middleware runs before any request body parsing to avoid accidental caching of malformed requests? Also suggest a clear error code for automation consumers.
Maya Patel (author): Reordered middleware chain so service_guard is executed immediately after auth. Added structured error code 'kms.service_bound' and included error docs link in response.
Ravi Desai: Approving after requested tests added. Logged a follow-up for console UX (ENG-9129).
Add service-scoped KMS guardrails to prevent cross-service key access and introduce an audit-ingestor that normalizes and deduplicates audit events. Backfill migration provided. Feature gated and rolled out in controlled cohorts.

title: Commitment gap auditor and rollback impact simulator
body:
Commitment gap auditor and rollback impact simulator

Add a runtime auditor that detects divergence between committed tenant throughput and observed delivery; include a rollback impact simulator and operator-facing visualization to validate safe decommit scenarios.
Context: Dedicated customers buy committed throughput and we must ensure the fleet honors commitments and can safely decommit/reschedule capacity when required. Motivation: recent support cases exposed hard-to-reproduce gaps between committed units and delivered throughput under bursty demand and transient preemptions. This PR adds a Commitment Gap Auditor service that continuously compares contract-level commitments to recent delivery (p50/p95 throughput and admission failures), and a deterministic Rollback Impact Simulator that lets operators run 'what-if' decommit scenarios against a sliding-window utilization model. Summary of changes: - new long-running service `commitment-auditor` (controller + API) that samples per-tenant reservation ledgers and emits gap alerts and suggested mitigations - a simulator binary (`rollback-sim`) that replays recent activity to estimate percent of tenant requests that would have been throttled under candidate decommit plans - operator UI endpoints (JSON + CSV) to fetch simulated outcomes and a small Prometheus metrics set for alerting - lightweight safety guards: automatic soft-hold when a decommit would cause >5% of active requests to regress past SLO for 5m - e2e tests and an integration scenario based test harness to reproduce regression locally Checklist: - [x] design doc (docs/design/commitment-auditor.md) - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] metrics + alert rules (basic) - [x] minimal operator UI endpoints - [x] rollout plan discussed with SRE and Sales Impact: This is an operator-facing feature that does not change runtime scheduling by default. New service runs as opt-in; default is disabled in Dedicated clusters until we complete a controlled rollout. Related: SUP-4312 (customer incident), ENG-1982 (autoscaler followup), RFC: decommit-safe-paths (internal).
Arjun: Nice incremental approach. Please call out invariants around partial decommits (what happens to reserved KV caches) — also add a unit test that simulates a preemption + decommit in the same window.
Maya: added test for preempt+decommit and documented KV cache assumption in design doc; clarified that auditor does not alter live reservations, only simulates and emits recommendations.
Sofia: Metrics look good. Can we expose a histogram for simulated throttled fraction to help threshold tuning?
Maya: added prometheus histogram and updated alert rule to use the 99th of simulated throttled fraction; addressed nits in the helm values file.
Jonah: ran the simulator against last 48h of production sample (sanitized) — output matched expectations, approving.
CI bot: flake detected in e2e: TestSimulatorDeterminism - rerunning jobs.
CI bot: rerun passed after deterministic seed fix.
Canary in dedicated-staging (1 cluster) -> opt-in beta for 5 customers -> expand to 20% of Dedicated fleet with monitoring gates (commitment_gap > 0.05 for 15m) -> global rollout disabled-by-default until SRE sign-off.
When auditor emits 'decommit-risk' alert: 1) fetch simulator CSV from /api/v1/simulate?plan=<plan_id> 2) inspect top affected tenants and simulated throttled fraction 3) consider smaller decommit or schedule maintenance window; call SRE on-call if >10% active requests impacted.
Decoupled simulation from live admission path. Future work: richer cost model (inc. spot preempt probability) and UI for ad-hoc scenario composition.

title: Add structured output example + JSON schema validation helper (Go)
body:
Add structured output example + JSON schema validation helper (Go)

Context: Support + Solutions Eng have repeatedly flagged that customers copy/paste a structured-output snippet, immediately hit JSON parse/validation errors, and then have no idea what the “safe” handling path is (SUP-18436). This PR adds a runnable Go example that demonstrates schema-constrained output, safe parsing/validation, and a pragmatic fallback/retry strategy. It also updates doc comments in the SDK to align terminology with the docs refresh ("structured output" / "schema-constrained"), and to warn against incremental JSON parsing during streaming.

What’s included: 1) New runnable example: examples/structured_output_jsonschema/main.go - Requests schema-constrained output from the model - Collects the final assistant message before parsing (no incremental parse) - Validates against a JSON Schema (type/required/additionalProperties) - On validation failure: logs a compact error, retries once with a tighter system message, then falls back to non-structured extraction 2) Lightweight validation helper (example-scoped): examples/internal/jsonschema/validate.go - Uses github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v5 to compile/validate a schema string - Returns a single error string suitable for end-user logs (keeps example output clean) 3) Doc comment updates: - client/response types: clarify that “structured output” is best-effort across models and should be validated - streaming notes: explicitly recommend assembling the final message before parsing JSON

Example schema used in the sample: The example constrains output to an object with required fields and no additional properties: {"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["title","priority","due_date"],"properties":{"title":{"type":"string","minLength":1},"priority":{"type":"string","enum":["low","medium","high"]},"due_date":{"type":"string","pattern":"^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$"}}}

User-visible behavior: Running the example prints a validated struct on success; on failure it prints a single-line validation error plus the raw model output (truncated to 1KB) for debugging.

How to test: - go test ./... - go run ./examples/structured_output_jsonschema (requires REDWOOD_API_KEY) - Force failure path by setting RW_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_FORCE_BAD=1 to validate retry + fallback branch

Notes / non-goals: - This does not change the API, only examples + doc comments. - We intentionally do NOT demonstrate streaming structured JSON parsing; we call that out as a pitfall and point to final-message assembly first.

Related: ENG-4821 (parity audit), ENG-4825 (Go examples refresh), PM-413 (support matrix language).
Ibrahim Khan: Can we make the retry behavior explicit about what changes between attempt 1 and attempt 2? Right now it looks like magic.
Mateusz Zielinski: Good call. Updated the example to show the exact additional system instruction for retry: we add “Output ONLY valid JSON matching the schema; do not include code fences or commentary.” and we log when we switch to attempt=2.

Brian Murphy: Please avoid implying a hard guarantee. Some models will still leak prose. Let’s make the docs comment say “validate and be prepared to retry/fallback.”
Mateusz Zielinski: Updated doc comments and README copy: “best-effort; validate; retry; fallback.” Also added a NOTE: do not parse incrementally during streaming.

Sabrina James: Can we keep example logs stable for golden tests later? The error formatting should be deterministic.
Mateusz Zielinski: Adjusted validation error formatting to a single-line, deterministic string (sorts fields where possible). Truncated raw output to 1KB to keep logs bounded.

Wei Chen: Naming: docs are standardizing on “structured output” rather than “JSON mode”. Please align in comments + README.
Mateusz Zielinski: Done. Replaced “JSON mode” phrasing in Go example and comments.

Sahana Iyer: go.mod diff adds a new dependency; ensure it’s scoped to examples only and doesn’t affect library consumers.
Mateusz Zielinski: Confirmed it’s only imported by examples/* packages. No exported API changes. CI now compiles the example to catch regressions.

Approvals: Ibrahim Khan (approved), Brian Murphy (approved), Sabrina James (approved).

title: Add idiomatic retry presets and lightweight stream control across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs
body:
Add idiomatic retry presets and lightweight stream control across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs

Motivation: We have accumulated several ad-hoc retry/backoff variants across SDKs and inconsistent streaming cancellation ergonomics. This PR introduces a small, opinionated set of language-idiomatic retry presets plus a lightweight stream control surface (cancel token + backpressure hint hook) implemented consistently in Python, TypeScript, and Go. Goals: 1) Provide three vetted presets (optimistic, balanced, conservative) for common production workloads so teams can pick sensible defaults without tuning; 2) Add a streaming control hook that surfaces a cancel token and an optional onBackpressure callback for consumer-driven pacing; 3) Keep implementations idiomatic per language (async context manager for Python, AbortSignal-friendly for TS, context.Context integration for Go); 4) Bump SDK minor versions and update changelogs and docs. Work done: - SDK surface: added retry presets as RetryPreset enum/classes and a small RetryConfig builder in each SDK. - Streaming: wire up cancel tokens to the existing stream iterators; expose onBackpressure callback that receives estimated queue depth (heuristic), does not block the runtime, and is opt-in. - Tests: unit tests for presets, integration tests exercising a simulated transient-error service, and end-to-end streaming cancellation/backpressure tests in the benchmark lab. - Docs: added how-to snippet per-language, migration notes, and a short decision rationale in the platform docs. Compatibility: Presets are opt-in; default behavior is unchanged unless a preset or config is supplied. Edge cases: the Go change required a small API rename (StreamHandle -> StreamCtrl) which is backwards-compatible via a shim for one release. Version bumps: python 2.5.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 1.12.1. Related: ENG-2049 tracks the cross-SDK spec; SUP-4321 logged a customer request for clearer streaming cancellation semantics.
Liam Patel (review): Good structure. Please make sure the TS AbortSignal approach is documented as the recommended upgrade path for consumers that currently pass AbortController to fetch-like helpers.
Maya Chen (reply): Added an explicit section in docs/sdk/streaming-control.md and a short migration snippet in examples/ts.
Diego Rivera (review): Go shim looks fine but please retain the old StreamHandle type for one release and add a deprecation note.
Maya Chen (reply): Added shim_streamctrl.go which aliases StreamHandle to StreamCtrl and added a deprecation comment and test ensuring both compile and pass linters.
Asha Gupta (review): Tests are comprehensive but CI flaked on the integration in the first run. Re-ran and green now. Consider adding a stress test in perf-canary later.
Maya Chen (reply): Noted; opened ENG-2097 to track perf-canary work as follow-up.

title: Horizon-driven kernel activation and pulse flush controller for more stable streaming TTFB
body:
Horizon-driven kernel activation and pulse flush controller for more stable streaming TTFB

Context / motivation: Streaming-first-byte latency (TTFB) for short, interactive LLM sessions remains noisy under mixed workloads. Prior work improved emitter tick pacing and KV prefetching, but we still observe sporadic 100-300ms spikes when kernels are cold or competing microbatches collide. This PR introduces two complementary runtime mechanisms: (1) a horizon-driven kernel activation heuristic that proactively brings up kernel execution contexts based on a compact prefix horizon prediction, and (2) a pulse flush controller that shapes flush cadence as a function of outstanding credits, kernel activation state, and observed downstream ACK latency. Together these reduce tail TTFB without increasing steady-state token-cost.

What this change does (single continuous description): Implements a lightweight KernelHorizon predictor that consumes per-request prefix length, recent token issuance rate, and model-config microprofile to compute a short horizon window (in tokens) that is likely to be requested within the next emission cycle. The KernelManager uses the horizon to start kernel activation (allocate workspace, populate sparse KV slices, pin working set) ahead of inevitable demand. Activation uses a low-overhead fast-path that avoids heavy warmup if prediction confidence is low. The PulseFlushController coordinates flush decisions: instead of a fixed tick or credit drain, the controller emits a flush pulse when (a) the current emitter microbatch is above a dynamic urgency threshold, (b) kernel activation readiness crosses confidence threshold, or (c) a deadline slack indicates we must send partial output to meet SLO. The pulse controller also feeds back to the request-level credit allocator to temporarily increase credits for streams that triggered kernel activation, preventing self-inflicted head-of-line blocking. The feature is behind a runtime feature flag (runtime.streaming.horizon_activation=true) and gated by an experiment rollout that uses per-pod sampling and progressive ramp to 100%.

Engineering notes: The KernelHorizon predictor is intentionally conservative: it prefers under-predicting to avoid unnecessary memory pressure. It uses a short exponential moving average on inter-token intervals with model-config priors (max generation length, typical chunk sizes). Activation state machines are idempotent and cancelable; if the horizon estimate changes, activation can be deescalated to a low-power hold. PulseFlushController uses a leaky-bucket-style urgency accumulator with hysteresis to avoid oscillation under variable network ACKs. We record new metrics (runtime.kernel_horizon.confidence, runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms, runtime.pulse_flush.count, runtime.pulse_flush.reason) and propagate them to tracing spans for waterfall analysis.

Performance summary: Bench results on q4-small (gpt-small-ish) workloads with mixed short chats and long completions: median TTFB improved 12%, p95 improved 18%, p99 improved 13% while token throughput remained within 1% loss. In microbench synthetic cold-start tests, the mean activation latency is 45ms (90ms 95th) with horizon pre-activation vs 170ms cold latency baseline. Cost impact: slight increase in transient memory allocations during activation windows (approx +2% GPU memory footprint on average for mixed workloads) but no measurable increase in per-token compute cost.

Compatibility & safety: Feature is disabled by default. Fallback behavior: if KernelManager cannot allocate activation resources within a short timeout, the pulse controller will revert to conservative flush cadence to prevent latency regressions. We added a kill-switch at pod-level to disable horizon activation in-flight. No API surface changes.

Testing: Unit tests for the KernelHorizon prediction logic and state machine, integration streaming tests that simulate varying ACK latencies and workload mixes, and an end-to-end perf harness run. Added deterministic replay tests to ensure activation cancellation doesn't leak resources. See tests/stream_perf_integration_test.py for scenarios.

Rollout plan: start with 5% of streaming pods for 48h, monitor runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms and runtime.pulse_flush.count, then 25% for 24h, and full ramp if no regressions. Post-merge follow-ups include adding model-specific horion priors for large-context decoders and a telemetry dashboard to correlate activation events with p99 TTFB.

Related work: builds on ENG-3128 emitter pacing improvements and complements previous KV-prefetch PRs by focusing activation timing rather than cache policy. Also ties into Observability tagging work (ENG-3201) to surface activation events in traces.
Liam O'Connor: left nit on atomics in KernelManager::activate - prefer relaxed loads only where safe; confirm no ABA hazard.
Ava Martinez: replied - switched to seq_cst for the state transition edge and added comment explaining tradeoff.
Priya Raman: requested a safety test where activation fails under OOM and ensure no leaking; also asked for clearer metric naming.
Ava Martinez: added deterministic OOM simulation test and renamed runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms to runtime.kernel_activation.activation_latency_ms for clarity.
Marcus Chen: approved after verifying integration test stability and that CI perf job shows no regression.
Pauline (SRE): asked to add a pod-level kill-switch; implemented and documented.
QA: found flakiness at very high ACK jitter - Ava added hysteresis and increased urgency decay window, re-ran tests.
Final: reviewers approved and requested squash merge.

title: Graceful Isolation Lattice and SLO Escort Hotfix
body:
Graceful Isolation Lattice and SLO Escort Hotfix

Hotfix: introduce lattice-based tenant isolation to enable staged soft-shedding and SLO Escort to preserve priority during regional failovers. Backwards compatible; feature gated. Includes telemetry tags and fast rollback path.
Motivation: an incident (SUP-7890) revealed oscillation when tenants were abruptly evicted during partial regional egress congestion. This PR introduces a lattice-based isolation model and an SLO Escort component to make evictions progressive, observable, and reversible without violating high-tier SLOs. Summary of changes: 1) isolation/lattice_manager: new lattice state machine that tracks tenant posture across soft, probationary, and hardened eviction levels; transitions are timeboxed and instrumented with causality IDs; 2) isolation/policy_evaluator: new scoring hook that computes a degradability score combining token-rate, latency quantiles, and recent KV pressure; 3) sleight-of-hand SLO Escort: a lightweight orchestrator that carries SLO priority markers across routing/region-fallback decisions so we avoid demoting high-priority tenants during transient egress spikes; 4) telemetry: add slo_escort_{decision,reason} metrics and a traceability tag for tenant lattice transitions; 5) tests and a fast rollback feature flag (FF_ISOLATION_LATTICE) to revert to previous behavior if needed. Checklist: [x] unit tests for lattice transitions, [x] integration test for region failover path, [x] CI smoke validated, [x] telemetry dashboards added, [x] feature-flag gating and documented rollback steps, [ ] docs: expanded operational runbook (follow-up small PR). Risk/rollout: gated behind FF_ISOLATION_LATTICE and staged rollout to a single region for 24h canary. Related: ENG-2345 for long-term scheduler work and PM-412 for customer impact tracking. Links: incident SUP-7890, runbook: internal/runbooks/soft-degrade.md. Why unique: lattice model decouples tenant health from immediate eviction decisions and the Escort ensures SLO priorities persist across routing fallback so a regional failover does not cascade demotions.
Diego Marquez: Nice approach. Two questions: 1) how is the lattice persisted across restarts? 2) can the SLO Escort marker leak into logs causing PII risks?
Priya Anand: Answered - lattice state is lightweight and persisted to existing tenant-meta KV with TTL; added a migration guard to avoid heavy writes. Escort tags are opaque IDs and will not contain tenant identifiers; added an extra audit gate to the telemetry writer as requested.
Hannah Li: Request change - add a 5s debounce before promoting from probationary -> hardened to avoid flip-flopping. Also please add a unit test for the debounce window.
Priya Anand: Updated policy_evaluator with 5s promotion debounce and added TestLatticePromotionDebounce in lattice_test.go. CI green locally.
Arun Patel: Approved after the debounce test and telemetry tag audit. (LGTM)
SRE-Alert-Bot: flagged metric slo_escort_decision as low-cardinality; confirm acceptable. Priya: confirmed and documented in telemetry YAML with retention guidance.

title: Document KMS error taxonomy in code and logs
body:
Document KMS error taxonomy in code and logs

## Summary
This PR adds inline documentation and concrete conventions for how we represent KMS failures in logs and traces. The goal is to make triage consistent across services (control plane + data plane) and to ensure dashboards/alerts can rely on stable field names.

This is intentionally “docs + conventions + guardrails”, not functional behavior changes. It complements the wrapper work in pr-18421 and metrics/spans work in pr-18434.

Linked: ENG-4822 (taxonomy + metrics tags), ENG-4823 (wrapper).

## What changed
- Adds a canonical KMS error taxonomy enum (with mapping notes) and documents when each category is used.
- Defines structured log field names + required fields for all KMS failures.
- Documents how errors should be surfaced to operators (what’s safe to include, what must be redacted).
- Adds a small helper that ensures required KMS log fields are present when logging wrapper errors (compile-time references + unit tests).

## Canonical taxonomy (required)
When a KMS operation fails, the wrapper MUST map to one of these kinds:
- `AccessDenied` (IAM/principal/key policy; includes `kms:Decrypt` denied)
- `NotFound` (key ARN/id not found, alias missing)
- `Throttling` (rate exceeded / quota)
- `Timeout` (client-side deadline, upstream hang)
- `InvalidCiphertext` (decrypt fails due to wrong key/material mismatch)
- `KeyDisabled` (key disabled/pending deletion)
- `DependencyUnavailable` (upstream service error/outage; retryable)
- `Unknown` (fallback bucket; should be rare and triggers follow-up)

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

## Required log fields
All logs emitted for KMS failures MUST include:
- `kms.provider`: `aws|gcp|azure|other`
- `kms.operation`: `Encrypt|Decrypt|GenerateDataKey|DescribeKey|GetPublicKey|...`
- `kms.key_id`: stable logical identifier (redacted if customer policy requires; see below)
- `kms.key_arn`: when available; may be redacted/hashed in Private (configurable)
- `kms.region`
- `kms.request_id`: provider request id if available
- `kms.error.kind`: one of the canonical taxonomy values above
- `kms.error.code`: raw provider code (e.g., `AccessDeniedException`, `ThrottlingException`)
- `kms.http_status`: when available
- `kms.retryable`: `true|false`
- `kms.retry.count`: retry attempts executed for this request
- `kms.latency_ms`: end-to-end wrapper latency

Optional but recommended:
- `kms.circuit_breaker.state`: `closed|open|half_open`
- `kms.timeout_budget_ms`: configured deadline for the operation
- `kms.throttle`: `true|false` (alias for filtering; derived from kind/code)
- `trace_id` / `span_id` (already standard, but called out here because dashboards depend on it)

Redaction guidance:
- Never log plaintext, decrypted payloads, or DEK material.
- `kms.key_arn` may be considered sensitive for some Private customers; if `KMS_LOG_KEY_ARNS=false`, log a stable hash in `kms.key_arn_hash` and omit `kms.key_arn`.

## Implementation details
Most changes live in the shared wrapper package (doc + constants), plus small call-site updates to align field names.

Example (Go) mapping and logging:

```go
// kmsx/errors.go
// KmsErrorKind is the canonical classification used for logs/metrics/alerts.
// See /docs/internal/kms-error-taxonomy.md.
type KmsErrorKind string

const (
  KmsErrAccessDenied KmsErrorKind = "AccessDenied"
  KmsErrNotFound     KmsErrorKind = "NotFound"
  KmsErrThrottling   KmsErrorKind = "Throttling"
  KmsErrTimeout      KmsErrorKind = "Timeout"
  KmsErrInvalidCiphertext KmsErrorKind = "InvalidCiphertext"
  KmsErrKeyDisabled  KmsErrorKind = "KeyDisabled"
  KmsErrDependencyUnavailable KmsErrorKind = "DependencyUnavailable"
  KmsErrUnknown      KmsErrorKind = "Unknown"
)

// When logging wrapper errors, include the required structured fields.
logger.Error("kms request failed",
  "kms.provider", provider,
  "kms.operation", op,
  "kms.region", region,
  "kms.key_id", keyID,
  "kms.key_arn", maybeKeyArn,
  "kms.request_id", reqID,
  "kms.error.kind", kind,
  "kms.error.code", code,
  "kms.http_status", httpStatus,
  "kms.retryable", retryable,
  "kms.retry.count", attempts,
  "kms.latency_ms", latency.Milliseconds(),
)
```

## Files / areas touched (high-level)
- `pkg/kmsx/errors.go`: taxonomy docstring + kinds
- `pkg/kmsx/log_fields.go`: constants for log field names + helper to attach required fields
- `pkg/kmsx/mapper_aws.go`: expanded mapping comments for common AWS KMS errors
- `docs/internal/kms-error-taxonomy.md`: internal doc referenced by runbooks and dashboards
- `services/controlplane/*`: update log field keys to match conventions
- `services/dataplane/*`: update log field keys to match conventions
- `pkg/telemetry/conventions.md`: adds note about `kms.*` namespace ownership and stability guarantees

## Why this is needed
We currently have multiple spellings for the same concepts (`kms_error`, `kms.err`, `kmsErrorCode`, `aws_request_id`, etc.). During recent triage (timeout spike + throttling investigations), on-call spent time normalizing logs by hand.

Stable field names enable:
- consistent runbook queries
- reliable alert conditions
- dashboards segmented by provider/operation/region
- faster “is this AccessDenied vs throttling vs invalid ciphertext?” answers

## Testing
- Added unit tests to ensure:
  - taxonomy values don’t change accidentally
  - required fields are present when logging a `KmsError`
- `go test ./...` in CI

## Rollout / compatibility
- Backwards compatible: old keys are not emitted by wrapper after this change, but existing consumers should use the new keys going forward.
- Follow-up PR will update runbook queries and dashboards to prefer `kms.error.kind` + `kms.error.code`.

## Checklist
- [x] Document taxonomy and mapping guidelines
- [x] Define required log fields
- [x] Update representative call sites (control plane + data plane)
- [x] Add unit tests for field presence
- [x] Security review for redaction guidance

## Reviewer notes / discussion highlights
- Allison requested we explicitly reserve the `kms.*` namespace and list “required fields” vs “recommended” to avoid churn. Done.
- Sean asked to ensure `kms.latency_ms` is wrapper end-to-end, not just provider call latency. Clarified in docs.
- Ethan requested `kms.operation` be normalized across services (string enum). Added list of supported operations + guidance.
- Hanae requested we add a note: do not include customer-provided ciphertext identifiers in logs. Added to redaction section.

## CI
Checks: build (pass), unit tests (pass), lint (pass), staticcheck (pass).

## Merge
Merged via squash to `main`.

Co-authored-by: Caleb Johnson (review suggestions + trace field alignment)
Standardizes structured log fields for KMS failures and documents the canonical error taxonomy used by the KMS wrapper; improves on-call triage consistency and dashboard filterability.

title: kv: fine-grained age histograms and spill-horizon controller for low-fragmentation eviction
body:
kv: fine-grained age histograms and spill-horizon controller for low-fragmentation eviction

Introduces tenant-aware age histograms for KV cache and a Spill-Horizon controller that reduces unnecessary spill traffic under moderate pressure; improves tail latency and reduces write amplification during compaction.
Motivation: We observed recurring tail latency spikes and excess spill I/O on multi-tenant hosts during short-lived memory pressure bursts. The current eviction logic is primarily LRU-like with coarse tenant quotas and lacks temporal fragmentation signal, which drives premature page spills and frequent small compactions. This PR introduces two complementary subsystems: (1) fine-grained per-tenant age histograms (AgeBuckets) that produce a compact fragmentation/temperature fingerprint for each tenant, and (2) a Spill-Horizon controller that uses age distributions, recent spill latency, and global reservation headroom to delay or coalesce spill actions until an adaptive horizon is crossed. Together they reduce unnecessary spill churn and make eviction decisions more locality- and age-aware.
Local stress ran with 64 tenants (mix of 90% cold / 10% hot distributions) for 30 minutes. Compared to baseline main: - p50 eviction latency unchanged (~1.2ms), - p95 spill latency reduced 28%, - p99 spill rate (spills/sec) reduced 3.6x, - write amplification during compaction decreased 22%. Memory overhead for AgeBuckets averaged +0.7% of heap on a 512GB node and stays bounded via sampling and caps.
Includes unit tests for histogram updates and spill-horizon backoff; integration test exercising deferred spills under fluctuating pressure; stress harness script to reproduce multi-tenant bursty workload. Ran full test matrix (linux/cgo) and the new stress scenario in CI; e2e run in staging for 48h before merge.
Feature gated behind kv.experimental.age_histograms and kv.spill_horizon_enabled flags. Default rollout is off for Dedicated until 2024-06-15, gradually enabled for 10% of hosted clusters, monitor spill_horizon_defer_total and compaction_write_bytes metrics before wider rollout. If regression detected, toggle flags to revert quickly.
- kv.age_buckets.num_buckets (default 8)
- kv.age_buckets.hotset_sampling_threshold (default 0.01)
- kv.spill_horizon.base_window_ms (default 150)
- kv.spill_horizon.backoff_multiplier (default 2.0)
- kv.spill_horizon.max_delay_ms (default 2000)
Risk: deferred spills could temporarily increase memory pressure and cause larger tail spikes if misconfigured. Mitigation: controller monitors reservation headroom and forces immediate spill if headroom < 5% or free pages below a safe threshold; operator flags enable immediate rollback.
Ethan Zhang (2024-05-15): Nice approach. Two questions: (1) How do we bound the memory cost of AgeBuckets for high-cardinality tenants? (2) Can you show a before/after p99 spill rate for the synthetic tenant workload?
Author (Anika) (2024-05-16): Answered inline. AgeBuckets are compact (8 fixed buckets + overflow counter) and cached in a contiguous slab per-tenant; we also cap tracking to heavy tenants behind a hotset sampling flag. Attached results in the description show p99 spill rate reduced ~3.6x on our emulator for mixed small/large requests.
Luis Martinez (2024-05-18): Request change: make the horizon backoff multiplier configurable and add a unit test for the backoff path when spill latency is high. Also add a metric that exposes how often Spill-Horizon deferred a spill.
Author (Anika) (2024-05-19): Added config and metric spill_horizon_defer_total; added unit test spill_horizon_backoff_test. PTAL.
Priya Patel (2024-05-20): Small nit: please prefer steady_clock for horizon timers to avoid system clock jumps. Also please add a short ops note for ops to tune the hist bucket thresholds.
Author (Anika) (2024-05-21): Switched timers to steady_clock and added ops section in docs. Thanks for the review; addressed all comments.
CI Bot (2024-05-22): Build failed on macOS: missing include in runtime/batcher.h. (automated)
Author (Anika) (2024-05-23): Fixed include and force-pushed. CI rerun.
CI Bot (2024-05-24): All checks passed.

title: airgap: offline credential rotation + delta-OCI-index sync with checkpointing
body:
airgap: offline credential rotation + delta-OCI-index sync with checkpointing

Context and motivation:
We need a robust mechanism for rotating container registry credentials and synchronizing incremental OCI index updates in air-gapped/private installs without requiring full re-seeding for every change. Customers operating in highly regulated environments require periodic credential rotation, auditable checkpoints, and a minimal-risk upgrade path. This PR implements a coordinated approach across Terraform, Helm hooks and the installer runtime to enable: 1) offline credential rotation using sealed/rotated secrets and a short-lived registry token bootstrap; 2) delta-based OCI index syncing with checkpoint manifests and tombstone handling for deletions; 3) preflight/upgrade/rollback hooks to ensure atomic promotion of new content and safe rollback to a previously checkpointed state.

Summary of changes (high-level):
- Terraform: new module modules/oci-seed that creates a seed manifest and a signed checkpoint object for registries; IAM/ACL placeholders for customer KMS to unwrap sealed tokens in air-gapped environments. Adds variables and docs for rotating credentials during scheduled maintenance.
- Installer runtime: delta-sync engine (pkg/deltasync) that reads an OCI index delta bundle and applies it to a local mirror using a checkpoint manifest; supports tombstone markers for removed images. The engine persists a monotonic checkpoint file and offers an idempotent resume when seed jobs are interrupted.
- Helm charts: chart/airgap/templates/preseed-job.yaml (pre-install hook) seeds the local registry from a signed checkpoint and performs a credential unwrap using a provided sealed-secret. chart/airgap/templates/promote-hook.yaml (post-upgrade hook) performs an atomic symlink switch in the registry mirror root to enable instant promote/rollback.
- CLI/operational: new commands in installerctl: 'installerctl seed --checkpoint <file>' and 'installerctl rotate-cred --sealed-secret <file>' which are simple wrappers around the runtime delta engine and the KMS unwrap flow.
- Docs: updated docs/airgap/rotation.md and docs/airgap/upgrade-rollback.md with operational playbooks and troubleshooting steps.

Commits (summary):
- 7cd4f13 add delta sync engine skeleton + checkpoint format docs
- ef1a2b0 add terraform oci-seed module and variables
- c3d9e8b helm: add preseed and promote hooks, chart values for checkpointing
- 51b2a4f impl installerctl rotate-cred + integration test scaffold
- a9f7e66 handle tombstone deletes in delta applier and idempotent resume
- d48b417 docs: rotation and playbook for safe rollbacks

Files changed (representative list):
- modules/oci-seed/main.tf (new)
- modules/oci-seed/README.md (new)
- pkg/deltasync/engine.go (new)
- pkg/deltasync/checkpoint.go (new)
- cmd/installerctl/rotate_cred.go (new)
- chart/airgap/templates/preseed-job.yaml (new)
- chart/airgap/templates/promote-hook.yaml (new)
- docs/airgap/rotation.md (modified)
- docs/airgap/upgrade-rollback.md (modified)
- test/e2e/airgap/delta_sync_test.go (new - scaffolding with mocks)

Small illustrative snippet (helm preseed job environment):

  env:
    - name: CHECKPOINT_PATH
      value: /work/checkpoints/seed.checkpoint.json
    - name: SEALED_SECRET_PATH
      value: /secrets/registry-sealed.json

(This snippet is intentionally small; the full hooks are in chart/airgap/templates.)

Review conversation (highlights):
- Priya Kapoor (reviewer): "Nice end-to-end design. I'm concerned about KMS token unwrap being represented as a placeholder; we need a concrete example for AWS KMS and HashiCorp Vault in the docs. Also request a unit test that simulates interrupted sync and resume behavior."
  - Marcus Li (author): "Added an AWS KMS example and a Vault recipe to modules/oci-seed/README.md; added unit tests for resume behavior and an e2e scaffold to validate interruption replay."
- Elena Ortiz (reviewer): "helm hooks look good but ensure the preseed job tolerations and imagePullPolicy are explicit for air-gapped clusters. Also call out a 2-step operator flow in the playbook for safety."
  - Marcus Li: "Addressed tolerations and set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent by default for all airgap hook images; added operator flow with explicit 'verify-checkpoint' step."
- Diego Ramos (owner): "Please add a migration note for existing installs so operators know the safe upgrade window (seed -> rotate -> promote). Once added, I will approve."
  - Marcus Li: "Added migration notes in docs/airgap/upgrade-rollback.md and the release notes block."

CI and testing notes:
- CI: unit, lint and chart tests passed on first run. Airgap e2e smoke failed initially due to an ordering bug in the checkpoint writer (race). Fixed in commit a9f7e66; reran CI. Final status: build: pass, unit tests: pass, e2e airgap smoke: pass, helm-lint: pass.

Upgrade and rollback workflow (operator-facing summary):
1) Upload new delta bundle and checkpoint to airgap media.
2) Run preseed hook or 'installerctl seed --checkpoint <file>' to apply delta to a staging mirror directory. This step performs checksum verification and writes a new checkpoint file with a monotonically increasing sequence id.
3) Operator runs 'installerctl rotate-cred --sealed-secret <file>' (optionally scheduled) to rotate registry credentials. The sealed-secret unwraps via customer-managed KMS (examples in modules/oci-seed/README.md).
4) Run promote-hook (helm post-upgrade) or 'installerctl promote' to atomically switch the live mirror to the new staging content. If anything goes wrong, promote-hook supports switching back to the previous checkpoint using the atomic symlink method.

Operational caveats and security considerations:
- The KMS unwrap is executed in the customer's environment during preseed; the PR includes examples for AWS KMS envelope decrypt and a Vault transit unwrap. Operators in fully air-gapped sites must ensure the unwrapping credentials are provisioned on a jump host with appropriate audit controls.
- Checkpoint manifests are signed (simple HMAC by default in this PR) to prevent replay attacks; customers can replace HMAC with an asymmetric signature in their fork.
- The delta engine is conservative about deletes: tombstones are applied only if the checkpoint sequence matches expectations to avoid accidental mass-deletion on a partial sync.

Backwards compatibility and migration notes:
- The new modules are optional. Existing bundles without checkpoint metadata continue to install via the previous code path (full-seed). During upgrade the operator should run the preseed step manually on an upgrade window to populate the first checkpoint, then follow the rotate/promote flow.

Follow-ups (future work):
- Add GPG/PKI-signed checkpoint manifests and a trust store model for multi-operator environments.
- Support delta compression and upload resume for extremely large repositories.
- Add an automated housekeeping job to prune stale checkpoints and expired sealed-secrets.

Merge details:
- Merge method: squash and merge
- Merged by: Diego Ramos

If you want to test locally: follow docs/airgap/rotation.md; the e2e scaffolding includes a small mock registry and recorded checkpoints to validate resume logic.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps KMS provider implementations as examples (AWS/Vault) rather than integrating them into the core to avoid embedding cloud credentials logic in the installer binary. The approach uses small, auditable wrappers to keep the air-gapped operator in control.
Adds offline credential rotation and delta-OCI-index checkpoint sync to the installer. Backwards-compatible on existing bundles; see operator notes for upgrade sequence.

title: consolidate-release-indexer-and-rollback-manifest-generator-for-private-installer
body:
consolidate-release-indexer-and-rollback-manifest-generator-for-private-installer

Introduce a single release indexer and rollback manifest generator for the private-installer packaging pipeline. Motivation: current release metadata for private deployments is fragmented across per-arch Helm indexes, tarball lists, and ad-hoc rollback blobs which complicates automated upgrades and makes rollbacks error-prone. This PR adds a deterministic release-index.json format that aggregates artifacts (helm charts, installer tarballs, OCI blobs), provenance pointers (cosign signatures, sbom hashes, attestation references) and a compact rollback-manifests/ directory with incremental patches used by the installer to perform atomic rollbacks. Changes: - add cmd/release-indexer: builds release-index.json from CI artifacts, computes deterministic stable IDs, attaches provenance bundle references, and emits signed index + incremental patch files - add cmd/rollback-gen: produces rollback-manifests/<release>-<seq>.json that the installer uses to roll back a specific component set - update private-installer Helm chart values and templates to read release-index.json and prefer pinned artifact URLs when present - terraform/modules/s3-buckets: add new prefixing and lifecycle policy used to host both indexes and incremental patches - CI: new workflow .github/workflows/release-indexer.yml that runs indexer on build artifacts, cosigns the index, generates SBOM deltas, and publishes to release-buckets - docs: document index schema, upgrade flow, and rollback semantics - tests: unit tests for stable ID generation, e2e test that simulates an upgrade then verifies rollback-manifests apply cleanly Notes on implementation: the indexer computes stable IDs using a canonical JSON serialization and sha256 over (artifact URL, arch, variant, semantic version, builder-provenance). The rollback-gen ensures patches are idempotent by using a three-way diff against the previous index and emitting reverse-apply steps. Security: cosign signing and sigstore attestations are integrated in CI; the installer verifies signatures and rejects unsigned indexes unless an explicit permissive flag is enabled. Backwards compatibility: indexer emits a legacy-compatible shim for older installer releases that still read per-chart indexes. Migration plan: CI will publish both legacy files and the new index for two release cycles; a follow-up PR will flip the installer default to prefer the index. See linked Linear ENG-3482 for rollout milestones.
Morgan Lee: This looks promising. Two high-level asks: (1) show compatibility guarantees in the README (what older installers will accept) and (2) ensure indexer emits a stable canonical ordering to avoid churn in signatures.
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Added a compatibility section in docs/private-installer/release-index.md and implemented canonical JSON ordering using encoding/json with a deterministic key sort before hashing.
Diego Ramos: The Terraform change needs a short migration note for customers with cross-account replication. Please make sure the lifecycle policy doesn't inadvertently expire rollback patches.
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Updated terraform/modules/s3-bucket/main.tf to set a 90-day minimum for the rollback prefix and added outputs to opt-in to cross-account replication. Also added a test that verifies patches survive lifecycle prune.
Anya Patel: CI step 'sbom-delta' flaked in the first run; I see you added retries. Can we add a smoke assertion that the delta is non-empty for every meaningful change?
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Added assertion in ci/scripts/sbom-delta.sh to fail if delta is empty when version changes. Also added retries and exponential backoff for the upstream sbom generator.
Diego Ramos: Approved after Terraform migration note and lifecycle tweaks. Morgan + Anya approved once docs and flaky CI flakiness were addressed.
Repository automation: merge queued (squash) after passing checks.
Introduce deterministic release-index.json and rollback-manifests for private-installer; CI publishes signed indexes and incremental rollback patches. Backwards-compatible shim included; operators should read docs/private-installer/release-index.md for migration steps.

title: tooling/execution: concurrency safeguards and tool-result-injection ergonomics
body:
tooling/execution: concurrency safeguards and tool-result-injection ergonomics

Motivation: Customers integrating complex tool chains reported flaky outputs when multiple tools ran in parallel and tool results were injected back into the model stream. This PR standardizes execution semantics for multi-tool calls, adds runtime safeguards for parallelism, and harmonizes behavior with our OpenAI-compat surface. Summary of changes: 1) Executor: introduce a per-request "tool-parallelism" cap (configurable at API/route level) that bounds concurrent tool invocations and provides backpressure hooks to the scheduler; 2) Injection protocol: formalize a deterministic injection ordering when multiple tool results arrive within the same model turn and attach an idempotency token to each injected result so retries do not duplicate content; 3) Retry semantics: new retry policy enum (none, best-effort, strict-idempotent) exposed via the API and respected by the runtime and OpenAI-compat shim; 4) Streaming stability: when streaming responses include tool-calls, we now atomically flush tool-invocation markers to the stream and gracefully resume generation once injected results are committed to the KV cache; 5) OpenAI-compat updates: function-calling payloads now accept an optional "execution_hints" map with parallelism and idempotency hints that the compat layer translates into our internal routing and executor options; 6) Observability: emit new metrics (tool.invocations.active, tool.invocations.queued, tool.injection.latency) and traces annotated with execution_hints for easier debugging. Implementation notes: - Executor changes are confined to runtime/executor/* and api/handlers/tool_call_handler.go; the executor preserves the previous scheduling algorithm but applies per-request parallelism caps before dispatching tool workers. - Injection order uses a deterministic comparator: (request_tool_sequence, tool_priority, start_timestamp). This avoids nondeterministic interleaving in model-visible outputs. - Idempotency tokens are short-lived UUIDs persisted in the request context and kept in the per-request token-cache; replayed tool results with matching token are ignored by the injection layer. - The OpenAI compatibility shim accepts additional fields but falls back to previous behavior when execution_hints are omitted to preserve backward compatibility. Checklist: - [x] Design doc updated with sequence diagrams and failure modes (ENG-1523) - [x] Unit tests for ordering and idempotency - [x] Integration tests simulating multi-tool fan-out and parallel retries - [x] Metrics/tracing added and tested in canary - [x] Backwards compatibility verified for existing function-calling clients - [x] Docs snippet for API surface added Notes on tradeoffs: We intentionally chose a conservative default parallelism cap of 4 to reduce burst load on downstream tool services; customers can raise this per-route with a warning in the console. The idempotency token approach requires minimal state but does not protect against cross-request duplicate side-effects (we call this out in the design doc). Migration: No action required from existing users; new execution_hints fields are additive. For customers wanting deterministic injection ordering across retries, they should include explicit tool priority in their tool manifest. Rollout plan: Canary on a small percentage of hosted traffic for one week with annotated traces and enhanced logging; force-enable flag included to accelerate rollouts for enterprise tenants. Backwards compatibility: tests included to ensure older SDKs (OpenAI-compat) do not break. Risk and mitigations: The biggest risk is increased latency when a tool result arrives slightly after generation — mitigated by configurable timeouts and an async-fallback policy that allows the generator to continue with a best-effort placeholder if strict-idempotent is not set. Local testing: see integration test harness in tests/integration/tool_invoke_fanout_test.go. CI: all unit/integration checks passed after two reruns (flaky test fix in metrics). Merge outcome: squash-merged to main with commit 0a9f3d2 (executor: add parallelism cap + injection protocol).
Improves safety and ergonomics for multi-tool and parallel tool calls: deterministic injection order, configurable parallelism limits, idempotent retry markers, and OpenAI-compat layer behavior tweaks.
