Priya Kapoor: please confirm backpressure behavior when downstream is saturated — implemented queue with max-wait and documented in design
Lars Müller: small nit on naming (strict-idempotent -> idempotent_strict) applied in second commit
Alyssa Chen (author): responded — kept public API as 'strict-idempotent' for readability, normalized internal name to 'idempotent_strict' to satisfy both
Jordan Blake: approved after CI green
Priya Kapoor: approved with one suggestion around logging verbosity (implemented)

title: jurisdictional-sink-orchestrator: idempotent reconciler + terraform module hooks for private installs
body:
jurisdictional-sink-orchestrator: idempotent reconciler + terraform module hooks for private installs

Motivation: Private installations running in multi-region VPCs need deterministic, auditable wiring of audit-log export sinks per jurisdiction and a reconciler that is safe to re-run during installer upgrades and rollbacks. Current behaviour relied on imperative hooks in the installer which caused drift when upgrades failed mid-flight and made it difficult to guarantee retention policies in cross-region setups. This PR introduces a jurisdiction-aware sink orchestration controller and wiring hooks for the private installer + Terraform modules so audit sinks are created and reconciled idempotently.

Summary of changes: 1) Add a small long-running reconciler (go controller) that watches AuditSink CRs and desired sink mapping from the installer; it performs create/update/delete with strong idempotency guarantees and emits detailed audit events (sink-reconciler.* metrics). 2) Extend terraform modules with new outputs and lifecycle-driven hooks so the private-installer can emit a desired-state manifest into the cluster (terraform/modules/audit_sink/*). 3) Helm chart changes: templates now include jurisdiction labels, retention annotations, and optional lifecycle hooks to defer reconciliation until KMS/secret rotation completes. 4) Installer: on the private-installer side we add a declarative sink-write step that applies the desired-state manifest and waits for the reconciler to report success; this replaces the previous ad-hoc shell provisioning. 5) Tests and e2e: add deterministic e2e that simulates mid-upgrade failures and validates rollback idempotency and retention enforcement.

Checklist: - [x] Controller implemented with retries and backoff, idempotent create/update path - [x] Terraform module hooks and docs added - [x] Helm templates updated for jurisdiction and retention annotations - [x] Installer wiring uses desired-state manifest for reconciliation - [x] Unit + e2e tests added and passing - [x] tfsec and helm linting addressed (one warning suppressed with justification)

Deployment notes: - This is backward compatible: the reconciler will adopt existing sinks by matching labels, so rollout can be done with a simple Canary (deploy reconciler -> enable terraform desired-state output -> flip installer to use manifest). - For air-gapped installs the reconciler image is included in the private registry bundle; ensure registry credentials are present prior to enabling the controller. - KMS-backed sinks: reconciler respects annotated kms_key_ref and will wait for secret readiness before finalizing sink wiring.

Rollback behavior: the reconciler is intentionally conservative: on deletion it removes only sink resources it created or owns (ownerReferences + managed-by label). If an installer rollback is triggered mid-upgrade, re-running the installer applies the same desired-state manifest and the reconciler converges back to the prior state without orphaning temporary resources.

Related work and references: Linear tickets ENG-2147 and ENG-2153 track the reconciler and terraform integrations. See internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-2147/jurisdictional-sink-orchestration and runbook: docs/private/audit-sink-orchestrator.md

Why this is different from previous PRs: previous changes focused on retention lifecycles and sink rotation; this change focuses on making sink wiring declarative and upgrade/rollback safe at the installer and terraform boundaries so compliance operators can guarantee retention and export topology after any control-plane operation.
Marco Chen (2026-02-15): Left a few nits on logging and a question on backoff constants — please make them configurable via Helm values.
Aisha Patel (2026-02-16): Responded — made backoff and max retries configurable, added HELM values and documented defaults in charts/values-private.yaml.
Lina Gómez (2026-02-19): Confirmed adoption strategy. Asked for explicit adoption migration notes for existing installs — requested a migration step in the runbook.
Aisha Patel (2026-02-20): Added migration steps to docs/private/audit-sink-orchestrator.md and a verification script to tests/e2e/verify-adoption.sh
Evan Brooks (2026-02-22): Verified e2e failure mode test. Approved after minor comments on test timing; requested CI to re-run integration job.
CI Bot (2026-02-24): Integration e2e failed on first run (timing flake). Rerun passed.
- Add jurisdiction-aware sink reconciler for private deployments (idempotent, adoption-safe).
- Terraform module outputs to emit desired-state manifests for installer-driven reconciliation.
- Helm chart updates: jurisdiction labels and retention annotations.
- Installer change: declarative sink apply + wait for reconciler.
- E2E tests for upgrade/rollback idempotency.
The reconciler enforces retention annotations and respects KMS key readiness. New controller requires role bindings; installer deploys a least-privilege service account. TFSEC flagged a potential IAM scope which is suppressed with justification — see tfsec/suppressions.yaml for details. Audit events emitted by the reconciler include sink create/update/delete with operator identity for forensic tracing.
Canary rollout recommended: deploy reconciler in a single region, enable desired-state output on terraform for one tenant, validate adoption via tests/e2e/verify-adoption.sh. For rollback, re-run installer with previous manifest — reconciler will converge back. Ensure private registry image is present for air-gapped installs before enabling controller.

title: Normalize function-invoke headers and introduce tool-selection backoff policy for OpenAI-compat
body:
Normalize function-invoke headers and introduce tool-selection backoff policy for OpenAI-compat

Context: We need stronger OpenAI-compat behavior for function/tool invocation metadata without changing user-facing API shapes. Previously the OpenAI adapter sent ad-hoc metadata in the streaming envelope which caused downstream consumers (proxies and third-party SDKs) to misinterpret tool selection cues and header ordering, leading to flaky tool handoffs during scaled traffic spikes. Motivation: unify invocation headers so the compat layer emits a canonical header set and introduce an exponential backoff policy when tool selection is congested to reduce duplicate/competing invocations and improve end-to-end stability.
Normalize: canonicalize invoke headers and add header-v2 schema
Runtime: honor header priority when framing streaming messages
Policy: implement tool-selection backoff controller and tests
Docs: add migration notes and example payloads for clients
Tests: integration tests for backoff and header preservation in retries
Amit Shah: Can we avoid changing the wire header name for existing clients? Suggest adding a versioned X-Redwood-Invoke header and preserving the old one for a deprecation window.
Carla Nguyen: Addressed — added X-Redwood-Invoke-V2 and mirror to X-Redwood-Invoke for one release. Kept mapping deterministic so proxies can upgrade smoothly.
Lena Ortiz: Backoff parameters look sane but add observability: counters for backoff triggers and per-tool contention gauge.
Carla Nguyen: Added metrics hooks and dashboard snippet in docs. Also tightened default max backoff from 10s to 5s per infra feedback.
Marcus Lee: Integration test failed on first CI run due to race in stream_framer; fixed by moving header normalization earlier in the pipeline.
CI Bot: rerun required after addressing flake in stream framing tests. All checks passed on rerun.
- OpenAI-compat: invoke header schema v2 (X-Redwood-Invoke-V2). The adapter mirrors v2 to the legacy header during a deprecation window.
- Stability: tool-selection controller now backs off competing handoffs on contention to reduce duplicate tool invocations and improve routing stability.
- Observability: new metrics redwood.tool_selection.backoff.count and redwood.tool_selection.contention.gauge

Clients: no immediate change required. Optional: switch to reading X-Redwood-Invoke-V2 to obtain structured invoke metadata (JSON object encoded as base64). The legacy X-Redwood-Invoke will be removed after two releases; watch redwood-announce for schedule.
Backport to release/2025-11 required for some enterprise clusters using private deploy. The header mirroring avoids immediate client changes but operations teams should schedule client SDK updates to consume v2 cleanly.
Small CPU overhead (~1-2%) from header normalization and backoff controller; expected reduction in wasted concurrent tool invocations under contention, improving overall tail latency during spikes.
If you see increased backoff counts, check tool capacity and routing policies. Emergency rollback: revert the feature flag compat.invoke_headers_v2 and disable tool_selection_backoff via runtime feature gate.
Header v2 example: X-Redwood-Invoke-V2: eyJ0b29sIjoi/qa-tool
Invoke payload example in docs: {"tool":"qa-tool","version":"1.3","memo":"trimmed"} (encoded)

title: Improve stream teardown, retry/backoff and reconnect semantics for OpenAI-compatible streaming
body:
Improve stream teardown, retry/backoff and reconnect semantics for OpenAI-compatible streaming

Fixes a class of customer-facing streaming failures observed when clients disconnect mid-stream and then reconnect or retry. This PR centralizes stream teardown logic, adds an explicit session idempotency token for resume/reconnect, implements server-side exponential backoff for automatic retry attempts, and updates the OpenAI-compatibility adapter to preserve in-flight function/tool-call state across reconnects. Key goals: 1) avoid duplicate function/tool calls on client reconnect, 2) ensure server timeouts produce a deterministic terminal event that client SDKs can use for cleanup, 3) make streaming retries safe under load without amplifying downstream work. This is implemented as a small runtime change plus adapter and SDK patches and includes unit+integration tests and a controlled rollout plan. Migration notes: server behavior is backward-compatible for clients that don't use resume tokens; SDKs should be updated to take advantage of resume and idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate tool calls. Rollout: staged on Dedicated for 48h, monitor stream-error-rate and duplicate-tool-call metrics, then full rollout to hosted API.
Maya Patel: Can we guarantee no duplicate tool invocations if the client retries while the server is still performing the call? Please add a test that simulates a long-running tool and a mid-call reconnect.
Author (Jinsoo): Added reconnect_test.go that simulates a long tool and asserts single invocation; we also added a server-side in-progress marker to prevent dupes.
Carlos Nguyen: The backoff defaults look conservative; suggest 100ms base, 2x multiplier, 1s max for hosted. Also, add metrics for retry_attempts to make rollout observable.
Author: Applied suggested defaults and exported retry_attempts metric; documented in console alert playbook.
Ethan Brooks: OpenAI adapter event naming changed from 'done' to 'complete' in one place; keep both for 2 releases for compatibility.
Author: Kept legacy 'done' event emission and added 'complete' alias with deprecation note in docs.
Stable streaming: deterministic teardown on disconnects; resume tokens to reconnect without duplicate tool/function calls; server-side retry/backoff to avoid thundering retries; OpenAI adapter preserves function call state across reconnects; SDK updates available for smoother migration.
Clients that want deduplicated reconnects should upgrade SDKs to the patched release and use the resume token exposed on stream start. Existing clients continue to work but will not benefit from resume semantics. Monitor metrics: streaming.duplicate_tool_calls and streaming.retry_attempts during rollout.

title: ci: generate release graph and manifest validator for private-installer artifacts
body:
ci: generate release graph and manifest validator for private-installer artifacts

Motivation: CI for private installer releases lacked a machine-readable release graph and a manifest-level validator that ties signed artifacts (images, helm charts, tf modules) back to the release manifest. This PR adds a release-graph generator and a manifest-validator stage to the private-installer CI pipeline to ensure provenance, enable safer upgrades/rollbacks, and block unsigned/unaligned manifests from publishing. Summary of changes: - new pipeline step 'build:release-graph' which produces a directed release graph (JSON) that maps artifacts -> helm chart values -> terraform module versions and includes cryptographic digests and SBOM references; graph is collated from build outputs and attestation metadata - new pipeline step 'validate:manifest' that consumes a release graph and enforces: cosign signature verification (keyless and KMS), SBOM presence, chart values checksum, and compatibility matrix checks for upgrades - small helper library under tools/release-graph that normalizes artifact metadata, computes canonical digests, and emits signatures-ready metadata for the signer job - Helm chart linting rules extended to emit a Helm manifest fingerprint (stable ordering) and surface mismatches between chart contents and release graph - Terraform module manifest extraction to include provider pins and a short policy check to prevent unsupported provider upgrades in the same release - CI orchestration changes: the validate step runs before artifact promotion and blocks publishing to the release bucket on failure - added an automated delta-rollback manifest generator which creates a minimal rollback plan from the release graph when a canary fails Why this is different: existing pipelines stamp artifacts and upload indexes, but we need a top-level release graph that can be consumed by Private control-plane for deterministic rollouts and by on-prem installers to reconcile manifests during upgrades. This PR focuses on making the release artifact a first-class, verifiable graph rather than loose indexes. Checklist: - [x] release-graph generator implemented - [x] manifest validator implemented and integrated into the CI workflow - [x] cosign verification (keyless and KMS) wired into validator - [x] Helm fingerprinting integrated - [x] Terraform module extraction implemented - [x] unit tests for tools/release-graph - [x] e2e run in staging that simulates signed artifact promotion - [x] added docs for ops on how to interpret the release graph Changes included (high level): tools/release-graph/* (new library and CLI), ci/pipeline/build-release-graph.yaml (new job), ci/pipeline/validate-manifest.yaml (new job), charts/private-installer/patches/manifest-fingerprint.yaml (helper), terraform/modules/release-metadata/README.md (docs), scripts/delta-rollback/gen-rollback.sh (new helper), tests/integration/release-graph-e2e (e2e harness). Testing and verification: - unit coverage for release-graph normalization functions - integration test that generates a release graph from staged artifacts, signs them with a test KMS key, then runs validator (CI job uses real cosign verification in staging) - staging rollout run that exercised the delta-rollback generator after a simulated canary failure - CI history shows two failed validator runs during early iteration (missing SBOMs) which were fixed by the chart/lint rule update Rollout plan: - merged to main and enabled in staging for one week; manual gating for production release (ops approval required) - enable automatic blocking on validator failures for subsequent releases; until then validator failures are opt-in via release-note flag Migration notes: - existing release index consumers must be updated to prefer release-graph.json; a small compatibility shim is provided under tools/release-graph/bin/compatify - operators must ensure cosign public key or KMS access is available in the Private control-plane to verify signatures Security considerations: - cosign key usage requires KMS scopes; the validator supports both keyless (OIDC) verification and KMS-backed verification; by default validator rejects unsigned artifacts - SBOM presence is mandatory for private installer releases; policy can be relaxed via a per-customer policy file if needed Documentation: - docs/private-installer/release-graph.md added explaining format and how to use the delta-rollback generator - ops playbook updated with steps to manually validate a release graph Known limitations & follow-ups: - release-graph currently serializes all digests in SHA256; we will add multi-algo support (ENG-6780 follow-up) - we do not yet have an automated remediation when validator fails (ENG-6723 will track a retry/auto-fix job) Related: ENG-6723 (release graph spec), ENG-6780 (multi-algo hashing), SUP-3048 (support ticket where customer asked for deterministic rollback plans).
Priya Nair: Please add a note about KMS key rotation impact on old releases; we shouldn't make old releases unverifiable.
Marcus Chen: Added rotation doc and compatibility shim for cached public keys. See tools/release-graph/compat.md
Sofia Alvarez: Validator should surface which rule failed in CI summary. Added structured failure reasons to job output.
Ethan Park: Confirmed that helm fingerprinting is order-stable across helm versions; added additional tests for templating edge cases.
Ops (comment): We need a small UX doc for operators to inspect release graphs; added docs/private-installer/release-graph.md
Add release graph generation and manifest-level validation to private-installer CI. This enforces signed artifacts, SBOM presence, and compatibility checks before promoting releases. Also introduces a delta-rollback manifest generator for safer rollbacks.
This PR intentionally keeps the release-graph format backward compatible via a small compat shim. Consumers are encouraged to migrate to release-graph.json.
Follow-ups tracked in ENG-6723 and ENG-6780.

title: Add deferred-indexing RAG playbook and streaming tool-proxy adapter
body:
Add deferred-indexing RAG playbook and streaming tool-proxy adapter

Summary: Adds a compact RAG playbook that demonstrates deferred (background) indexing semantics combined with a streaming tool-proxy adapter for tool-calls.
Motivation: many production RAG pipelines need to accept writes (ingestion) while keeping the serving index stable; fully reindexing synchronously is expensive and causes visible latency spikes.
This playbook shows a pragmatic pattern: 1) ingest -> enqueue -> optimistic-serve from a hot prefix cache; 2) background indexer that performs incremental merges and emits cleanup/metrics; 3) a streaming tool-proxy that forwards tool calls to external services via a websocket-backed relay and exposes a local replay hook for offline tests.
What this PR contains:
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/README.md: conceptual notes, sequence diagrams (ASCII) and runbook for tradeoffs.
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/docker-compose.yml: minimal local stack (producer, indexer, redis queue, preview server).
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/examples/ingest_client.py: small Python client that demonstrates optimistic reads and enqueue semantics.
- adapters/tool-proxy/streaming-relay.ts: TypeScript websocket relay and proxy adapter used by the playbook.
- adapters/tool-proxy/README.md: integration notes for connecting external tools (auth patterns, backpressure).
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md: docs site snippet with recommended config flags for Redwood Optimize (batch/kv-cache hints).
- tests/integration/deferred_index_smoke.test.ts: basic e2e smoke tests for local run.
- examples/workflows/deferred-index-github-actions.yml: simple GH action to exercise the local smoke test.
Notable behaviors and examples:
- The playbook intentionally demonstrates an 'optimistic serve' where new documents are queryable from a short-lived prefix cache before a full index merge completes; this is annotated with caveats in the README.
- The streaming-relay supports an ACK/receipt flow and a fallback HTTP webhook mode for environments without websockets.
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md includes recommended Redwood API routing policy snippets to route low-latency reads to cached shards while background merges are underway.
Checklist:
- [x] Design doc and sequence diagrams included
- [x] Local stack + smoke tests
- [x] Adapter with replay hooks for testing
- [x] Docs snippet for console and Optimize guidance
- [x] Basic perf notes (cost/latency tradeoffs)
How to run locally (short):
1) git clone && cd playbooks/deferred-indexing
2) docker compose up --build
3) python examples/ingest_client.py --sample
4) open http://localhost:8080/preview to see optimistic reads
5) run npm run test:smoke from repo root to execute the integration smoke test
Implementation notes and tradeoffs:
- Background index merges intentionally batch writes with a small window (500ms default) to minimize merge amplification; the README explains tuning knobs for batch size and TTL.
- The optimistic prefix cache is TTL-based and uses sequence numbers to avoid serving uncommitted partial writes; we document consistency tradeoffs and recommended SLOs.
- The streaming tool-proxy was implemented in TypeScript to mirror many frontend integrators; a Python minimal shim is left as an exercise in the README.
Security: the adapter includes an optional HMAC handshake for websocket relay auth; README outlines how to replace with KMS-signed tokens in Private deployments.
Migration and docs site: the docs snippet adds a new sidebar entry under "Authoring -> Playbooks" and references Redwood Optimize recommendations (batching, kv-cache sizing) so that customers can reproduce the topology.
Related work: ENG-7291 (deferred indexing experiment) and PM-402 (RAG authoring patterns).

Sofia Patel (2026-02-19): Added a 'Tuning and SLO' section with numbers from our dev runs (see README).
Mei Zhang (2026-02-22): Tests flaked once in CI due to a race in the indexer startup; suggested a healthcheck-based wait in the GH action. See requested change.
Sofia Patel (2026-02-23): Added healthcheck wait step and increased retry timeouts for the local redis queue; reran CI.
Carlos Rivera (2026-02-25): Security review: HMAC handshake looks fine but add a short example on rotating keys; minor nit on naming in streaming-relay.ts
Sofia Patel (2026-02-26): Addressed key rotation snippet and renamed `relayClient` -> `toolRelayClient`.
Mei Zhang (2026-02-27): Approve after CI green.
Adds a new deferred-indexing RAG playbook demonstrating optimistic-serving patterns and a streaming tool-proxy adapter; includes local stack, smoke tests, and docs snippets with tuning guidance.
This example is intentionally opinionated; it's intended as a template rather than a drop-in production system.
Follow-up: add a Go shim for the relay and a small benchmark harness to compare optimistic serve latency vs synchronous indexing (follow-up ENG card).

title: Introduce batch-pattern compiler and compact quant telemetry
body:
Introduce batch-pattern compiler and compact quant telemetry

Motivation: Tenant workloads show recurring micro-patterns that are not well captured by the existing static batch templates. This PR adds a batch-pattern compiler that consumes recent request traces and emits compact, tenant-scoped batching templates plus a paired compact quantization profile telemetry pipeline so the Optimize layer can recommend lower-cost model variants without losing quality. Scope: 1) batch-pattern compiler service (server component and CLI to compile patterns from trace snapshots); 2) compact quant telemetry exporter that aggregates per-pattern token distributions and per-model quantization sensitivity metrics; 3) lightweight simulation harness used by CI to validate unit economics vs baseline; 4) minimal Console integration: a read-only API endpoint surfaces the top-3 generated patterns for a tenant. Implementation notes: the compiler is conservative by default (max batch-size delta +/− 20%) and emits safe fallbacks. The telemetry export uses a compact protobuf envelope and ships via the existing telemetry pipeline with optional batching disabled for immediate visibility. Rollout plan: staged deploy to canary tenant group -> 48h metrics observe window -> ramp to 20% -> full. Includes feature flag redwood.features.batch_pattern_compiler and a tenant opt-in tag. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-4572) - [x] Compiler server + CLI - [x] Telemetry exporter + aggregator - [x] CI harness and smoke bench - [x] Console API + minimal UI stub - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Docs: runbook and operator notes What this PR is not: it does not change default batching in production (only suggests defaults via Optimize), it does not auto-apply quant profiles without a manual review. Backwards compatibility: existing batch templates remain untouched; compiler outputs are stored under tenant preference namespace v2. Related work: ENG-4572 (design), ENG-5031 (Optimize integration), SUP-1209 (customer request), RFC-2025 (telemetry envelope). Risks & mitigations: risk of overaggressive batching -> mitigated by conservative deltas and canary. Risk of telemetry volume -> mitigated by compact envelope, sampling, and off-peak upload window. QA notes: simulation harness compares cost-per-100k-tokens and p95 latency against mainline presets and fails CI if cost drops >30% with latency increase >15%. Merge: squash. Release notes included below.
Diego Morales: Can we guarantee the compiler will not increase median latency for small payloads? Suggest a regression test in sim harness.
Alyssa Chen: Added a latency regression check to CI harness; compiler has a small-sample guard that forces fallback to tenant preset for payloads < 64 tokens.
Priya Singh: Telemetry envelope looks good but we need retention spec; please add TTL and sampling notes to runbook.
Alyssa Chen: Added TTL=30d by default and sampling config. Updated docs/oncall/batch-pattern-runbook.md.
Evan Brooks: Code looks good, minor nit on variable naming in compact_aggregator_service.go (renamed in follow-up commit). Approved.
Final approval after CI was green and bench smoke passed. Diego and Priya signed off after latency & TTL mitigations were added. Plan: canary deploy 2026-03-02, observe 48h, ramp per runbook.
Introduce batch-pattern compiler: generates tenant-specific batching templates and compact quant telemetry to enable Optimize to recommend cost-saving model/quant profiles. Rollout is gated behind a feature flag and tenant opt-in. No automatic changes to production batching; operators can review recommended patterns in the Console. Includes CI simulation harness to prevent regressions.
Feature flag: redwood.features.batch_pattern_compiler. Tenant opt-in via tag 'batch-pattern-v2'. Canary cluster and helm values updated in charts/helm/redwood-values-cost-telemetry.yml. Monitor p95 latency, token cost, and telemetry ingress volume. If regressions detected, flip feature-flag-off and rollback helm release.

title: unify-credential-modes-and-peekable-stream-iterator-cross-sdk-ergonomic-bump
body:
unify-credential-modes-and-peekable-stream-iterator-cross-sdk-ergonomic-bump

Introduce CredentialMode enum across Python/TS/Go SDKs, add a peekable streaming iterator to improve ergonomic consumption of chunked responses, harmonize retry/backoff presets, and bump SDK package versions to align with the new session APIs.
Context: Multiple SDK consumers requested clearer credential behaviors and a simpler streaming consumer pattern. This PR introduces a small, explicit CredentialMode enum (AUTO|PINNED|DELEGATED) across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs, harmonizes default retry/backoff presets to match runtime SLOs, and adds a peekable stream iterator abstraction to make chunk-aware consumers easier to write. Motivation: reduce accidental double-refreshes, improve cross-lang parity for session lifecycle, and reduce user code complexity when implementing lookahead on streaming responses. Summary of changes: - Add CredentialMode contract and adapter in core session layer (sdks/*/session) - Implement CredentialMode-aware credential provider fallback chain with telemetry hooks - Add PeekableStreamIterator (py: IterablePeek, ts: PeekableAsyncIterator, go: PeekableChan) with small memory bounds and deterministic close semantics - Align retry presets and expose an ergonomic RetryProfile builder for advanced use - Add compatibility shim for Node backpressure (ts) preventing unbounded in-memory buffering - Update docs and migration notes and bump package versions (py 2.8.0, ts 1.16.0, go v0.10.0) Checklist: [x] unit tests for credential modes and adapter chains [x] integration tests for stream iterator under chunked responses [x] e2e smoke on hosted API against a Canary model [x] docs: cross-sdk migration guide and examples [x] changelog entries Impact: API surface additions are additive (new enum, new iterator helper). There is a recommended migration for advanced users who previously relied on implicit token refresh side-effects. See release notes for steps.
High-level: 1) If you previously relied on implicit refresh side-effects, set CredentialMode=PINNED to preserve behavior or migrate to AUTO with tests. 2) Replace legacy StreamHelper.peek hacks with PeekableStreamIterator for lookahead. 3) Update retry presets only if you used custom backoff - new defaults are safer for low-latency workloads.
Unit tests added for edge cases: stale token during long-lived stream, peek after close, concurrent peek+next races. Local fuzzing run (1000 randomized message boundaries) showed stable memory under the configured peek window. Manual verification: python example consumer using IterablePeek consumes first N tokens without needing to buffer the rest; TS sample shows backpressure preserved when piping to a writable stream. Go integration ran on a small Dedicated cluster and showed no deadlocks after the token fetch mutex fix.
Priya: Can we avoid shipping both Peekable and the older StreamHelper to prevent confusion? Author: Kept StreamHelper for backwards compatibility but marked deprecated and added a migration note. Liam: The CredentialMode.Auto fallback still triggered two refreshes in a race when the session lease expired; added a token fetch mutex in Go and a guarded promise in TS to serialize refresh. Diego: Request to expose telemetry tag for credential_mode in metrics; added tag and unit tests. Priya: CI flake on the typescript backpressure test; root cause was the Node stream draining order — added a small delay to the test and hardened the shim. Approvals: Priya approved after fixes, Liam approved after addressing double-refresh races, Diego approved with telemetry change.

title: introduce-guided-sprint-quickstart-with-local-probe-and-telemetry
body:
introduce-guided-sprint-quickstart-with-local-probe-and-telemetry

Motivation: provide a compact, opinionated RAG quickstart that teams can run locally to iterate on retrieval, prompt steps, and lightweight telemetry. The Guided Sprint quickstart is intentionally small: it demonstrates a stepwise RAG pattern (index -> retrieval -> refine -> tool call) with deterministic seeds and a local probe harness for reproducible smoke tests and telemetry sampling. This PR adds the quickstart scaffold, a tiny local probe that simulates user flows and emits simple structured telemetry, and a short doc snippet for the dev docs site.

What changed (summary): added quickstarts/guided-sprint/README.md with step-by-step setup, added a sprint.yml authoring manifest describing step contracts and assertion hooks, added probe/local_probe.py which runs deterministic sessions and records JSON traces to /tmp/guided-sprint-traces, added examples/simple-agent.ts showing how to wire Redwood SDK tool-calls and structured output checks, added docs/snippets/guided-sprint-embed.md with docsite copy and a short inline gallery, and added ci/quickstart-smoke.yml to run the local probe in CI smoke.

Checklist: - [x] Quickstart scaffold and README - [x] Deterministic probe with seed control - [x] Telemetry lightweight JSON trace format documented - [x] CI smoke job that runs probe (non-blocking, optional rerun) - [x] Inline doc snippet for docs site - [x] Tests: basic smoke assertions in probe

How to run locally: 1) python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate 2) pip install -r quickstarts/guided-sprint/requirements.txt 3) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=<key> 4) python quickstarts/guided-sprint/probe/local_probe.py --seed 42 --count 10 5) Inspect JSON traces at /tmp/guided-sprint-traces and run quickstarts/guided-sprint/validate_traces.py for basic assertions.

Telemetry and expectations: traces are intentionally minimal: each step emits {"step": "retrieve|refine|tool", "lat_ms": <int>, "tokens": <int>, "status": "ok|warn|fail"} and an overall session summary. The README documents how to plug the traces into Console by uploading the JSON or using the small adapter script included.

Compatibility: the example agent uses the public Redwood SDK patterns (prompts -> structured JSON -> tool calling) but avoids any private APIs. The quickstart is suitable for hosted and local flow testing; it does not assume Dedicated or Private deployment.

Related work: ENG-4123 (guided sprint quickstart), PM-988 (quickstart prioritization).

Notes: kept scope narrow to avoid maintenance cost: no new SDKs, no heavy telemetry backend integrations, CI job is opt-in and non-blocking to upstream e2e runs.
Arjun Patel: Please add a short code sample in README showing how to set deterministic seed; also flagged that telemetry schema should be versioned (v1) — can you add a minimal spec?
Maya Chen: responded: added telemetry v1 spec to README and a --seed flag to local_probe.py; left a note about future schema migrations.

title: Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace
body:
Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace

Motivation: In production we observed recurring OOMs and large transient workspace peaks for long-sequence (>=4k) generation and KV-heavy batched workloads. Previous work focused on per-layer checkpointing and arena sizing; this PR targets three complementary levers to reduce peak GPU footprint without changing numeric behavior: 1) interleaved activation checkpointing that staggers recompute windows to shrink concurrent activation sets, 2) scratch buffer coalescing that merges short-lived per-op scratch allocations into a reusable sub-arena, and 3) scheduler hints that adjust continuous-batching flush thresholds to avoid pathological peak overlaps with KV cache refill phases.

Summary of changes (commits):
- commit 1: implement interleaved checkpoint planner and unit tests (planner/ckpt_planner.{cpp,h}, tests/ckpt_planner_tests.cpp)
- commit 2: introduce coalesced scratch allocator and sub-arena lifecycle (runtime/scratch_coalesce.{cpp,h}, runtime/sub_arena.{cpp,h})
- commit 3: hook allocator into kernel queue; add allocator metrics and tracing points (runtime/kernel_queue.cpp, observability/metrics_registry.cpp)
- commit 4: scheduler hint API and continuous-batching adjustments (scheduler/flush_policy.{cpp,h}, api/scheduler_config.md)
- commit 5: perf harness & benchmarks (perf/bench_long_seq.py, perf/bench_report_24678.md)
- commit 6: address review comments, test flakiness fixes, additional microbenchmarks (various)

Files/areas changed (high level):
- runtime/*: new scratch coalescing allocator, sub-arena management, updated kernel queue to use sub-arena
- planner/*: new interleaved checkpoint planner for grouped layers
- scheduler/*: new flush threshold heuristics and opt-in scheduler_hint config
- tests/*: unit tests for planner and allocator, end-to-end perf harness
- perf/*: benchmark scripts and result artifacts
- docs/api: scheduler config doc and short rationale

Key implementation notes:
- Interleaved checkpointing preserves existing deterministic recompute semantics; it schedules which layers are recomputed together to minimize the live activation set. The planner uses a simple greedy grouping heuristic with a max-concurrent-activation target derived from a per-model profile.
- Scratch coalescing introduces a short-lived sub-arena that consolidates fast scratch allocations from kernels that previously carved many small temporary buffers. Sub-arena size is auto-sized from recent epoch allocation histograms and is reclaimed per-batch. The allocator implements a small freelist and uses 8- or 16-byte alignment to avoid fragmentation.
- Scheduler hints are opt-in via the scheduler_config and default to conservative values for existing deployments. When enabled, the scheduler slightly reduces continuous-batching accumulation when the planner predicts a high KV-cache refill overlap (important for chat/history workloads).

Benchmarks (high level):
- Long-sequence generative (seq_len=8192, batch=1): peak GPU memory reduced by 24% (median across 5 runs), workspace allocation spikes reduced by 38%. End-to-end latency unchanged +/- 2%.
- Standard throughput workload (seq_len=2048, batch=4): throughput improved by ~6% due to reduced fragmentation and fewer transient allocations; median latency improved 4%.
- KV-heavy batched chat test: mean memory footprint down 18%; lower variance in tail latency under sustained load.

Compatibility & testing:
- Numeric equivalence tests added for a representative transformer block; recompute paths validated against baseline determinism tests.
- New unit tests cover planner heuristics and allocator corner cases (fragmentation, sub-arena resize). Perf harness includes CI smoke checks; full perf suite runs in infra-perf job.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for planner and allocator
- [x] Perf harness & representative benchmarks
- [x] Observability hooks (metrics/traces) for allocator and planner
- [x] Documentation for scheduler hint configuration
- [x] No API/public surface changes

Review conversation (condensed):
- Jonah Reed: "Can you explain how this interacts with existing arena checkpointing heuristics? Will this ever increase recompute cost beyond threshold?"
  - Aisha: "Interleaved planner uses the same cost model as existing arena checkpointing; it adds grouping constraints to limit concurrent activations. In our microbenchmarks recompute time increased by <3% while peak memory dropped significantly. Added unit tests and perf samples to perf/bench_report_24678.md to illustrate."
- Priya Nair: "Allocator looks good but we should expose an escape valve for customers on tight perf SLAs."
  - Aisha: "Added scheduler_config.scratch_coalesce_enabled=false toggle and documented behavior in api/scheduler_config.md; default remains enabled for cloud internal images."
- Marco Silva: "CI perf job showed a regression on one long-running canary run (flaky) — can you add more robust warmup to the bench script?"
  - Aisha: "Added additional warmup iterations and retry logic; CI perf now passes consistently."
- Jonah Reed (approve): "LGTM, nice memory wins, tests and metrics look adequate. Approving for merge."

CI history:
- Initial push: unit tests passed, infra-perf job showed a regression on one 30-minute long run (investigated as a warmup issue) -> perf fail
- Followup push: adjusted perf harness warmup and fixed allocator edge-case -> CI rerun passed
- Final status: all required checks passed (unit, integration, lint, infra-perf smoke)

Migration/ops notes:
- No runtime config change required for existing clusters. Operators can opt-out of scratch coalescing via scheduler_config and should observe a short warmup where sub-arena sizes are profiled (few minutes under steady traffic).
- Added alerting: a new high-cardinality metric runtime.scratch_coalesce.retries indicates sub-arena resize thrashing; documented recommended thresholds in docs/ops/scratch_coalesce.md

Risk assessment:
- Low: changes are behind opt-in flags and have unit/perf coverage. The planner is conservative by default and the coalescing allocator falls back to per-op allocations if sub-arena cannot satisfy requests.

Why unique from prior work: Unlike prior arena-checkpointing or dynamic scratch PRs, this change 1) interleaves checkpoint recompute windows to minimize live activations concurrently, 2) coalesces many ephemeral small scratch buffers into a purpose-built sub-arena with auto-sizing, and 3) ties scheduler hints to KV-cache refill patterns to avoid peak overlap. The combination yields both lower peak and lower variance in memory usage for KV/continuous-batch heavy workloads.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI. Follow-up items created ENG-8644 (tune coalesce defaults per model family) and ENG-8650 (add telemetry dashboard for sub-arena heatmap).
Reduced peak GPU memory and workspace for long-sequence workloads via interleaved activation checkpointing, scratch buffer coalescing, and scheduler hints. Expect 20-30% peak memory reduction on typical transformer loads; no API changes.
Enable by default for hosted clusters v21+, opt-out available. Expect up to ~30% peak memory reduction on long sequences; monitor runtime.scratch_coalesce.* metrics.

title: Introduce per-turn microtimeline, cost-slab annotator, and alert-playback tool
body:
Introduce per-turn microtimeline, cost-slab annotator, and alert-playback tool

Motivation: customers often need to correlate per-conversational-turn latency spikes with exact token-cost patterns and the alerts that fired. Existing rollups show per-invocation aggregates but do not surface intra-turn hotspots or let SREs replay alert conditions against synthetic traffic. This PR introduces three complementary pieces: (1) a per-turn microtimeline metric set (lightweight per-token latency and kernel-path tags), (2) a cost-slab annotator service that maps token streams to discrete cost bands for compact storage and alerting, and (3) an alert-playback utility that replays historical traces against new threshold configs to measure alert churn and false-positive risk before changing SLOs.

What this changes: Adds a microtimeline exporter in the runtime that emits compact per-turn sparklines and per-token phase markers; a background annotator that consumes those streams and emits cost_slab labels (low/medium/high/peak) with references to kernel execution path and quantization profile; a new CLI/tooling endpoint in observability-playground that can ingest a time window and run an alert-playback to produce an AP/recall style report for alert configs.

Checklist:
- [x] Runtime: microtimeline exporter (sampling: deterministic 1:50 + priority hotpath overrides)
- [x] Annotator: cost-slab algorithm + deterministic hashing for stable slab ids
- [x] Storage: compact slab label + sparkline rollup schema migration (backfill support included)
- [x] UI: dashboard panels and sparkline widgets (draft)
- [x] Tooling: alert-playback CLI + HTTP endpoint for automated runbooks
- [x] Tests: unit tests for slab binning, end-to-end playback against synthetic traces

Related: ENG-2314 (microtimeline spec), ENG-2378 (alert-playback UX). See design notes: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2314/microtimeline-spec and a short demo notebook linked in the PR comments.

Notes on storage/retention: cost-slab labels are small (1 byte tag per invocation with 128-bit trace anchor) and can be downsampled at ingestion. Default retention for raw sparklines is 7d; rollups retained 90d. This balances debugging needs and disk costs.

Rolling behaviour: nothing is enabled by default for all tenants. The runtime flag is gated behind an org-config boolean and experimental in dedicated/private.
Ethan Park: Can we make the sampling deterministic per-invocation so debug traces are reproducible?
Maya Kline: Yes — sampling uses a 64-bit hash of (tenant_id, invocation_id) with a configurable modulus; added tests to assert determinism.

Ravi Singh: How will this affect tenant billing queries (cardinality)? Concern about explosion if we store per-token vectors.
Maya Kline: We don't store per-token full arrays by default — runtime emits 1:50 sampled vectors; annotator collapses to slab labels and a compressed sparkline (run-length compressed per-phase). Also provided a migration script and retention defaults in the PR.

Ana Morales: Alert-playback looks excellent. One UX ask: include a per-alert 'expected fallout' metric (how many invocations would have been suppressed by the new rule).
Maya Kline: Added that metric to playback reports and surfaced it in the dashboard mock.

Ethan Park (on CI failure): test_alert_playback.py::test_replay_noise is flaky locally; observed time-dependent flakiness.
Maya Kline: Added deterministic timestamps and mocked clock in the test; reran CI.

Approvals: Ethan Park approved after minor test fix; Ravi and Ana gave LGTM.
Added experimental per-turn microtimeline telemetry and a cost-slab annotator to summarize token-level billing into compact bands. New alert-playback tooling lets SREs simulate threshold changes against historical traces to estimate fallout and false positives. Gated behind org-config; enabled by opt-in.
If alerts spike after enabling cost-slabs for a tenant, run alert-playback against a 24h window to see likely causes. Use the microtimeline dashboard to identify kernel_path hotspots and consider enabling prefetched warmup for the route.

title: Introduce header probing + prefetch bridge for streaming tool-calls and structured-output OpenAI-compat adapter
body:
Introduce header probing + prefetch bridge for streaming tool-calls and structured-output OpenAI-compat adapter

Motivation: customers reported intermittent failures when using browser-based streaming tool/function-calls behind proxies or CDNs that drop or re-order custom auth headers. The failures manifest as aborted streaming sessions or tool-call rejections during the initial tool metadata exchange. This PR adds a small, backward-compatible probe-and-bridge flow that reduces the likelihood of mid-stream failures and clarifies the header contract for OpenAI-compatible clients.

Design summary: we introduce an OPTIONS-based 'header-probe' that the client MAY issue prior to establishing the streaming WebSocket/HTTP stream. When supported, the probe negotiates which of the following headers will be preserved across the proxy path: X-Redwood-Signed-Nonce, X-Project-Key, X-Org-Scoped-Token. If the probe detects header preservation issues, the client can use the 'prefetch bridge' endpoint (/_prefetch_bridge) which accepts the signed nonce via a short-lived POST and returns a one-time session token tied to the tool-call handshake. The session token is compatible with existing signing semantics and is safe to include in standard Authorization headers and cookie-based proxies.

Compatibility layer: to preserve OpenAI-compatibility we add a structured-output adapter for tool and function call handshakes. The adapter maps legacy header names (openai-internal-* and api-key variations) to our canonical headers, and normalizes nonce/signature frames emitted in stream chunks so older clients and proxies that split text frames do not lose signature context.

What changed (high-level commits):
- add header-probe controller and OPTIONS handler
- add /_prefetch_bridge token issuance handler (short-lived, single-use tokens)
- structured-output adapter for stream frames and legacy headers
- client SDK helper for JS (prefetchBridge helper + probe fallback)
- end-to-end tests simulating proxies that strip headers; unit tests for signature chaining
- docs and migration notes for the compat adapter

Files of note changed: api/http/probe_handler.go, api/http/prefetch_bridge.go, runtime/stream/adapter/structured_adapter.go, sdk/js/prefetch_bridge.ts, docs/auth/header_probe.md, tests/e2e/proxy_strip_headers_test.js, ci/config.yml

Testing and QA: added E2E tests that spin up a lightweight proxy that optionally strips X-* headers and validates the prefetch bridge flow. Manual test plan in docs includes: (1) browser streaming through Cloudflare worker that strips custom headers, (2) server-to-server streaming with preserved headers, (3) tool-call with function metadata larger than 8KB to verify chunked signature frames are re-assembled. Also ran perf microbenchmarks: prefetch bridge adds ~0.7ms median to cold connection establishment but reduces mid-stream abort rate to 0.02% in our proxy simulations.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind 'auth.probe' and 'auth.prefetch_bridge' flags. Default behavior: probe disabled, bridge available. We will enable probe gradually in canary clusters and monitor streaming-success-rate and auth-fallback-count in the first 48 hours. If rollout is clean, we will enable probe by default for SDKs with version gte 1.23.0.

Notes: this PR is intentionally conservative about token lifetime (30s single-use) and logs minimal nonce metadata to avoid PII. See docs/auth/header_probe.md for threat model. Related: ENG-1229 (streaming stability), ENG-1304 (auth header semantics).
Adds a lightweight header-probing handshake to improve browser preflight behavior, a prefetch-bridge to stabilize streaming tool/function calling in proxied environments, and an OpenAI-compat structured-output adapter that canonicalizes nonce/signed headers for legacy clients.

Author (Maya): TTL made configurable via config/auth.prefetch_bridge_ttl and validated in tests. Kept default 30s but added min=5s guard.

Eve Thompson: CI flake on e2e proxy test — looks like race in proxy shutdown. Suggest retry fixture. (comment)

title: Introduce sequence-length-transition-emulator and tail-amplification detector
body:
Introduce sequence-length-transition-emulator and tail-amplification detector

Motivation: existing synthetic workload runners focus on fixed sequence-length distributions or simple bimodal mixes. Real traffic often exhibits abrupt shifts in token-length distribution (for example, a UI change that causes prompts to include an extra context block) which can amplify tail latency due to cache fragmentation and kernel scheduling. This PR introduces a small, configurable suite that emulates sequence-length transitions and a lightweight detector that flags 'tail amplification' events during benchmark runs.

What this PR adds (high level): 1) seqlen_emulator: a runner that generates workload traces with controlled Markov-style sequence-length transitions (configurable transition matrix, dwell time, burstiness). 2) tail_amplification_detector: streaming detector that computes amplification ratio (p99_after / p99_before) and issues annotated events for the reporting pipeline. 3) integration harness: glue to run the emulator against existing perf-canary clusters and produce JSONL time-series for the reporting pipeline. 4) docs and example profiles.

Checklist: [x] emulator core + config schema, [x] detector + unit tests, [x] integration harness and example Linear job, [x] perf CI workflow that can replay saved traces against baseline, [x] docs.

Why different: unlike sequence-mix synthetic runners this tool models transitions (the temporal dimension of distribution change) and explicitly measures amplification of tail quantiles rather than just absolute p99. This helps identify scenarios where short bursts of longer sequences cause disproportionate cost/latency impact.

Related: ENG-7342 (perf-signal-detection), ENG-7561 (benchmark-suite-refactor). Also links to internal doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-7342/seqlen-transition-emulator (internal).
Marcus Li: please ensure the emulator can run deterministically for CI comparisons — request added seeded_sampler (addressed in d12a8c4)
Ritu Sharma: detector window length needs to be configurable and documented; suggested default values — added window param + docs update
Daniel Park: memory usage looked high when replaying multi-hour traces; optimize by streaming JSONL and reusing buffers (addressed in d12a8c4)
Author (Aisha): responded to all comments, added unit tests covering determinism and a small nightly replay job to validate detectors against stored traces
Adds a benchmark lab tool that emulates temporal transitions in sequence-length distributions and a detector that quantifies tail amplification; includes example profiles and CI replay workflow to compare amplification ratios against baseline. Useful for identifying bursty prompt changes that disproportionately affect p95/p99 latency.
New emulator + detector to surface amplification-of-tail events caused by rapid sequence-length distribution changes; integrated into perf CI with example traces.

title: add-constrained-retrieval-quickstart-and-cli-runner
body:
add-constrained-retrieval-quickstart-and-cli-runner

Context: teams building retrieval-augmented generation frequently need patterns for constrained retrieval (budgeted token windows, timebound indexes, and candidate pruning) to meet latency and cost targets. This quickstart provides a compact, opinionated template demonstrating windowed retrieval, candidate scoring, and a tiny offline CLI runner so engineers can iterate locally without provisioning cloud infra. Motivation: reduce developer onboarding time for production-practices that combine retrieval constraints, lightweight vector stores, and streaming generation. What this PR includes: 1) a new quickstart directory with README, step-by-step tutorial, and a minimal dataset; 2) an opinionated CLI tool (rust/ts shim) that runs indexing, constrained retrieval, and a simulated Redwood API streaming client; 3) examples showing SQLite+annlite and an in-memory L2 fallback; 4) telemetry hooks that emit compact probe events to the Redwood Console local adaptor; 5) a small eval harness and smoke tests used by CI. title: Unify session telemetry and introduce compact SDK adapter bridge
body:
Unify session telemetry and introduce compact SDK adapter bridge

Summary: This PR introduces a compact adapter layer across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that standardizes session telemetry envelopes, simplifies the streaming handoff surface, and provides a compatibility bridge so existing consumers can opt into the new ergonomics incrementally. Motivation: Multiple internal integrations observed inconsistent session envelope shapes, duplicated telemetry keys, and slightly different retry defaults between SDKs leading to confusion for platform teams and noisy alerting. This was called out in ENG-2143 and tracked as part of cross-SDK parity work in ENG-2199. Goals: (1) standardize the session telemetry payload and sampling keys across SDKs; (2) provide a minimal adapter that consumers can layer over existing session code to get the new semantics with zero downtime; (3) align retry default presets for streaming and token refresh so cross-language clients have comparable behavior; (4) bump SDK minor versions that contain the ergonomic API surface. Changes: - Core: new compact adapter module implemented in each SDK repo (redwood-sdk-python, redwood-sdk-typescript, redwood-sdk-go) and exported from the polyglot 'redwood' root package so examples can import a single compatibility shims path. - Telemetry: unified envelope format: {"session_id","span_id","sampling_rate","client_version","env_tags"} and a lightweight sampler hook. Existing telemetry keys are preserved as aliases for backwards compatibility. - Streaming ergonomics: introduced 'CompactSession.handle' API that wraps existing pullstream/pushstream handles and provides a small set of methods (start, pause, drain, handoff) with clearer lifecycle semantics. - Retry presets: converged streaming retry presets to 'aggressive' (low-latency, limited retries), 'balanced' (default), and 'durable' (longer tail, idempotent workloads). SDKs ship default 'balanced' to avoid changing runtime behavior for most users. - Version bumps: python -> 2.6.0, typescript -> 1.9.0, go -> 1.5.1. - Tests: added cross-sdk unit tests for envelope normalization and an interop smoke test that runs in CI job 'sdk-interop'. Commits: - 7b1c3d1: add compact adapter interface and shared docs - 2aa9d4f: implement telemetry envelope normalization + sampler - e3f8b2a: converge streaming retry presets and add presets test - 5c9f6a4: add TS/Go adapter implementations and examples - a9d2f11: interop smoke test CI job + fixture changes - d1c7b52: docs and examples for migration guide Files changed (high level): - python: redwood_sdk/compact_adapter.py, tests/test_compact_adapter.py, setup.cfg - typescript: packages/sdk/src/compactAdapter.ts, packages/sdk/test/compactAdapter.spec.ts, package.json - go: sdk/compact_adapter.go, sdk/compact_adapter_test.go, go.mod - root redwood: docs/sdk/compact-adapter.md, examples/compact-adapter/* - ci: .github/workflows/sdk-interop.yml Testing & CI: First CI run: lint failures in python (docstring/typing) and a flaky TS unit test. Action: fixed typings and tightened test timing assertions in 2aa9d4f. Reran CI: all checks passed including 'sdk-interop' smoke test on linux-1 and linux-2 runners. Performance: microbenchmarks against the prior streaming surface show median latency unchanged and p50 token processing within 3%; memory overhead from the adapter is negligible for typical session sizes. Review thread (selected): - Samir Gupta (review): "Good shape overall. Please justify the chosen defaults for the retry presets in the PR body and add a short note on why 'balanced' is default." - Lena Park (author): "Added presets rationale to the PR description and unit tests that assert behavior. Balanced chosen to prioritize low-risk migration: ~3 retries with jitter for transient errors, preserves prior median latency in our benchmarks." - Priya Nair (review): "Please add a short migration snippet in docs showing how to opt-in with existing code (hand-off example). Also, add a telemetry alias map so that legacy dashboards can continue to work." - Lena Park: "Added examples/docs and telemetry alias map. Updated release notes accordingly." - Ethan Cole (approve): "Approvals from me after CI green and docs added. Small nit left about one TS naming choice; not blocking." Merge details: - Merge method: squash and merge - Merged by: Priya Nair - Merge commit message: "unify(session+telemetry): compact adapter bridge + sdk bumps" Post-merge actions and TODOs: - Backported minimal compatibility shims to the 2.5.x python branch for a critical partner (follow-up PR tracked in Linear ENG-2261). - Monitor telemetry for increased span_count/alerts for first 48 hours (feature flagging gated rollout). - Follow-up: add migration helper that converts historical telemetry in the ingestion pipeline (ENG-2230). Why this is unique from prior parity work: previous PRs focused on individual SDK surface parity (handshake and backoff semantics). This change is a small-footprint adapter + telemetry unification that lets teams adopt new ergonomics piecemeal without large refactors. It also surfaces an explicit compatibility story (alias map + migration docs) to reduce operational flash.
Adds a compact cross-sdk adapter to standardize session telemetry envelopes and reduces SDK surface for streaming handoff; bumps Python/TS/Go SDK versions to align UX. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via feature flag.

title: converge-sdks-backoff-telemetry-ux
body:
converge-sdks-backoff-telemetry-ux

Context and motivation: This PR brings a cross-SDK convergence change set across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs to standardize backoff semantics, emit richer retry/streaming telemetry events, and smooth a few ergonomic rough edges in stream consumers. The goal is parity for default retry behavior (exponential+jitter with an optional max_elapsed config), clearer telemetry for upstream callers to reason about retries and resumptions, and small UX improvements that avoid surprising edge cases observed in recent incidents. Primary user-facing improvements: (1) unified default backoff parameters and an explicit opts.backoffConfig/BackoffConfig typed object in all SDKs; (2) new telemetry hooks that emit structured retry/stream events (retry_attempt, retry_backoff_ms, stream_resume_token, stream_graceful_fallback) which are lightweight and safe to enable in production; (3) TypeScript: introduce async iterator helper that returns a single unified StreamResult shape and avoids orphaned promise rejections when consumers bail early; (4) Python: contextmanager for streaming responses so that KV cache and network resources are deterministically released; (5) Go: connection pooling opt-in flag and graceful drain on iterator Close to reduce spurious reconnect storms during scale-downs. Non-goals: changing server-side protocol or adding new server features. Implementation notes and trade-offs: to keep runtime overhead minimal, telemetry events are emitted through the existing metrics bridge with a new compact schema (no heavy JSON payloads) and a per-client sampling rate controlled by client options.
