title: atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts
body:
atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows. This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer. Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics. CI changes: new pipeline job ci/pipelines/release-stager.yml validates packing/compression, runs signature verification, and performs a smoke deploy to minikube in under 6 minutes. Security: signing routine ensures reproducible tar order before cosign signing and inserts a small attestation with build-info and builder git-ref. Backwards compatibility: published archives include both packed zstd artifact and legacy uncompressed blobs to allow older private-installer clients to continue fetching if necessary; rollout plan includes a two-week dual-read window before deprecating legacy path. Testing: unit tests for packer and signature validator, integration tests for staged swap and Helm preflight, and manual canary in a staging VPC. Rollout: merge -> pipeline produces staged artifact -> run canary promotion job -> after 24h and monitoring approval, auto-swap active pointer for production. See release_notes for more details and migration steps.
Diego Ramirez: Great direction — two questions: (1) how do we guarantee the atomic swap across S3/GCS and avoid partial reads during swap? (2) can we keep a short-lived dual-read window by default?
Asha Patel: Response: swap implemented by an object-replace with versioned buckets and a linearizable head object; we add a small retry backoff (100ms) during installs to handle eventual consistency edge-cases. Dual-read window set to 48h by default configurable via TF module.
Sophie Nguyen: Can we validate KMS availability earlier? Helm hook runs a KMS health-check and fails fast; added unit tests for simulating KMS timeout.
Evelyn Clark: Nit: packer code needs a deterministic file ordering comment and a test. Addressed in commit 'test(pack): add deterministic-order test'
Diego Ramirez: CI failure on first run (integration timeout) — re-run fixed it and logs show transient minikube image pull issue. Verified in subsequent run. Approved after green CI.
Pipeline: release-stager (pack -> sign -> verify) passed; e2e minikube smoke test passed; linters passed. First CI run timed out on minikube image pull, rerun was green.
- Introduces atomic release staging: publishes a packed, signed artifact and atomically swaps the active release pointer in object storage.
- Adds deterministic packing and zstd compression for release manifests and provenance, reducing release size and improving upload latency.
- Adds Helm preflight hooks (pre-install, pre-upgrade) to validate cluster preconditions and abort unsafe rollouts.
- Upgrade tool now generates a deterministic rollback plan from staged indexes to make rollbacks reliable and fast.
- Backwards compatibility: staged artifacts include legacy uncompressed blobs for a configurable dual-read window.
- CI: new release-stager pipeline with minikube smoke test and signature validation.
Unit: packer deterministic order, zstd roundtrip, signature verify. Integration: staged swap + Helm preflight on minikube. Manual: canary promoted to staging VPC and monitored for 48 hours before prod promotion.
1) Operators: update terraform module for release bucket to enable versioning and object-lock suggested setting. 2) If you run on very old installer clients: keep legacy-read enabled (env RELEASE_LEGACY_READ=true) until clients are upgraded. 3) To opt into atomic swap immediately, set release_stager_enabled = true in tf module and run apply. 4) To roll back a staged release: use tools/upgrade/plan_and_rollback --release <name> --rollback-to <timestamp> which calculates deterministic steps from the packed index.
This PR is intentionally conservative about compression level to prioritize install speed on constrained customer networks. We plan to introduce optional higher compression for air-gapped distribution in a follow-up change.
If a production install reports 'manifest-signature-mismatch' after promotion, fall back to previous active pointer (stager.undo_swap) and open SUP ticket; artifacts remain in the staging bucket for forensic analysis.
installer: atomic release staging, deterministic manifest packing, Helm preflight hooks, and deterministic rollback plans (Asha Patel)

title: Introduce telemetry-gradient and cost shingle inspector for prompt-shape drift detection
body:
Introduce telemetry-gradient and cost shingle inspector for prompt-shape drift detection

Motivation: We see recurring low-signal cost regressions tied to prompt-shape shifts (different prompt lengths / role-token mixes). Existing token-level cost metrics show totals but do not surface subtle distributional drift across segments of the prompt. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a telemetry-gradient metric that tracks per-invocation changes in token-cost density across prompt segments (head/mid/tail) so we can detect gradual drift; 2) a 'cost shingle inspector' abstraction that slices invocations into fixed-size token shingles, computes lightweight histograms, and emits compact sketches for downstream aggregation and dashboarding.

Goals: - Detect prompt-shape drift earlier without full trace sampling. - Provide actionable panels in the Console to show which prompt segments and model stages (embedding/encode/generate) are driving cost changes. - Add tuned alerts for gradual drift (low-amplitude, long-window) and a higher-sensitivity alert for sudden spike in tail-cost.

Summary of changes: - telemetry/gradient: new metric generator in the observability pipeline. Computes per-invocation gradients between head/mid/tail cost densities and emits incrementally aggregated counters and sketches. - telemetry/shingle: shingle extractor that emits token-shingle sketches (count-min + percentile sketch) keyed by route + prompt-shape-bucket. Light-weight, safe for high QPS. - console/dashboards: new "Prompt Shape Drift" dashboard with:  * Shingle heatmap (fractional cost per shingle)  * Gradient trend lines (head vs tail)  * Attribution panels (by model stage and kernel) - alerts/rotation: new alert rules and suppression windows to avoid noisy alerts for stable seasonal prompts. - tests: unit tests for shingle extractor, integration test harness (synthetic replay) to validate drift detection and alert thresholds.

Backwards compatibility: instrumentation tags are additive; feature can be controlled by runtime flag telemetry.shingle.enabled=false for on-prem.

Rollout plan: - Stage 1: feature flag off in prod; enable for canary tenants (5%) with verbose sampling. - Stage 2: increase to 25% and enable dashboard ingestion. - Stage 3: global rollout with tuned alerting and canary auto-disable if cost overhead exceeds 1.5%.

Related: ENG-3412 (prompt-shape drift pilot), SUP-789 (customer incident that motivated tail cost alerts).
Evan: Can we bound the extra cardinality introduced by shingle keys? Priya: Shingle key is route + prompt_shape_bucket (3-5 buckets) + stage; we also apply reservoir sampling at 1% by default for high QPS tenants. Maria: Alert thresholds look aggressive for multi-tenant bursts. Suggest adding a rolling baseline with seasonal smoothing. Priya: Added seasonal baseline and a low-sensitivity 'warm' alert group; kept the 'spike' alert high-sensitivity. Samir: Nit: move constants to config and document default cost oversight. Priya: Addressed, moved to helm values and documented. Post-merge: Observability SRE to watch canary and adjust suppression windows on first week.
Added prompt-shape drift detection: telemetry-gradient metric and cost shingle inspector. New Console dashboard ‘Prompt Shape Drift’ and tuned alert rules. Feature gated; default sampling is conservative. Useful for teams tracking token-cost regressions tied to prompt changes.

title: runtime-validate-response-schemas-and-stream-rewind
align-auth-ttl-heartbeat-and-stream-facade-across-sdks
body:
align-auth-ttl-heartbeat-and-stream-facade-across-sdks

Context & motivation: Multiple SDK consumers reported subtle mismatches between server-side session TTL propagation, streaming heartbeats, and SDK-side retry/keepalive semantics. This caused short-lived production flakes where long-lived streaming clients were reauthorized unexpectedly or experienced silent stalls. This PR harmonizes the contract across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs: 1) explicitly propagate server-issued session TTL to SDK session managers; 2) provide an optional lightweight heartbeat/ping helper on streaming handles to keep ephemeral sessions alive without user-managed timers; 3) expose a compact consumer-facing StreamFacade that simplifies reconnect + backoff + credential refresh for most application scenarios. Work items completed: - Add session TTL propagation path (server -> SDK session cache) - Implement StreamHeartbeat helper with jittered pings and backoff-aware suppression - Introduce StreamFacade in each SDK with ergonomic defaults (auto-reconnect, credential refresh hook, graceful drain) - Add deterministic retry presets for transient auth failures and integrate into facade - Add unit/integration tests across tri-SDK CI matrix - Bump SDK versions (python 0.43.0, typescript 1.12.0, go v1.5.2) Commits (high-level): - 3a7f8d2: session: surface server ttl in session envelope and client hints - 7b21c4a: sdk-common: introduce ttl-aware SessionManager and TTL expiry events - f4d0b9e: py-sdk: add StreamHeartbeat and StreamFacade; tests + docstrings - d12e6b1: ts-sdk: compact StreamFacade, heartbeat shim, export types - a9c6e3f: go-sdk: session TTL handling and lightweight facade implementation - c8b0d2f: tests: add e2e streaming fixture to exercise reauth and heartbeat - e1b3f75: docs: add stream-facade quickstart and migration notes Changed areas (high level): - sdk-common/session/* (new helper & interfaces) - python/redwood_sdk/streaming/facade.py (new) - typescript/packages/sdk/src/stream/facade.ts (new) - go/sdk/session/facade.go (new) - sdk-common/tests/* (new cross-sdk fixtures) - docs/quickstarts/stream-facade.md (new) - changelogs/* (version entries) Review conversation summary: - Priya requested clearer guarantees around TTL semantics: author added explicit contract notes and unit tests showing TTL extension vs. renewal semantics. - Liam flagged potential race in the Go facade's reconnect path where inflight token rotation could be dropped; addressed by serializing credential handoffs and adding a small integration test. - Diego found a lint failure in the TypeScript heartbeat jitter implementation; fix included to use crypto-safe jitter on Node/browser. - One CI run initially failed on ts lint and py flake; author pushed fixes and re-ran. Approvals: Priya Rao (approved after test additions), Diego Martínez (approved), Liam O'Connor (approved). CI: initial run: fail (ts lint, py flake); subsequent run: pass across linux/macos/windows tri-matrix. Migration notes & developer guidance: - New StreamFacade is opt-in; existing streaming APIs remain supported. - If you previously implemented custom heartbeat, consider switching to StreamHeartbeat for consistent jitter and suppression behavior. - Session TTL is now delivered via session.envelope.ttl_seconds; SDK session managers will emit TTL_EXPIRE events to allow graceful drain. Testing & observability: - Added new e2e fixture that simulates auth server issuing short TTLs and verifies StreamFacade reauth flow. - Instrumented metrics: sdk.session.ttl_updated, sdk.stream.heartbeat_sent, sdk.stream.reconnect_attempt. Risk & rollback: feature is guarded behind a facade and opt-in defaults; can be disabled by setting facade: { enabled: false } in SDK config. If a regression is found, revert commit f4d0b9e / d12e6b1 / a9c6e3f depending on language. Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main after approvals. Notes on uniqueness: This PR focuses on aligning server->SDK TTL semantics and introducing a minimal heartbeat helper plus an ergonomically opinionated StreamFacade that collapses several previous extension points into a single, well-tested entrypoint for most customers. 
Unify session TTL handling and streaming heartbeat across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs; introduce compact stream facade UX and bump SDK versions (py 0.43.0, ts 1.12.0, go v1.5.2).

title: Seed synthetic traffic generator for demo dashboards (job + presets)
body:
Seed synthetic traffic generator for demo dashboards (job + presets)

Problem: our demo tenant Console views (usage, latency percentiles, error analysis, cost breakdown) frequently show empty/flat graphs right before a live demo, and the distributions look obviously “fake” when we do a quick manual warm-up. This PR introduces a synthetic traffic generator that continuously produces realistic, policy-driven demo traffic and emits the same telemetry path as real inference (usage + latency + error + trace hooks) so dashboards stay populated and believable. What’s included: (1) a k8s CronJob + ad-hoc runner that hits the demo org’s routes via the public gateway (not direct ingestion) to exercise auth, rate limits, routing, and fallbacks; (2) preset configs (steady, executive-10min, spike, rollout-canary) to cover common demo narratives; (3) a small library for sampling realistic request shapes (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming mix, tool-calling frequency, structured output schema usage) and injecting controlled error rates (timeouts, 429s, tool validation failures) without overwhelming the tenant; (4) guardrails to ensure this can ONLY target the demo org/project allowlist and cannot run against prod/customer orgs. Motivation: make the demo tenant resilient to “dashboard emptiness” and give SEs a one-command way to warm up the tenant prior to a call, while also generating data that makes cost/latency tradeoffs and reliability/fallback flows visible in the Console. Rollout plan: merge behind DEMO_SYNTH_TRAFFIC_ENABLED, enable in demo env only, then let SRE tune the default schedule/caps after a week of observation.
Traffic is generated via the same public gateway path used by the demo app (so we get auth, quotas, routing, retries, and streaming behavior); requests are labeled with `x-redwood-traffic-source: demo_synth` and scenario tags (scenario=steady|spike|rollout_canary, feature=streaming|tool_calling|structured_output, region=us-east|eu-west). Presets control: QPS target + jitter, streaming ratio, model mix weights, token length distributions, tool-call rate, structured output schema selection, and “controlled failure” knobs. Guardrails: hard allowlist on org_id + project_id, environment check (must be DEMO env), and a max spend cap per hour (tokens + embeddings units) with immediate stop on breach. The CronJob uses a dedicated service account with egress restricted to the gateway; it does not have permissions to call internal admin endpoints.
Unit: distribution sampling (p50/p95 bounds), config parsing, allowlist enforcement; Integration (staging): `rw demo traffic run --preset executive-10min --dry-run=false` against staging demo org, verified dashboards populate within ~2–4 minutes; Load sanity: steady preset capped to avoid triggering 429s (unless explicitly enabled via spike preset).
Logan Wright: Can we confirm these events follow the same aggregation windows as real traffic? If we’re tagging them, we should make sure dashboards default include them (or at least demo views do).
Mei Lin (author): Yep—these are real gateway requests, so telemetry is emitted through the normal pipeline. I added `source=demo_synth` as a tag, but dashboards are not filtering it out. We can add a future improvement to let Console toggle “exclude synthetic”.
Chloe Martin: Please avoid creating new “special” ingestion paths. Looks like this is using gateway, which is good. One concern: structured-output scenario should not depend on any flaky schema validation service; can we keep it self-contained?
Mei Lin (author): Agreed. Structured output uses inline JSON schema and validates locally in the runner (and still sends the schema in the request). No external dependency besides the inference route.
Allison Grant: For the spike preset, can we ensure it doesn’t page us by default? We should route alerts for demo env separately, but until that’s fully in place I’d prefer spike preset disabled unless explicitly run.
Mei Lin (author): Updated presets: CronJob only runs steady; spike preset is manual-only via CLI and has an explicit `--i-understand-this-may-trigger-alerts` confirmation gate.
Sean Gallagher: Add a hard cap to prevent runaway spend if someone bumps QPS. Also, if gateway returns 401/403 (key rotated), runner should fail fast and surface a crisp error message.
Mei Lin (author): Added `max_tokens_per_hour` + `max_requests_per_run` caps and fail-fast on auth errors with a remediation message pointing to the key rotation runbook. Also added a health summary at end of run.
Markus Klein: This is exactly what the SE team needs. Please include a quick-start snippet for ‘dashboards empty’ so we can paste into Slack during a panic.
Mei Lin (author): Added `docs/internal/demo/demo-dashboards-warmup.md` with a 30-second copy/paste section and expected time-to-first-graph.
Merged via squash into main; follow-up task: tune CronJob schedule and caps after observing a week of demo usage (ENG-4879 alerts will land separately).
Internal-only: Demo environment now has a synthetic traffic generator (CronJob + CLI) to keep Console dashboards populated with realistic distributions; supports presets for steady traffic and common demo narratives.

title: Introduce RBAC anomaly detector, KMS usage ledger, and jurisdictional pin gate
body:
Introduce RBAC anomaly detector, KMS usage ledger, and jurisdictional pin gate

Motivation: customers operating in regulated jurisdictions require stronger evidence about access decisions and KMS usage, plus automated detection of unusual privilege changes. This PR adds three coordinated pieces: 1) an RBAC Anomaly Detector that samples policy decisions and surfaces statistical deviations (new service + control plane telemetry), 2) a KMS Usage Ledger that records per-tenant, per-key KMS call metadata for non-repudiable audit and residency verification, and 3) a Jurisdictional Pin Gate that enforces region-pin policies at the KMS allocation layer and emits canonical audit events for downstream compliance pipelines. The goals are: reduce investigation time for policy breaches, provide provable KMS usage trails for compliance audits, and enforce region pin constraints at the decision point to avoid accidental cross-region key use. Changes in this PR touch: policy evaluation path, audit forwarder, KMS allocation middleware, migrations for the ledger schema, the console telemetry surface, and operator-facing rollout flags. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-9485) - [x] Unit + integration tests for policy sampler - [x] Ledger write path is idempotent and signed - [x] Backwards-compatible migration and feature flag - [x] Console telemetry panels added - [x] e2e scenario for region-pin enforcement (simulated cross-region request) Backwards compatibility: the anomaly detector is opt-in and behind "rbac_anomaly_enabled" feature flag. KMS ledger writes are opt-in per-tenant until a migration window closes. Rollout plan: gradual enablement by tenant cohort, tie ledger writes to audit retention throttles, monitor error rates and key write latency. See commits for incremental scope and the review thread for design clarifications.
Liam Nguyen (2025-02-13): Nice direction. Two asks: (1) how do we bound false positives for the anomaly detector so SRE doesn't get paged? (2) ledger writes need to be resilient to transient DB errors. Can you add backoff and non-blocking fallback?
Aisha Patel (2025-02-13): Replied: added exponential backoff + circuit breaker for ledger writes, detector uses an adjustable baseline window and an anomaly-confidence threshold; default is conservative (only P>0.999 alerts). Added config to route low-confidence alerts to a noiseless 'review' stream instead of pages.
Sofia Alvarez (2025-02-14): We need a clear privacy/legal review for storing KMS call metadata. Please ensure tenant opt-in and a data-retention TTL per-tenant. Also: mandate KMS key-id hashing before storing any identifier in non-secure stores.
Aisha Patel (2025-02-15): Replied: implemented per-tenant opt-in flag, retention TTL, and HMAC-prefix hashing of key IDs before writing to ledger. Sensitive raw IDs are only stored in the sealed PostgreSQL column encrypted with CMK; non-sensitive indexes use hashed prefixes.
Marcus Reed (2025-02-16): Test comment: e2e simulated tenant with region pin should reject cross-region KMS allocation and emit a signed audit event; test flaked once in CI (timing).
Aisha Patel (2025-02-16): Flakiness debug: extended the test timeout and added an eventual consistency assertion for the fanout queue. Reran locally and CI.
Liam Nguyen (2025-02-18): Approve after nit fixes.
Sofia Alvarez (2025-02-19): Approve. Note: legal signoff attached to the Linear ticket SEC-223.
Added opt-in RBAC anomaly detection service, per-tenant KMS usage ledger for verifiable audit trails, and a jurisdictional pin gate preventing KMS allocations across pinned regions. Feature is behind flags; see docs/compliance/kms_ledger_guide.md for tenant opt-in, retention controls, and migration steps.

title: Introduce first-class lease auth profiles, named retry flavors, and pullstream clarifications across SDKs
body:
Introduce first-class lease auth profiles, named retry flavors, and pullstream clarifications across SDKs

Context and motivation: We've received recurring feedback that SDK consumers want an explicit, ergonomic concept for short-lived auth leases, and a small set of named retry profiles that can be wire-mapped across Python/TS/Go to avoid subtle divergence. This PR introduces a lightweight 'lease' lifecycle API (acquire/renew/release/annotate) and a compact mapping of retry 'flavors' (optimistic, balanced, aggressive) that the SDKs expose in parity. It also clarifies pullstream semantics: deprecates the older opaque resume-token surface in favor of a checkpoint cursor and documents recommended migration paths.

What this changes (high level):
- Adds a Lease abstraction to SDK core (py/ts/go) + low-overhead heartbeat shim for long-running streams.
- Introduces named retry flavors and a small declarative adapter so platform defaults can be propagated across languages.
- Pullstream: replace ResumeToken v1 surface with CheckpointCursor v2; provide compat shim that translates legacy tokens at runtime to minimize breakage.
- Adds cross-sdk integration tests that exercise lease renewals during streaming disconnects.
- Minor telemetry/metrics labels to differentiate lease renewals vs token refreshes for cost/ops visibility.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked, [x] unit tests added, [x] cross-sdk integration tests, [x] update changelogs/versions, [x] migration notes for users.

Migration notes: docs/sdk/migration/lease-and-checkpoint.md

title: introduce-reservoir-based-decentralized-scale-synthesizer
body:
introduce-reservoir-based-decentralized-scale-synthesizer

Motivation: production fleets see many short-lived microbursts from tenant traffic patterns which cause oscillatory autoscaling and wasted headroom. This PR implements a lightweight reservoir-based "decentralized scale synthesizer" that runs alongside the existing autoscaler to smooth short spikes while preserving throughput guarantees and predictable tail latency. Design summary: 1) each node maintains a small local reservoir credit accounting window that decays over time and is topped up by observed idle capacity; 2) the synthesizer aggregates ephemeral credits across replicas via a gossip-style delta protocol to create a soft, decentralized pool without a central control plane lock; 3) scaling decisions use a two-stage policy: local fast-path uses reservoir credits to accept short bursts without triggering scale-up, while the slow-path falls back to the cluster autoscaler when sustained demand exceeds reservoir thresholds. Key properties: bounded amplification (reservoir caps per-tenant and per-node), graceful decay to avoid persistent overcommit, and deterministic backoff in preemption scenarios. Telemetry and observability: added reservoir inflow/outflow metrics, reservoir_utilization_percentile by tenant, reservoir_credit_evictions, and a debug endpoint to snapshot local reservoir state. Feature flags: env FLAG_RESERVOIR_SYNTHETIC=true enables the synthesizer and FLAG_RESERVOIR_GOSSIP controls gossip interval. Backwards compatibility: autoscaler API unchanged, synthesizer registers as an optional operator. Rollout plan: gated behind feature flags, start with canary on dedicated fleets for low-risk tenants, monitor latency and headroom burn rates for 72 hours, then progressive rollout. Tests: unit tests for credit accounting and gossip reconciliation, integration tests simulating mixed-duration microbursts, and a synthetic benchmark showing 18% reduction in unnecessary scale-ups and 12% lower 99th percentile latency for bursty workloads in our lab. Risk and mitigations: gossip divergence detected in tests fixed by introducing monotonic vector clocks and periodic full-state reconciliation. Migration notes: no live migration required; operators can toggle off to immediately disable accepting reservoir credits. See docs/design/reservoir-synthesizer.md for detailed algorithms and math. Checklist: - [x] design doc - [x] unit tests - [x] integration tests - [x] telemetry dashboards - [x] canary rollout plan
Daniel Kim: 'Can you elaborate on how vector clocks prevent split-brain in high churn clusters?' Author: 'Vector clocks are scoped to reservoir deltas and we only accept deltas with monotonically increasing sequence numbers per node; in practice this prevents applying stale negative deltas. We also fallback to full-state reconciliation on mismatch which is in the implementation.' Priya Shah: 'Need a clear knob to stop credit acceptance per-tenant for compliance customers.' Author: 'Added per-tenant opt-out via tenant metadata and feature flag checks in the admission fast-path.' Connor Lee: 'Telemetry looks good but add a gauge for reservoir headroom impact on node memory to catch leaks.' Author: 'Added reservoir_memory_bytes metric and a unit test around memory reset after reconciliation.' After fixes reviewers approved and requested squash merge.
CI pipeline: unit tests (pass), lint (pass), integration (initially failed due to timing flake in reservoir_scaling_test, fixed by adding deterministic clocks and retry backoff) rerun (pass), e2e benchmark optional job (pass). Total CI duration ~34m.
Add optional reservoir-based decentralized synthesizer to smooth short-duration bursts and reduce unnecessary autoscaler churn. Enabled via FLAG_RESERVOIR_SYNTHETIC. Recommended for bursty workloads on Dedicated fleets. Non-breaking; opt-in behind feature flags.

title: Introduce hierarchical smoke-sampler and late-fail attenuator CI hook
body:
Introduce hierarchical smoke-sampler and late-fail attenuator CI hook

Motivation: intermittent prompt-set failures (spikes driven by small cohorts) are causing noisy CI alerts and unnecessary rollbacks. This PR adds a hierarchical smoke-sampler that builds a two-tier sampling plan (cohort-level followed by intra-cohort sampling) to increase coverage of high-variance prompt families while keeping smoke evaluation budgets bounded. It also introduces a late-fail attenuator CI hook that downweights isolated failures that occur late in a sliding window and only escalates when failure weight persists across windows. Design: sampler computes cohort disruption scores using historical eval variance and recent error-rate deltas; top-K cohorts are sampled proportionally to disruption with a minimum floor to avoid starvation. The attenuator consumes per-prompt failure history and a tunable half-life to compute an effective failure weight; single-window blips are suppressed, sustained deviations trigger the existing quality gate. Rollout plan: feature-flagged in CI config, dry-run for two weeks producing annotation-only reports, then opt-in for branch protection gating. Tests: unit tests for sampler statistics, integration scenario with synthetic prompt drift, end-to-end CI scenario recorded in artifacts. Checklist: implement sampler and hook, add feature flag, tests, docs and examples, update alerting thresholds. Adds hierarchical smoke-sampler to prioritize prompt cohorts by disruption score; introduces late-fail attenuator CI hook to avoid escalating one-off intermittent failures while still surfacing persistent regressions; includes unit+integration tests and docs; rollout behind feature flag; no immediate production gating change unless enabled.

title: Add shared KMS client abstraction with explicit timeouts + standardized retries
body:
Add shared KMS client abstraction with explicit timeouts + standardized retries

Summary: Introduces a shared KMS client abstraction used across control-plane + data-plane services to standardize timeouts, retries/backoff, and error mapping. The current KMS call sites implement timeouts inconsistently (or not at all) and several retry policies amplify load during provider-side latency spikes, which contributed to elevated 5xx during throttling events.

Key goals: - Make KMS dependency behavior predictable (bounded latency, bounded retries) - Provide a canonical error taxonomy for downstream policy (circuit breaker + degrade-mode followups) - Improve observability: metrics + structured log fields to enable on-call triage

Scope of this PR: - New library package `pkg/kmsclient` with:   - explicit deadlines for Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/DescribeKey (per-operation defaults)   - retry policy w/ exponential backoff + jitter and a hard retry budget (max attempts and max elapsed)   - structured error mapping into a small set of categories (Timeout, Throttled, AccessDenied, NotFound, InvalidCiphertext, Internal, Unknown) - Minimal integration in two representative services to prove wiring + config surface (more migrations tracked in ENG-4823) - Adds unit tests for error mapping + retry budget behavior and a small fake KMS transport for deterministic tests

Non-goals: - Circuit breaker and degrade behavior (follow-up ENG-4824) - Metrics/tracing spans (follow-up PR; this keeps the wrapper API stable first) - Rotation / dual-read (ADR-008 work)

Configuration: - Defaults are conservative and aimed at production safety. Services can override via config, but values are validated and clamped to safe ranges in a later PR (ENG-4823 subtask). - Default budgets (v1):   - Encrypt/GenerateDataKey: timeout 2s, max attempts 3, max elapsed 3s   - Decrypt: timeout 2s, max attempts 2, max elapsed 2.5s (intentionally tighter to avoid fan-out storms) - Retryable errors: network timeouts, 5xx from provider SDK, explicit Throttling/RateExceeded

Error mapping: - Wrapper returns `KmsError` with fields: `category`, `provider_code`, `provider_message`, `is_retryable`, `request_id` (when available) - Logs should include: `kms.op`, `kms.category`, `kms.provider_code`, `kms.request_id`

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping (AWS-style error codes), retry budget accounting, and jitter range (non-deterministic aspects bounded via seeded RNG) - Adds a small integration-ish test using the fake transport to simulate throttle then success and assert we do not exceed max elapsed

Rollout plan: - Land wrapper, then migrate call sites incrementally behind a service-level config toggle where practical - SRE requested we ship metrics prior to broad rollout; follow-up PR will add `kms_client_latency_ms` histogram and `kms_client_errors_total` counter with tags

Refs: - Linear: ENG-4823 (wrapper), ENG-4822 (taxonomy) - Related support context: SUP-19377 (throttling leading to elevated 5xx) - ADR-007 draft in review (this PR implements the proposed API surface; final knobs may adjust slightly)

Screenshots / logs: - Example structured log emitted by wrapper on AccessDenied: `{"msg":"kms call failed","kms.op":"Decrypt","kms.category":"AccessDenied","kms.provider_code":"AccessDeniedException","kms.request_id":"2a4f...","err":"kms: access denied"}`

Checklist: - [x] Bounded timeouts for all KMS operations used in codebase today - [x] Standard retry policy with jitter - [x] Error taxonomy + mapping - [x] Unit tests + lint - [x] Docs in code (package README + godoc) - [ ] Metrics/tracing spans (next PR) - [ ] Circuit breaker integration (next PR)

Ethan Park (review): Can we ensure Decrypt has a tighter retry budget than Encrypt? Decrypt is on the request path for several flows and we can’t afford tail latency + retry storms.

Diego Santos (author): Yep. In this PR I set Decrypt max attempts=2 and max elapsed=2.5s (Encrypt/GenerateDataKey are 3 attempts / 3s). Also added a unit test that asserts Decrypt never exceeds the tighter budget.

Sean Gallagher (review): Retry policy looks reasonable, but jitter must be default-on. Also please confirm we are NOT retrying AccessDenied/InvalidCiphertext.

Diego Santos (author): Confirmed. Only retry categories are Timeout/Throttled/Internal (provider 5xx/network). AccessDenied/InvalidCiphertext/NotFound are non-retryable. Jitter is applied on every backoff step; test asserts bounds.

Allison Grant (review): I like the taxonomy, but we need stable field names in logs. Can you add `kms.op`, `kms.category`, `kms.provider_code`, `kms.request_id` consistently? (Even before metrics.)

Diego Santos (author): Added those fields in the wrapper logger helper; callers just pass a logger and we attach consistent fields. Metrics will come in the next PR.

Kevin Osei (review): Please make sure error objects don’t include plaintext/ciphertext or key material. Also confirm request_id is safe.

Diego Santos (author): Wrapper never logs payloads. We only log provider request_id, op name, and error code/message. No key IDs are logged by default (call sites can add separately, but we should audit those later).

Jordan Lee (review): Config knobs: can we keep naming consistent with existing config conventions? (timeouts as durations; retry as max_attempts + max_elapsed.)

Diego Santos (author): Updated config names to `kms.timeout.decrypt`, `kms.retry.max_attempts`, `kms.retry.max_elapsed` (duration strings). README documents it.

Sean Gallagher (follow-up): Please add a note in README about expected behavior under KMS throttling and why we cap elapsed time.

Diego Santos (author): Added a short section under “Operational notes”.

Approvals: Ethan Park approved; Sean Gallagher approved; Allison Grant approved; Kevin Osei approved.

title: Add dead-letter queue + guarded replay CLI for failed export batches
body:
Add dead-letter queue + guarded replay CLI for failed export batches

Summary: This PR introduces a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for audit export batches that fail delivery after exhausting retries, and adds an operator-facing replay tool with guardrails. This is a reliability/safety feature for the SIEM-ready audit export beta (Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs / S3) to ensure we never silently drop events while still protecting the platform and customers from accidental replay storms. Context / Motivation: During downstream outages (e.g., sustained 429s from Splunk HEC or 403s from mis-scoped Datadog keys), the exporter currently retries with backoff and then surfaces a per-destination error. Without DLQ persistence we risk either (a) losing batches on process/queue churn or (b) having no safe operational path to replay specific failures once a customer fixes credentials/quotas. ENG-5164 calls for a DLQ + replay tooling with explicit operator controls. Design highlights: (1) DLQ record model: When a batch hits max_delivery_attempts OR we detect a non-retryable adapter error, we persist a DLQ record keyed by (tenant_id, export_config_id, checkpoint_range) and store the batch payload (newline-delimited JSON events) in object storage under a structured prefix. DLQ record includes: dlq_id, created_at, tenant_id, export_config_id, destination_type, reason_code, reason_detail (redacted), first_event_ts, last_event_ts, event_count, byte_size, last_attempt_at, attempt_count, and a payload_ref. (2) At-least-once compatibility: Replays may cause duplicate deliveries. We intentionally do not attempt exactly-once; downstream should dedup using event_id (per ADR on delivery semantics). Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion. Guardrails include: required --tenant-id and --export-config-id; default is dry-run; interactive confirmation unless --yes is provided; bounded selection via --since/--until and --max-items; token-bucket rate limiting (--max-events-per-minute) to avoid spiking adapters; refuses to replay if export config is disabled OR if exporter feature flag is off for that tenant (unless --override-feature-flag is provided, which is restricted to on-call breakglass role). (4) Safety checks: Replay validates destination configuration hash matches the DLQ record by default (prevents replaying old payloads into a newly re-pointed sink). Can be overridden with --ignore-config-hash-mismatch for incident response, but emits a prominent warning. (5) Redaction: DLQ reason_detail is run through the same redaction helper used by adapter logs to avoid accidentally persisting tokens/keys/PII. Payloads contain audit events only (already subject to audit schema/PII policy); we do not include request/response bodies. (6) Observability: Adds metrics: audit_exporter_dlq_enqueued_total{tenant_id_hash,destination_type,reason_code}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_items{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_events{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_replay_total{result}, and audit_exporter_dlq_replay_latency_seconds. Also adds structured logs for DLQ enqueue and replay runs (with correlation_id). User-visible / Ops workflow: - When an adapter can’t deliver a batch and we exceed retry limits, exporter transitions the batch to DLQ and advances the live pipeline checkpoint to prevent system-wide backpressure. - On-call or Support can instruct customer to fix auth/limits, then run replay for the impacted tenant/config/time window. - Replay is incremental and rate-limited; any failures during replay are re-DLQ’d with a new reason_code (replay_failed_*). Example commands: - List backlog: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq list --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --until 2025-02-09T06:00:00Z - Dry-run replay (default): ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 10 - Execute replay with explicit acknowledgements: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 50 --max-events-per-minute 12000 --ack-duplicates --yes Testing: - Unit tests for DLQ persistence, reason_code mapping, and redaction - Integration tests using adapter stubs: force 429/403/non-retryable to verify DLQ enqueue and payload roundtrip - Manual: replayed a synthetic backlog into Splunk stub with rate limiting and verified dedup by event_id Related: - Linear: ENG-5164 - ADR: delivery semantics and idempotency (at-least-once + event_id) - Support context: SUP-18531 (perceived missing events during throttling) Notes / Follow-ups: - Dashboard panels/alerts for DLQ backlog are tracked separately (we add metrics here, panels in observability-pack). - For beta, replay CLI is intended for on-call / SRE / Support escalation only; we are not exposing self-serve replay in Console.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can we confirm advancing the live checkpoint after DLQ enqueue won’t violate at-least-once? If we advance, aren’t we skipping events? Diego Santos (author): We’re not skipping generation; we’re persisting the batch payload + checkpoint range and treating replay as the at-least-once path. Without advancing, a stuck tenant can backpressure worker resources and starve other tenants. This matches ADR guidance: preserve payload, allow replay, accept duplicates. Marcus Lin (Security): Please ensure DLQ reason_detail doesn’t store adapter error blobs that may include tokens. Also confirm payload only contains audit events (no request bodies). Diego: Added redaction on reason_detail and a unit test that simulates Splunk error strings containing 'Authorization: Splunk <token>' and verifies it is redacted. Payload is the normalized audit event schema only; no HTTP request/response is serialized. Hanae Suzuki (Secrets/KMS): Where are DLQ payloads encrypted? Diego: Uses existing object storage client with SSE-KMS enabled in beta environments; added config validation to refuse startup if DLQ payload store is configured without encryption in hosted/dedicated. Aisha Bello (SRE): CLI needs stronger guardrails. Can we require --ack-duplicates and make dry-run default? Also add a cap to prevent replaying >N events unless explicitly set. Diego: Updated CLI: dry-run is default; execution requires both --ack-duplicates and --yes; added --max-items default 100 and hard cap 10k unless --breakglass is used. Logan Wright (Telemetry): Metrics label cardinality: do not label by raw tenant_id. Diego: Updated to tenant_id_hash and destination_type/reason_code only. Added note in docs about support workflow for identifying tenant via internal tooling. Approvals: Sean approved after guardrails changes; Marcus approved after redaction changes; Hanae approved after encryption validation; Logan approved after label change.
Exporter now persists terminal delivery failures to a dead-letter queue and provides an operator replay CLI with safety guardrails (beta feature; intended for on-call/support use).

title: Responses protocol adapter: stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff for OpenAI compatibility
body:
Responses protocol adapter: stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff for OpenAI compatibility

Motivation: New OpenAI Responses variants expose streaming fragmentation semantics, RNG/seed hints, and richer metadata that must be faithfully represented in Redwood's Responses compatibility layer. Without an adapter, hosted customers see reordering and truncated toolcall boundaries in streamed responses and cannot reproduce outputs when a seed is provided. This PR implements a protocol adapter that stabilizes fragment reassembly, preserves explicit tool/function-call boundary markers in the stream, and forwards RNG/seed hints plus metadata passthrough to the sampling layer. Design highlights: 1) Introduce lightweight fragment framing (frag_id, seq, final_flag) on the bridge to detect out-of-order chunks and perform deterministic reassembly with minimal buffering. 2) Emit and consume explicit toolcall boundary tokens at the adapter layer so function/tool callers receive well-formed call begin/end events even when the underlying runtime shards streams. 3) Map OpenAI-style "seed"/"deterministic" hint fields to an internal RNG-hint header and expose a seed proxy that pins sampling when requested for reproducible debug runs. 4) Preserve response-level metadata (request_id, model_attrs, user_metadata) by passthrough on the adapter and tag primary streaming frames with metadata headers so the console and observability pipelines retain attribution. 5) Fail-open fallback: when fragment integrity cannot be verified within a configurable timeout, the adapter falls back to per-chunk best-effort delivery and flags the event in logs/metrics. Implementation notes: Changes are concentrated in services/bridge/openai_adapter.go (adapter logic and framing), runtime/stream/framer.go (framing helpers), runtime/stream/reassembly.go (reassembly state machine), runtime/sampling/seed_proxy.go (seed handoff and validation), api/compat/responses_adapter_test.go (unit/integration tests), and docs/compat/openai-responses.md (compatibility guide). The adapter is feature-flagged under "openai_responses_adapter_v2" and gated behind a canary rollout. Tests and validation: added deterministic integration tests that replay recorded fragment orders, end-to-end tests against an OpenAI-compat harness, and a small perf canary to verify latency impact under 99th-percentile SLOs. Observability: new metrics added: adapter.frag_reassembly.latency_ms, adapter.frag_reassembly.reorders, adapter.toolcall.boundary_mismatches, and adapter.seed_forward.count. Rollout plan: 1) enable on internal canary; 2) run for 48h comparing toolcall event counts and reassembly metrics; 3) enable on hosted region eu-west-1 with gradual traffic ramp; 4) flip feature flag for Dedicated customers based on contracts. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] integration tests, [x] canary config, [x] docs updated, [x] rollout plan added. Impact: backward compatible for existing calls, minor latency increase in worst-case reassembly situations, improves streaming stability and deterministic reproduction for debugging. Related: ENG-3241 tracks the adapter work; SUP-9123 references a customer case where streamed toolcalls were split across fragments.
Compatibility adapter: stable streaming reassembly across Responses variants, explicit tool/function-call boundary markers, and passthrough of RNG/seed hints to Redwood sampling for deterministic debug runs. No API breaking changes.
Eliot Wong: Looks solid overall. Two asks: (1) tighten the reassembly buffer cap and expose as config; (2) add a small fuzz test that randomly reorders fragments to validate the state machine. Also please add a short migration note for Dedicated customers.
Marissa Cole (author): Addressed buffer cap and exposed via adapter.max_reassembly_buffer; added fuzz test suite under api/compat/fuzz_reassembly_test.go; added dedicated migration note in docs. PTAL.
Diego Alvarez: Approve after the perf numbers are posted from the canary run. Concern: seed passthrough must never override customer KMS restrictions; ensure validation rejects externally-supplied seeds if KMS-policy forbids it.
Marissa Cole (author): Added validation gate in runtime/sampling/seed_proxy.go that checks customer seed policy via authz call; updated tests to cover the restricted case.
Samir Patel: Left a nit on log level for boundary-mismatch (info -> warn) and a small comment about metric cardinality. Resolved by adjusting to warn only when mismatch rate > threshold.
7 commits: initial adapter scaffold and feature flag; framing helpers and proto changes; reassembly state machine with tests; seed proxy + sampling integration; toolcall boundary markers and console tagging; docs and compatibility guide; canary config and CI pipeline adjustments.
Squash and merge. Merge commit message: 'openai(compat): responses protocol adapter with stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff. Closes ENG-3241.'

title: introduce slab-grafting reclaimer and spill-rate cap to reduce KV cache fragmentation and spill storms
body:
introduce slab-grafting reclaimer and spill-rate cap to reduce KV cache fragmentation and spill storms

Motivation: In high-concurrency tenant workloads we continue to see transient spill storms driven by large numbers of small, fragmented slot allocations. These storms increase peak GPU memory usage and cause cascading evictions that harm latency. This PR introduces two orthogonal mitigations: (1) a slab-grafting reclaimer that coalesces adjacent free slots into larger usable extents with low CPU overhead, and (2) a spill-rate cap controller that rate-limits and smooths background spill operations to avoid sudden IO spikes. Design: slab-grafting is implemented as a background, incremental pass that scans per-shard free lists and attempts opportunistic graft operations when fragmentation score exceeds a threshold. Grafting is lock-free with respect to normal alloc/free paths by using a CAS-based two-phase promotion that marks ranges as 'staging' before atomically linking them into larger slabs. The spill-rate cap is a token-bucket controller in the KV spill scheduler; it enforces a soft cap on MB/sec of spill throughput and exposes a spill_smoothing_window_ms knob. When cap is hit, the scheduler prefers reclaiming contiguous grafted slabs and defers noncritical spill tasks. Compatibility: the grafting path is gated behind a runtime flag enable_slab_grafting and defaults off for older clusters; the spill cap has a conservative default of 128 MB/s but is tunable per-deployment and can be disabled. Testing: unit tests validate graft correctness across races and simulated concurrent frees; a stress harness (tools/kv_stress) demonstrates a 45% reduction in maximum concurrent spill IO during mixed-read/write tenant workloads, and a 12% P99 latency improvement on the generation path in our benchmark-lab scenarios. Rollout plan: staged canary to 10% of pods for 48h, monitor memory residency and spill_io_mbps metrics, then 50% for 24h, then global. Related work: follows the fragmentation detection work in ENG-3983 and complements the asynchronous compactor (ENG-4620). Known limitations: grafting is not effective for highly interleaved small live objects; in those cases we still rely on the compactor and eviction heuristics. Safety: feature flags and conservative defaults provided; metrics to watch: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.graft_ops, kv.spill_mbps, kv.eviction_count. 
Maya Patel (2026-02-16): Can you clarify the invariants around the 'staging' mark? I'm worried about a window where an allocator can see the range and try to reuse before graft completes.
Jordan Keane (2026-02-16): Answered: allocator checks a lightweight epoch bit and will fail allocation if range is marked staging; added comment and assertion to ensure allocation paths skip staging ranges.
Arjun Singh (2026-02-17): Performance nit: the graft scan poll interval defaults to 200ms; on our internal workloads that adds measurable CPU jitter. Can we make it adaptive (backoff when idle)?
Jordan Keane (2026-02-17): Implemented exponential backoff when graft rate drops below threshold; added tests and updated bench results.
- Added slab-grafting reclaimer to reduce KV cache fragmentation and improve allocation efficiency.
- Added configurable spill-rate cap to smooth spill IO and prevent spill storms.
- New metrics: kv.graft_ops, kv.graft_latency_ms, kv.spill_rate_limit_mb_s.

title: runtime: make optimization config applier idempotent + retry-safe (partial rollout safeguards)
body:
runtime: make optimization config applier idempotent + retry-safe (partial rollout safeguards)

Context: As part of Safe apply + rollback for Optimization Configs, the control plane will issue apply operations that may be retried (network timeouts, controller restarts) and can be delivered out-of-order relative to worker restarts and shard movement. Prior implementation applied configs as a best-effort "set current" and would re-run side effects on every delivery (cache invalidation, batcher reinit), which increased tail latency and could leave mixed worker states during partial rollout. This PR makes the runtime Optimization Config applier idempotent and resilient to retries, and adds explicit safeguards for partial rollout states.

What changed: 1) Introduced apply_operation_id and deterministic apply keying. The runtime now consumes ApplyOptimizationConfig(scope, version, apply_operation_id, reason) and records a durable ApplyRecord per (scope, version). If the same apply_operation_id is delivered again, the operation is treated as a no-op after verifying the recorded checksum. 2) Added a small durable state store (RuntimeOptimizationConfigState) to persist last_desired_version, last_applied_version, last_apply_operation_id, and an apply_status enum (PENDING/APPLIED/FAILED). This survives worker restarts and prevents "double apply" side effects after process crashes. 3) Side-effect gating: cache invalidation and batch scheduler resets now run only on transition from one applied version to another, and are skipped on idempotent retries. 4) Partial rollout safeguards: if a worker receives an apply for an older version than its recorded desired_version, it will reject it with a conflict response unless reason=ROLLBACK (explicit rollback) or allow_downgrade=true from control plane. This prevents late/stale apply messages from reintroducing a regressed version mid-rollout. 5) Repair behavior: if apply_status is FAILED for the same (scope, version) and the controller retries with a new apply_operation_id, the runtime will re-attempt apply (previously a failed apply could wedge workers until manual restart). 6) Observability: added metrics and structured logs to make retry/no-op/conflict behavior visible: optimization_config_apply_total{result=applied|noop|conflict|failed}, optimization_config_apply_duration_ms, and optimization_config_state_gauge{state}. All are tagged with tenant/model/region/config_version/apply_operation_id (apply_operation_id only in logs to avoid high cardinality metrics).

Why this is safe: The new behavior is strictly more conservative. Duplicate deliveries become no-ops, stale messages are rejected, and only explicit rollbacks can downgrade. Persisted state ensures crashes don’t cause reapplication storms (and the associated cache flush latency spikes). Unit + integration tests cover retry ordering, crash/restart, and conflict semantics.

Follow-ups: - Control plane rollout controller will start supplying apply_operation_id everywhere (tracked in ENG-4824). - Console will surface conflict/failed reasons using the error codes introduced here. - We should consider promoting apply_operation_id into trace spans once tracing propagation is in place for the apply pipeline.

Related: ENG-4823 (idempotency guarantees), PR #19915 (apply transaction checkpoints), PR #19933 (gate hooks/metric tags).
Omar El-Sayed (review): The state store worries me a bit — is this per-worker local disk? What happens on ephemeral workers or when a pod is rescheduled? Also please confirm we’re not adding a high-cardinality metric label with apply_operation_id.

Noah Patel (author): Yes, this is local to the runtime pod (same path as other small runtime state; falls back to in-memory if not writable). If the pod is rescheduled, we lose the record, but idempotency still holds per-process; the controller retries will reapply cleanly. The durable store mainly prevents re-running side effects after a crash/restart on the same node and avoids repeated cache flushes. apply_operation_id is logs-only; metrics are tagged with tenant/model/region/config_version and result.

Sofia Ivanova (review): Can you clarify the stale apply rule? I’m concerned about a canary controller that pauses and then resumes: will workers start rejecting legitimate apply calls if desired_version advanced?

Noah Patel (author): Rule is: if incoming.version < desired_version, we return CONFLICT unless reason=ROLLBACK (or allow_downgrade). If the controller pauses/resumes the same operation, desired_version doesn’t change, so no conflict. Conflicts happen when a newer version was already declared desired (e.g., fast follow apply or rollback) and an older message arrives late.

Ethan Park (review): Please add explicit error codes so the controller can distinguish conflict vs transient failure; otherwise we’ll treat it as retryable and spam the runtime.

Noah Patel (author): Added OptimizationConfigApplyError with codes: CONFLICT_STALE_VERSION, CHECKSUM_MISMATCH, VALIDATION_FAILED, APPLY_FAILED_TRANSIENT. Updated client to propagate codes up.

Sean Gallagher (review): Can you add an annotation log line with a stable message for dashboards? We want to key alerts on "optimization config apply failed" events.

Noah Patel (author): Added structured log event "opt_config_apply" with fields result, scope, version, error_code, and request_id. Metrics also emit result=failed.

Benji Okafor (review): Proto change adds apply_operation_id — any backwards compat concerns with older runtimes during rollout?

Noah Patel (author): Field is optional; runtime treats missing apply_operation_id as "legacy" and derives one from (scope, version, request_id) but marks it non-dedup-safe across retries. The controller will only enable retry semantics after runtime fleet is upgraded (feature flag in control plane). Documented rollout plan in internal runtime doc.

Omar El-Sayed (review): One more request: when checksum mismatch occurs, should we hard fail and require operator intervention? That seems like a data integrity issue.

Noah Patel (author): Agreed — checksum mismatch returns non-retryable CHECKSUM_MISMATCH and does not change desired/applied state. This should surface as a hard stop in the rollout UI. Added a unit test.

Chloe Martin (comment): Thanks — Console will need the conflict/failed codes surfaced on the rollout timeline. Please ensure error strings are user-safe.

Noah Patel (author): Errors are code-first; messages are short and don’t include internal paths. Console can map codes to friendly text.

Final approvals: Omar El-Sayed (approved), Sofia Ivanova (approved), Ethan Park (approved).
- Runtime now treats Optimization Config apply as an idempotent operation keyed by (scope, version, apply_operation_id). Retries and duplicate deliveries will no-op safely; partial apply states are detected and repaired.

title: Introduce ephemeral circuit limiter with paced reopen for regional soft-failover
body:
Introduce ephemeral circuit limiter with paced reopen for regional soft-failover

Context and motivation: In several recent incidents we observed rapid flip-flopping of regional circuits during noisy partial outages. That behavior amplified client retries and triggered downstream capacity cascades. This PR introduces an ephemeral circuit limiter that enforces a short-lived, tenant-aware deny window with a paced reopen strategy to smooth recovery and avoid mass reopen storms. The aim is graceful degradation: let high-priority SLO-bearing tenants continue where possible, slow-roll reopen lower-priority tenants, and surface telemetry to trace circuit lifecycle decisions.

What this changes (single-line continuous body including checklist, testing, and rollout): Implement ephemeral CircuitLimiter that tracks per-tenant deny-windows (TTL), a pacing controller that schedules staggered reopen tokens based on tenant weight and recent success rate, an opt-in config flag in cluster config (runtime.ephemeral_circuit.enabled), and metrics/traces for circuit decisions. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-3421) and reviewed, [x] unit tests for limiter and pacing policy, [x] integration test for multi-tenant reopen pacing, [x] added telemetry (circuit_events, pacing_backoff_ms, tenant_priority) to console dashboards, [x] feature flag + gradual rollout strategy. Testing: unit tests + small cluster integration run on perf-canary; e2e flaky test (region-sim) was rerun twice before green; CI shows all checks passing on final run. Rollout plan: enable feature flag in prod for 10% of traffic per region for 24h, monitor circuit_events and p50/p99 latency; expand to 50% then 100% if no regressions.

title: paged-kv: implement soft-pin block allocator and reuse heuristics to reduce fragmentation
body:
paged-kv: implement soft-pin block allocator and reuse heuristics to reduce fragmentation

Motivation: long-lived KV cache entries and block fragmentation were causing elevated tail latency and increased GPU memory pressure under mixed-sequence workloads. This PR introduces a 'soft pin' block allocation strategy and stronger reuse heuristics for the paged KV block manager to reduce allocation churn and eviction storms. Summary of changes: 1) New soft-pin concept for blocks: blocks can be marked soft-pinned when referenced by in-flight decode contexts; they are excluded from immediate eviction but eligible for reuse by same-owner contexts to avoid duplication. 2) Segregated free lists per size class with compact LRU buckets to improve reuse locality. 3) Eviction ranking that factors in last-access timestamp, owner affinity, and live-kv-count to avoid evicting hot multi-token KV pages. 4) GC/compaction path to coalesce small free fragments when fragmentation exceeds threshold. 5) Runtime knobs: kv.soft_pin_v2 (bool), kv.free_list_threshold (int), kv.compact_fraction (float). Design notes: the soft-pin is a lightweight per-block ref-bit plus ownership tag; ownership is used only as a hint for reuse and does not bypass safety checks. Reuse is conservative: blocks reclaimed for reuse must not have active external pointers. Benchmarks: local microbench (mixed chat + completion load, seq distribution 8-1024) shows 10-14% reduction in p99 token-latency and ~12% throughput improvement on T4-equivalent nodes; memory overhead reduced ~6% due to less duplicated KV pages. Rollout plan: feature gated, canary on 5% of hosted traffic, ramp to 50% after 48h if perf signals stable. Backout: revert kv.soft_pin_v2 or set kv.free_list_threshold high. Related work: follow-ups planned to integrate with continuous batching's slot-aware scheduling to further co-locate reuses. Linear tickets: ENG-2143, ENG-2178. Risks: potential subtle race during concurrent eviction and decoder handoff; mitigated with additional CAS checks and stress tests. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] perf benchmarks, [x] canary script, [x] doc update.
Ravi Gupta: Can you explain why we prefer soft-pin over exclusive pin? I'm worried about stalling eviction under bursty load.
Ava Martinez: Soft-pin is intentionally low-friction; it prevents immediate eviction only for active handoffs and still allows reuse for same-owner contexts. We observed exclusive pins increased memory pressure because pages couldn't be reused quickly.
Marta Lopez: Nit: add a test for concurrent reuse where two decoders race to acquire the same reclaimed block.
Ava Martinez: Added block_allocator_unit.cc to cover that exact race and added CAS checks in reclaim path.
Kenji Sato: lgtm for allocator design; please add a metric for 'soft_pin_reuse_hits' to track benefit post-rollout.
Ava Martinez: Added metric kv.soft_pin_reuse_hits and a perf dashboard row in docs/architecture/kv_cache_design.md.
Improved paged KV block manager with 'soft-pin' allocation, better reuse heuristics, and compaction to reduce fragmentation; expected p99 token latency improvements and reduced memory duplication. Feature gated behind kv.soft_pin_v2.
Canary config provided in scripts/perf/canary_kv_softpin.yaml. Watch metrics: kv.evictions, kv.soft_pin_reuse_hits, kv.compaction_runs, gpu_memory_peak, request_p99_token_latency. Backout: disable kv.soft_pin_v2 and reroute canary traffic.
Local perf: 12% throughput increase under mixed-seq load; p95 improved ~6%, p99 improved 10-14% in T4-like environment. Canary early signal: 8% p99 improvement on 5% traffic after 24h with no increase in evictions.

title: Introduce TimeWarp RAG Simulator quickstart: synthetic user & structured-output linter
body:
Introduce TimeWarp RAG Simulator quickstart: synthetic user & structured-output linter

Motivation: Reproducing user-facing RAG regressions that depend on network latency, index freshness, or multi-tool interactions is time-consuming. This quickstart introduces the TimeWarp simulator — a lightweight local harness that lets engineers run deterministic, time-scaled RAG scenarios and assert structured outputs against expected contracts. The goal is a low-friction developer loop to reproduce flaky tool-calls, evaluate output stability under synthetic delays, and run quick regressions in CI. What this PR adds: 1) quickstarts/timewarp-simulator/README.md — end-to-end guide and expected workflows; 2) a compact TypeScript runner (runner/ts/) that drives synthetic user sessions with configurable latency/timewarp factors and replayable corpora; 3) a structured-output linter (examples/linting/structured-output-linter.py) that validates JSON/YAML responses against field-level contracts and fuzzy string expectations; 4) telemetry probes (telemetry/probes.yaml) and a CI smoke job (ci/smoke-timewarp.yml) that runs a short scenario on PRs to catch regressions; 5) docs site registration (docs/quickstarts.yml and docs/snippets/timewarp-setup.md) so quickstart appears in the docs sidebar. Security & privacy: The runner uses seedable, local-only corpora (examples/playback/sample-corpus.json) and never ships customer data; a note in the README explains sanitization for real-indexed corpora. Quickstart highlights and commands: - Install node and python (README includes minimal versions). - From the quickstart dir: npm ci && npm run build && node dist/run.js --corpus examples/playback/sample-corpus.json --timewarp 0.5 --seed 42 This runs a session that simulates accelerated token/latency pacing (0.5x wall clock). - To run with a 2x slow-down: --timewarp 2.0 - Lint responses: python3 examples/linting/structured-output-linter.py --input out/session-001.json --schema quickstarts/timewarp-simulator/contracts/session-schema.yaml - CI smoke: ci/smoke-timewarp.yml runs the runner against a short scenario and fails the job if structured-output linter finds contract divergences. Developer notes & checklist: - ✅ Deterministic seeds added to runner and sample corpus for reproducibility. - ✅ Minimal telemetry hooks (span ids + latency histograms) added so SRE can wire into existing dashboards. - ✅ Docs snippets and usage examples included with copyable CLI commands. - ✅ Small sample corpus and a guide for sanitizing real corpora are included. - Known limitations: The simulator is not a substitute for full-scale load testing; it targets functional/regression scenarios and structured-output stability. It currently supports HTTP-based tool stubs and the Redwood hosted API compatibility layer; adding grpc tool stubs is tracked in ENG-3330. Migration/upgrade notes: The quickstart is opt-in; it does not change runtime behavior. To adopt, teams can copy the quickstart folder into their repos or reference the runner as a submodule. Linear tickets: ENG-3214 tracks simulator enhancements and instrumentation; PM-78 tracks product docs and a short tutorial. Testing & CI summary: A new smoke CI job was added and is gated on docs and lint passing on PRs touching quickstarts. Full unit tests live alongside the runner and were executed as part of this PR's CI. Merge summary: squash-merged to main after reviewers signed off and CI green.

title: Add reservoired burst-accountant and steady-window SLO profiles for Dedicated fleets
body:
Add reservoired burst-accountant and steady-window SLO profiles for Dedicated fleets

Customers observed intermittent microburst patterns that repeatedly pushed Dedicated tenants past short-term P95 latency SLAs despite healthy long-window utilization. This PR introduces a reservoired burst-accountant and a configurable steady-window SLO profile to explicitly decouple short burst allowances from steady throughput guarantees.

What this changes: added a credit reservoir model (per-tenant, per-fleet) that accrues credit when observed usage is below a configurable steady-window baseline, and draws down when short-term bursts exceed nominal throughput. Credits are persisted in the reservation ledger with TTL and soft-eviction semantics. A new steady-window SLO profile (window length, baseline qps, burn-rate caps, recovery rate) can be attached to tenant reservations and accepted by the autoscaler and admission controller. The admission controller now consults the accountant to allow transient overcommit within the credit budget, and emits telemetry so ops can see effective burst headroom and expected exhaustion times.

Why: previous autoscaling heuristics conflated short-term spike handling with long-window capacity planning, leading to noisy scale-ups and SLA flapping. The reservoir model reduces unnecessary scale churn, improves tail latency consistency, and provides an audit trail for transient overages.

Compatibility and opt-in: new behavior is gated behind the feature flag "reservoired_burst_accountant" and is enabled by default for Dedicated fleets started after the release date. Existing fleets will remain on traditional burst heuristics unless opt-in is performed via the Console or API. Backward-compatible admission paths exist: if the accountant data is unavailable, the system falls back to current conservative limits.

Testing and validation: unit tests for ledger persistence, integration tests simulating realistic burst profiles, and a small-scale canary (10 fleets) run in perf-lab. Load tests show P95 latency improvements of 12-18% on bursty workloads and reduced autoscale events by ~28%.

Rollback plan: revert feature flag (ops) to disable accountant and fall back to baseline burst limits. Post-merge tasks: telemetry dashboard, Console opt-in UI, and a follow-up PR to add a per-tenant dry-run mode that reports but does not enforce credit draws.

title: Introduce inference health scorer and token-cost forecast panel
body:
Introduce inference health scorer and token-cost forecast panel

Motivation: Production teams want a single, explainable signal that summarizes invocation health (latency, cost, cache-warmth, model-fallbacks) and a short-term forecast of token burn to reduce noisy alerts during predictable bursts. This PR introduces a lightweight per-invocation 'inference_health_score' (0-100) plus a token-cost forecast panel that surfaces 1h/6h/24h EWMA forecasts and a confidence band.

What this changes (high level):
- Instrumentation: runtime emits 'inference_health_score', and additional tags: token_cohort, kernel_slot, hw_tier, prefix_warmth. Implemented in serving/telemetry/health_scorer.rs and runtime/tracing/span_enricher.cpp.
- Aggregation/worker: observability/pipelines/forecast_worker.go computes per-tenant EWMA forecasts for token-cost (tokens/sec and token-cost/sec) and writes forecast series to the metrics cache. Forecasts use an EWMA with adaptive alpha (short/long windows) and a confidence band from recent variance.
- Dashboard: grafana/dashboards/inference_health_and_forecast.json adds: health-summary heatmap, forecast sparkline (1h/6h/24h), cohorted bar (by token_cohort), and a causal-log-mosaic link column that deep-links into the trace inspector.
- Alerts: alerting/rules/forecast_slo_rules.yaml includes a forecast-aware alert rule that defers paging if projected 1h burn is within hysteresis threshold; it still fires if the health_score drops below 30 or if a critical fallback rate is observed.

Design notes:
- health_score composition: 40% latency SLO distance, 25% token-cost z-score, 20% prefix_warmth (higher is better), 10% kernel_queue_penalty, 5% recent-model-fallback-rate. The metric is normalized to 0-100 with guarded NaN handling. The algorithm is intentionally transparent (implemented as a deterministic rule in health_scorer.rs) to make RCA easier.
- Forecasting: we opted for EWMA-based forecasting to keep compute cheap in the ingest tier. The worker maintains short (1h), medium (6h), and long (24h) windows and exposes a 'forecast_confidence' derived from window variance.
- Alert tuning: new rule adds a 'forecast_quiet_window' if the projected burn explains the deviation; an 'explainability' label is attached listing the dominant contributor (e.g., "arrival_profile", "kv_cache_cold").

Backward compatibility & opt-out: default is enabled. For Dedicated/Private customers we provide an opt-out via config: observability.features.health_scorer=false. Metric names are stable and documented in docs/observability/metric_catalog.md.

Testing & validation:
- Unit tests: health_scorer unit tests cover composition edge cases, NaN handling, and bucket assignment (tests/health_scorer_test.rs).
- Integration: forecast_worker was run in a staging replay (replaybench) for a 72h synthetic workload; dashboard panels validated against the replay and matched expected forecasts within 3% on average.
- Load: worker CPU and memorystore usage measured on staging 2x baseline with no observable impact on ingest pipeline; added a 50ms budget cap per-window evaluation to avoid tail amplification.

title: perf: cross-batch dequant fusion with amortized per-token rescale for mixed-precision kernels
body:
perf: cross-batch dequant fusion with amortized per-token rescale for mixed-precision kernels

Motivation: Long-context workloads show fragmentation across microbatches that prevent effective dequant fusion and cause repeated dequant/rescale operations per token. This PR introduces a cross-batch dequant fusion pass plus an amortized per-token rescale step that cooperates with the KV cache and continuous batching coordinator to reduce redundant dequant work for INT8/FP8 mixed-precision serving.

Summary of changes: implemented a new CrossBatchDequanter that tracks compatible contiguous microbatch windows and emits a fused dequant operation for stacked tokens; added an AmortizedRescale operator that defers fine-grained scale adjustments until token groups exceed a stability threshold; extended the scheduler with a cross-batch affinity hint and modified the KV cache interface to expose per-layer scale metadata needed by the fused path. Also added kernel-level fastpaths for fused int8->fp16 conversion targeting long prefix reuse patterns.

Design notes: the fused path is opt-in behind a runtime feature flag (RUNTIME_FUSED_DEQUANT). When enabled the scheduler annotates queued requests with batch-affinity tags; CrossBatchDequanter periodically probes the queue to form mergeable windows constrained by latency SLO heuristics. AmortizedRescale computes a combined scale factor and only applies per-token micro-adjustments when the cumulative quantization error crosses a configurable threshold (defaults tuned from benchmarks). Compatibility: falls back to existing per-request dequant for heterogeneous model variants and when KV cache indicates incompatible scale signatures.

Benchmarks: microbench on p4d.24xlarge with a 16k context evaluation harness showed up to 22% throughput improvement and 18% average token-latency reduction on customer-like chat load (95th percentile latency remained within SLO). FP8/INT8 combined workloads saw better utilization due to fewer kernel launches and improved KV cache hit patterns. Detailed numbers included in /docs/perf/crossbatch-dequant-run-2026-02-20.md.

Testing: unit tests for CrossBatchDequanter and AmortizedRescale (kernel emulation mode), end-to-end CI smoke against the runtime with synthetic traffic, and a canary rollout configuration for Dedicated. Stress tests included kv-cache warm/cold cycles and continuous-batching scenarios. CI initially reported a flaky scheduler test (test_scheduler_affinity) which was fixed by adding a deterministic queue snapshot during window formation.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag, canary on dedicated pools with low-priority routing, opt-in for private deployments via config toggle. Observability: new metrics added (dequant_fused_windows, amortized_rescale_ops, per_layer_scale_mismatch) and alerting thresholds proposed in SLO dashboard PR.

Related: follows up on ENG-3962 and complements earlier kernel fusion work (see ENG-1538). Notable tradeoffs: slightly increased memory for temporary fused buffers; however the overall token compute/launch overhead drops substantially for long prefix reuse.

title: Differential audit sampling + KMS call-path reconciliation for RBAC v2 operator scope
body:
Differential audit sampling + KMS call-path reconciliation for RBAC v2 operator scope

Motivation: Reduce sensitive-audit volume while preserving forensic fidelity and ensuring per-call KMS provenance for operator-scoped actions. This PR implements a differential audit-sampling layer (route + risk aware) integrated with an end-to-end KMS call-path reconciler to ensure any sampled event carries provable KMS metadata that can be traced back to the operator credential used. Changes include a sampling policy engine, hooks in the RBACv2 enforcer to emit sampling signals, and a background reconciler that annotates audit events with KMS proofs and retries failed attestations. Checklist: - [x] Sampling engine core + config (feature flagged) - [x] RBAC enforcer hooks for per-request risk tagging - [x] KMS call-path reconcilier with exponential backoff and backfill - [x] Integration tests for sampled vs full-audit behavior - [x] Docs + migration notes - [x] Performance microbenchmarks to validate <3% p50 overhead Related tickets/links: Linear ENG-4820, SEC-900; design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4820/differential-audit-sampling-design; compliance note (internal): https://redwood.internal/docs/compliance/kms-provenance. Rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag rbacv2.diff_audit_sampling; default off for enterprise accounts. When enabled, low-risk routes use probabilistic sampling, high-risk routes (policy change, KMS key ops, operator escalation) are always retained. The reconciler runs asynchronously and attaches kms_proof:{provider,region,key_id,nonce,signature} when available. If reconciliation fails after configured retries the audit event is marked audit_status:reconciler_failed and forwarded to a high-priority fanout for compliance reviewers. Backwards compatibility: existing audit consumers see an added metadata block but retain old fields. Migration note: operators that rely on 100% audit capture must set force_full_audit:true per-route in console before enabling this flag.
