title: Add RAG mosaic authoring stubs and live-preview quickstart
body:
Add RAG mosaic authoring stubs and live-preview quickstart

Introduce a compact quickstart that demonstrates a 'mosaic' authoring pattern for RAG scenarios: template stubs, a live preview server, telemetry probes, and a devcontainer for local onboarding.
Motivation and summary: Add a lightweight quickstart that shows authors how to compose retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios using a 'mosaic' layout: small, composable step templates (retrieval, transform, tool-call, finalization) that can be arranged and previewed in real time. This is targeted at developer-first product teams who want fast iteration cycles when authoring multi-step agents and tool-calling flows. The quickstart includes: 1) starter templates for step types, 2) a tiny live-preview server that streams intermediate step outputs into a mosaic UI, 3) telemetry probes and example probes for Redwood Console, 4) a devcontainer and scripts to run locally, and 5) CI e2e smoke tests.

What changed (high-level): commits: - Add mosaic authoring templates and README (initial scaffolding) - Add live-preview server (FastAPI + SSE) and browser UI - Wire telemetry probe hooks and example telemetry config - Add devcontainer, Makefile and local-run scripts - Add CI smoke test that runs quickstart e2e in headless mode - Docs site section and short how-to guide

Changed areas/files (representative): - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/README.md (new authoring guide and examples) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/templates/*.yaml (retrieval/transform/tool/output stubs) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/server.py (SSE endpoints + example runner) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/static/index.html (mosaic UI) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/devcontainer.json + .devcontainer/Dockerfile - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/telemetry/probes.yaml - .github/workflows/quickstart-e2e.yml (added smoke job) - docs/site/content/quickstarts/rag-mosaic.md (documentation and screenshots)

Design notes and rationale: - Mosaic layout: each step emits a compact envelope {type, summary, tokens_used, result_preview}. The UI displays envelopes tiled so authors can quickly inspect how retrieval, rerank, transform, and tool calls interact. - Live preview uses SSE to avoid full-page polling; server-side runner replays a seeded conversation and emits step-level deltas to the UI. This mirrors production tracing while remaining lightweight for local runs. - Telemetry probes: small hooks are emitted from the runner with route and token-level metadata; default probes are no-op but wired to Redwood Console examples in telemetry/probes.yaml. - Templates: YAML-based step templates were chosen for readability and copy/paste ergonomics in docs and repos. Templates include sensible defaults for caching/batching hints and an example quantization/throughput note.

title: Signed Terraform Plan Artifacts and Helm-diff Rollback Gating
body:
Signed Terraform Plan Artifacts and Helm-diff Rollback Gating

Context and motivation:
This PR implements a reproducible, signed artifact workflow for Terraform plans and a Helm-chart-diff-driven rollback gating mechanism for the private installer CI/CD. Recent customer upgrades highlighted two operational gaps: (1) lack of a verifiable plan artifact to attest exactly what will change during an upgrade, and (2) upgrades failing to generate deterministic rollback anchors when chart/value drift occurs in airgapped environments.

Summary of changes:
- Generate a canonical, reproducible terraform plan JSON during staging, canonicalize it (strip timestamps, sort maps), and sign the blob with cosign using the org KMS key. Signed artifacts are uploaded to the release bucket under /plans/<release>/<cluster>.plan.json.sig and recorded in the release manifest.
- Add a lightweight plan-verifier binary (tools/plan-verifier) used in CI and in the installer preflight to validate signatures and ensure the on-cluster state matches the plan fingerprint before applying.
- Add a Helm chart diff preflight that computes a normalized diff between current deployed chart+values and the candidate release, identifies changed template keys that are rollback-risky (stateful migration hooks, volume changes), and produces a rollback anchor entry to include in the release manifest.
- CI: new pipeline step ci/pipelines/verify-signed-plan.yml to gate merges for private-installer changes that touch upgrade paths. The pipeline verifies signatures, runs the helm-diff preflight against a live staging cluster simulator, and publishes the artifacts.
- Docs: docs/upgrade-runbook.md extended with a signed-plan troubleshooting section and instructions for on-prem operators on how to rotate signing keys.

Design notes and security posture:
- Artifact signing uses cosign with KMS-backed keys (AWS KMS / GCP KMS interchangeable). The plan JSON canonicalization is intentionally strict: deterministic ordering of resources and consistent provider addresses to ensure reproducible fingerprinting across CI runs.
- The plan artifact and helm-diff anchor are stored with provenance metadata (git ref, pipeline id, signer id) and included in the release manifest so the installer can make allowlist decisions during an airgapped apply.
- The preflight runs in two modes: CI-mode (simulator) and runtime-mode (installer preflight). The latter defaults to fail-closed when signatures or anchors are absent, but an operator flag --allow-unsigned-upgrades is available for troubleshooting with audit logging.

How to test locally:
1) ./scripts/generate-plan.sh --cluster test-cluster --out /tmp/plan.json (creates canonical plan JSON)
2) ./scripts/sign-plan.sh /tmp/plan.json (produces /tmp/plan.json.sig)
3) tools/plan-verifier verify --plan /tmp/plan.json --sig /tmp/plan.json.sig --kms-key $KMS_KEY
4) Run helm diff preflight: tools/helm-diff-preflight --current ./staging/chart --candidate ./charts/private-installer --values ./staging/values.yaml
5) Execute the CI simulation job locally: ./ci/local-run verify-signed-plan.yml

Migration and rollout plan:
- Feature is behind a flag (ENABLE_SIGNED_PLANS). We will enable CI gating for all release branches for two weeks in staged mode. During the first week, the pipeline will publish signed artifacts but not block merges; during week two it will block merges if signatures are missing.
- Operators will be notified via release notes and the private-installer Slack channel with instructions for key rotation and preflight diagnostics.

Related work and references:
- Related Linear tickets: ENG-7382 (plan attestation), ENG-7390 (helm rollback anchors).
- Inspired by upstream reproducible-plan work and cosign best practices.

Checklist:
- [x] Generate canonical plan and signer hook
- [x] Implement verifier for CI and runtime
- [x] Add helm-diff rollback anchorer
- [x] CI pipeline integration and tests
- [x] Docs + runbook updates

Introduce signed terraform plan artifacts for upgrade gating and add a Helm chart diff-based preflight that computes a safe rollback anchor. Adds verification tooling to CI and runtime verification for private deployments.

Sofia Alvarez (reviewer): Will preflight cause false positives for clusters with drift? We should provide an escape hatch for manual intervention.

title: Sliding canary with composite SLO gates, shadow validation and automated rollback choreography
body:
Sliding canary with composite SLO gates, shadow validation and automated rollback choreography

Motivation: Customers running mixed-quality-sensitive workloads asked for a rollout mode that can: (1) evaluate live traffic quality (semantic/regression metrics) alongside traditional SLOs (p50/p95 latency, error rate), (2) apply a gradual sliding window increase in traffic rather than fixed steps, and (3) wire automated rollback choreography when any composite gate trips while preserving an audit trail and optional shadow replay for offline bisect.

This PR implements a new rollout strategy named 'sliding-canary' in the rollout controller and adds telemetry-driven composite gates that aggregate signals across latency, error rate, and configured application-level quality checks (e.g., eval-set regression score). The strategy supports: sliding traffic ramps (percent per minute), safety holdpoints with manual approval, shadow capture for failing slices, and coordinated rollback with tokenized rollback-playbook events for operator playbooks.

Key user-visible changes:
- New rollout.strategy.type = "sliding-canary" with fields: start_percent, max_percent, slide_rate_per_min, hold_points[], composite_gates[]. Each composite_gate can reference latency/error thresholds and quality metric expressions.
- New API endpoints: POST /rollouts/:id/snapshot and POST /rollouts/:id/force-hold for operator intervention.
- Shadow capture toggle at rollout level to mirror traffic for offline replay and automated bisect.
- Automated rollback choreography: when a composite gate trips, controller emits a rollback token and sends a structured event to the playbook queue; optional dry-run replays can be configured.

Design summary:
- Controller: implements time-windowed sliding window sampler (defaults to 60s windows) collecting per-route aggregated signals. Composite gates evaluate historical windows with configurable decay to prevent single-spike noise.
- Telemetry: added new rollup metrics (rollout.window_latency_p95, rollout.window_error_rate, rollout.window_quality_regression) and tags for rollout_id, cohort. These feed into the composite gate evaluator and the console dashboards.
- Shadowing: lightweight capture stores request metadata + model-output fingerprint in compressed sstable and emits a pointer to object storage. Replay harness reuses existing replay infra but tags traces with original rollout cohort for bisect.
- Safety: built-in backoff policy on rollback that respects operator holdpoints and supports an autorecover mode if upstream transient issue resolves (configurable cooldown).

Migration/backcompat: existing rollout configs are unchanged; sliding-canary is opt-in. Controllers running older versions ignore sliding-canary rollouts and return a validation error prompting users to upgrade. Migration doc included.

Tests & CI: unit tests for gate evaluation, e2e integration tests for sliding ramp behavior and rollback choreography, and a small load test simulating mixed-quality degradation.

Commits (summary):
- add: rollout strategy implementation (controller + reconciler + leader-election safety)
- add: composite gate evaluator and config schema + validation
- add: telemetry metrics and console dashboard panels
- add: shadow capture writer and replay tagging
- add: API endpoints for snapshot/force-hold
- fix: reconciliation race on concurrent rollout updates
- chore: docs + migration guide + rollout strategy examples

Changed files (high level):
- controller/rollouts/strategy_sliding_canary.go (new)
- controller/rollouts/gate_evaluator.go (new)
- api/rollouts/routes.go (api additions)
- telemetry/metrics_rollouts.prom (metrics defs)
- observability/dashboards/sliding_canary.json (dashboard)
- replay/harness/capture_writer.go (shadow capture)
- docs/runbooks/sliding-canary.md (user guide + migration)
- tests/integration/sliding_canary_e2e.test (test harness)
- ci/workflows/rollout-integration.yml (updated to include new e2e)

Short code snippet (controller):
- sliding window aggregator uses exponential-decay on per-window aggregates to reduce sensitivity to one-off spikes.

Testing notes: e2e run against local dev cluster simulates a regression in 'semantic-fidelity' quality metric between 0.86 -> 0.72 which correctly trips the composite gate after three sliding windows and triggers the rollback token and shadow capture pointer. The replay harness successfully replays captured traffic slice and reproduces the regression in offline evals.

Security & perf considerations: shadow capture stores only fingerprints and minimal context by default (PII scrubbed); customers can opt into full request store under explicit consent. The sliding window evaluator is bounded-memory and runs on controller leader only. Benchmarks show <5% controller CPU increase at 1000 concurrent rollouts.

Rollback playbook example: 
1) Gate trips -> controller emits rollback token with metadata
2) Orchestrator pauses traffic ramp and issues rollback command to serving plane
3) Shadow capture pointer is sent to replay service for bisect
4) Operator can either approve autorecover or approve manual revert

Docs & examples: docs/runbooks/sliding-canary.md shows example YAML, A/B experiment mapping, and guidance for tuning composite gates (weighting latency vs quality).

Why this is different from existing canary strategies: rather than incrementing in fixed steps, sliding-canary performs continuous ramping evaluated in sliding windows and uses a composite evaluation function that can incorporate domain-specific quality signals (not just latency/error), enabling safer ramping for quality-sensitive models such as summarization or reranking.

Related: ENG-3245 (composite SLOs), ENG-3310 (shadow replay improvements).
Introduce sliding-canary rollout strategy with composite SLO gates (latency/error/quality), shadow validation hooks and automated rollback choreography. Backwards compatible with existing canary config; new strategy opt-in via rollout.strategy.type="sliding-canary".

title: introduce-econ-orchard-mini-sampler-and-quant-curator
body:
introduce-econ-orchard-mini-sampler-and-quant-curator

Motivation: This PR adds the 'Econ Orchard' suite — a compact, production-safe set of tools that generate conservative default batching/caching presets, a lightweight micro-sampler for workload-shaped telemetry, and a small quantization profile curator to recommend safe quant variants per SKU. The goal is to accelerate onboarding for customers who want unit-economics-aware defaults without running large-scale profiling jobs.

What this PR does (single continuous description): Implements a mini-sampler agent (orchard-sampler) that runs lightweight request sampling in the runtime path to collect sequence-length distributions, prefix reuse ratios, and short-term tail latency histograms; introduces a Quant Curator service that maps observed telemetry to a small set of tested quantization presets with a safety score; adds an econ-defaults generator that synthesizes tiered batch/cache/quant defaults per deployment SKU (burst, steady, latency-sensitive) and exposes them via the CLI and the Console defaults API; includes a new 'unit-econ quick-checker' CLI command that simulates expected cost/latency delta for candidate presets against recorded traces.

Files and surface changes: - runtime/orchard/mini_sampler.py: sampling agent with extremely small overhead path and failsafe circuit. - runtime/orchard/kv_prefetch_policy.py: new conservative prefetch policy for small caches. - optimizer/quant_curator/*.py: mapping and scoring logic for quant presets. - cli/econ_tool.py: `redwood econ quick-check` and `redwood econ apply-defaults` commands. - docs/quickstarts/econ-orchard.md: one-page guide and safety guidance. - tests/unit/test_mini_sampler.py, tests/integration/test_econ_cli.sh: end-to-end smoke tests.

Operational safeguards: sampling runs at 0.5% by default (configurable), includes an opt-out header for privacy-sensitive customers, and uses moving-window aggregation with caps to avoid memory blowups. The Quant Curator only recommends profiles that were previously exercised on a compatible architecture; every recommendation carries a 'safety_score' and default action is conservative (prefer higher precision when score < 0.9).

Compatibility and rollout: Feature-flagged behind runtime.feature.econ_orchard; we add a canary rollout sequence in the deployment manifest. Defaults generated by this tool do not auto-roll out — they are surfaced in Console and can be applied manually or via the CLI.

Testing and benchmarks: Adds microbenchmarks for sampler overhead (observed ~0.12% median CPU uplift at 0.5% sampling rate), integration test that runs quick-check simulations against a recorded trace and verifies unit-econ delta within expected bands, and end-to-end CI coverage for CLI flows.

Notes and follow-ups: - Follow-up ticket ENG-3301 will add the automatic suggestion card to the Console. - We intentionally keep the quant-curator rule set small (4 presets) to limit complexity and allow easier A/B testing.

title: Add residency-proofing middleware and audit entropy hashing
body:
Add residency-proofing middleware and audit entropy hashing

Motivation: Customers operating under strong data residency constraints need cryptographic proof that KMS operations and key usage occurred in the expected region without exposing deterministic audit identifiers that could be used to correlate requests across tenants. This PR introduces a residency-proofing middleware that records signed, region-anchored statements for KMS operations and an audit entropy-hashing layer that salts audit identifiers before logging to reduce cross-tenant correlation risk.

What this change does: Adds a lightweight middleware component in the frontdoor service that: (1) validates KMS provider region against tenant policy, (2) emits a residency proof blob signed by the platform's attestation key, and (3) attaches a short immutable nonce reference to the outgoing audit envelope. Introduces an audit hashing pipeline stage that applies HMAC-SHA256 with a per-tenant entropy seed (rotated periodically) to resource identifiers before they hit the audit log. Adds RBAC v2 enforcement rules that require the new residency-proof scope for operators who can override region pins. Feature-flagged rollout: residency-proofing is behind feature flag feature.residency_proofs and audit-hash behind feature.audit_entropy_hashing.

Risk and mitigation: New cryptographic material is added (attestation key and per-tenant entropy seeds). Keys are provisioned via the KMS provisioning flow and stored in the secrets store with restricted ACLs. CI includes integration tests that exercise seed rotation and residency proof verification. We ship a migration that backfills proof metadata where possible but does not change existing audit formats unless the feature flag is enabled.

Checklist: - [x] Middleware impl + unit tests; - [x] Audit pipeline stage + e2e test; - [x] RBAC v2 policy updates + policy unit tests; - [x] Migration and feature flags; - [x] Docs and changelog entry; - [x] Security review completed.

Related: Linear ENG-1792; security review ticket SEC-45.
Anil Kapoor: Can we avoid adding region strings directly to the proof blob? Prefer region IDs to reduce leak surface. Requested change: use region id mapping table.
Marina Cortez: Reply: switched to region IDs and added mapping table in infra/regions.go; updated tests to assert canonicalization.
Rhea Singh: Please add an emergency rollback path for the feature flag in case key provisioning fails during rollout. Requested change: docs + api to force-disable.
Marina Cortez: Reply: added admin API endpoint /internal/flags/disable and documented rollback steps in docs/ops/rollouts/residency_proofs_rollout.md.
Benji Wu: Concern about tenant entropy seed rotation window and audit continuity. Suggested change: provide a seed-epoch in the proof metadata so older logs can be re-hashed for queries.
Marina Cortez: Reply: included seed_epoch in signed proof and added backfill job skeleton in infra/secrets/migration_20250220.go.
Security team (SEC): Approved after review; asked for cryptographic algorithm callouts in docs (HMAC-SHA256, RSA-2048 attestation). Added to docs.
- Added residency-proofing middleware to attest KMS operations per-tenant; feature-flagged behind feature.residency_proofs.
- Introduced audit entropy hashing to salt resource identifiers in audit logs; feature.audit_entropy_hashing controls rollout.
- RBAC v2 update: new residency_proof operator scope required to override region pins.
New keys and per-tenant seeds are introduced. Mitigations: keys provisioned through existing KMS provisioning flow with limited ACLs, feature flags for gradual rollout, integration tests that exercise rotation/backfill, and an admin rollback API. Security reviewed and approved.
1) Enable feature.audit_entropy_hashing in staging and run audit search regression; 2) Enable feature.residency_proofs behind a canary for 1% of requests with non-blocking enforcement; 3) Monitor SLOs and audit query latency; 4) Gradually increase canary and enable enforcement; 5) Run backfill migration for seed_epoch where requested by customer support.
Ops should watch the secrets store quota during onboarding (provisioning creates per-tenant seeds). If provisioning fails, use the admin endpoint to disable the feature and run migration rollbacks. See docs/ops/rollouts/residency_proofs_rollout.md for detailed steps.

title: Introduce Econ Optimizer Runbook with Auto-apply Curation
body:
Introduce Econ Optimizer Runbook with Auto-apply Curation

Motivation: Customers repeatedly ask for safe, repeatable ways to adopt cost-reduction defaults (batching, prefix caching) and curated quantization profiles while preserving serving SLOs. This PR introduces a human-readable runbook + an 'auto-apply' curation flow for tenant defaults that is conservative by default and observable via telemetry. The runbook ties together: 1) declarative preset profiles (batch/cache/quant) for common workload archetypes; 2) a dry-run simulator that evaluates unit-economics and SLO risk; 3) an opt-in auto-apply path that materializes safe changes as tenant overrides; 4) telemetry hooks and audit records for traceability.
Design summary:
- Presets: new YAML schema under services/econ-runbook/presets/ describing batch_shape, cache_policy, target_quant_profile, acceptable_latency_delta_pct, and rollout_guard. Presets map to tags (e.g., "interactive-small", "batching-high-thr").
- Dry-run simulator: leverages existing workload traces to simulate token-cost, GPU utilization, and 95/99 latency shifts; generates an econ delta report with suggested confidence bands.
- Auto-apply: an operator-approved flow. A runbook action produces a proposed tenant override set stored in the config service; the operator may 'apply' which triggers a canary rollout (5% traffic) followed by a 1h observation window. Automatic rollback if latency/SLO breach or error rate spike > 2x baseline.
- Telemetry: new metrics and spans (econ.runbook.proposal.*, econ.runbook.apply.*, econ.runbook.simulation.summary) with links to correlated traces and the tenant audit log entry.
- Quant profiles: introduce a curated whitelist of quant strategies (q8_qat, q4_vnni-lite, q6_mixed) tied to model families and validated by the simulator. For model families not whitelisted, the runbook recommends fallback-safe profiles.
- Safety: rollout_guard enforces 'no more than X% unit cost reduction per 24h' and refuses aggressive quant profiles for low-latency SLO tenants.
Implementation notes:
- Added a small service (services/econ-runbook) that owns presets, simulation, and runbook state machine.
- Integrations: runtime change applier (runtime/config-applier) which applies overrides to serving runtime; simulator reuses workload-synth from perf-canary.
- UI: console/ops shows proposals and simulation artifacts (CSV and charts).
Checklist:
- [x] Preset schema and example presets
- [x] Simulator implementation and unit tests
- [x] Auto-apply workflow with canary + rollback hooks
- [x] Telemetry and audit log entries
- [x] API surface: POST /runbook/propose, POST /runbook/apply, GET /runbook/simulate
- [x] Docs: runbook README and console help
- [x] Dry-run-only flag for customers to preview without applying
- [x] End-to-end smoke test in CI
Caveats and tradeoffs:
- The simulator is trace-driven; corner cases with extreme tail distributions require conservative rollout_guard thresholds.
- Auto-apply is intentionally gated behind an operator approval in the first rollout; we can relax to fully automated in a later follow-up when we have more historical validation.
Related work and links: Linear ENG-4219 (preset catalog); ENG-4301 (simulator improvements); perf-canary reuse: services/perf-canary/workload-synth; console ticket: DES-88.
Migration: existing tenant defaults are left untouched; proposals create tenant override entries in config service so rollback restores prior state.
Rollout: merged to main, enabled behind feature flag runbook.auto_apply_v1 for a small set of early customers.

title: Add Terraform plan guard and Helm airgap shim with migration simulator
body:
Add Terraform plan guard and Helm airgap shim with migration simulator

Motivation: Private/on-prem customers running air-gapped or tightly controlled environments need deterministic upgrade outcomes. Two common failure modes we've seen in incidents are (1) unintended Terraform resource churn during apply and (2) missing chart artifacts or image references in airgapped clusters. This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: a Terraform plan guard (installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard) that enforces an allowlist and diff threshold before apply; a Helm airgap shim (installer/helm/airgap-shim) that stages and validates all chart assets and image digests ahead of rolling upgrades; and a migration simulator tool (installer/tools/migration_simulator) that can run DB/KV schema migrations in dry-run mode against a snapshot to detect incompatible changes before an in-place upgrade. Summary of changes: - installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard: new module that wraps terraform plan/apply with a preflight validator (configurable thresholds, allow/deny rules, and auto-approve gating). - installer/helm/airgap-shim: small utility and chart hooks to bundle required tarballs and image digests, validate registry replacement maps, and produce a signed asset manifest for offline clusters. - installer/tools/migration_simulator: Go binary that can replay migration SQL/transform logic against a detached DB snapshot and emit a regression report with row-level checks and schema diffs. - installer/docs/upgrade-playbook.md: updated step-by-step including how to run the plan guard, use the airgap shim, run the migration simulator, and perform the orchestrated rollback if needed. - ci: added tests for plan_guard logic and a unit test harness for migration simulator using SQLite snapshots. Backwards compatibility: Plan guard is opt-in via a top-level flag in the Terraform root (guard_enabled = false by default) so existing automation is unaffected. The Helm shim is additive; it exposes an alternate release flow for airgapped installs. Migration simulator does not change runtime migration code; it is strictly a preflight tool. Testing and verification: - Local integration tested against a reproducible example cluster and a synthetic DB snapshot (see installer/examples/airgap-smoke). - Terraform plan guard tested with scenarios: benign diff, resource rename, and unexpected deletion; guard thresholds behaved as expected, blocking destroy-heavy plans. - Helm shim validated on an offline KIND cluster (chart assets served from local registry) and through OCI tarball manifests. - CI: unit tests and a small integration job passed on re-run; one flaky test in early runs (migration_simulator/sql_parser_test) was stabilized by simplifying the parser and adding a fixture. Rollback/runbook: The playbook documents a staged rollback orchestrator that leverages the plan guard's dry-run mode to detect residual drift and the airgap shim's manifest to re-seed missing artifacts. Steps include: 1) mark tenant for maintenance (installer/scripts/quarantine.sh), 2) snapshot current DB and object storage, 3) run migration simulator to verify revert path, 4) apply rollback release using Helm shim with signed manifest, 5) validate with smoke prompts and metrics. Security notes: Signed manifests use the existing KMS/HSM integration; the migration simulator never ships snapshots off-cluster unless explicitly exported by an operator. Known limitations: - Simulator currently supports primary Postgres schemas and a subset of KV transforms; complex stored procedures are not simulated. - Plan guard thresholds require tuning per customer workload. See upgrade-playbook for mitigation. Links: Linear ENG-2124 for the feature epic; a follow-up is tracked under INF-403 to add Postgres stored procedure simulation.
Add an optional pre-upgrade Terraform plan guard that blocks apply when drift or unexpected resource churn is detected; introduce a Helm 'airgap shim' that stages chart artifacts for disconnected clusters; include a local migration simulator that runs schema migrations in dry-run mode against an exported DB snapshot; provide an updated upgrade playbook documenting safe dice-roll rollback steps and verification commands.
Priya Nair: This looks good overall — can we make the plan guard threshold configurable per-resource?
Aisha Khan: Yes — added resource_level_thresholds and documented examples in plan_guard/README.
Samir Patel: Migration simulator is a great safety net. Can we add an explicit disclaimer about not running simulator in production DBs?
Aisha Khan: Added warning in simulator README and playbook; emphasized operator-only execution and snapshot requirement.
Miguel Ortega: CI flaked on sql parser; pushed a fix and re-run. Approving post-fix.
Priya Nair: Approve after docs update.
Miguel Ortega: Merged via squash after approvals.

title: add-provenance-anchors-and-version-notary-workflow
body:
add-provenance-anchors-and-version-notary-workflow

Motivation: onboarding workflows currently lack compact, verifiable provenance snippets and a lightweight version notarization step that ties a model upload to deterministic metadata and a stable version token. This PR introduces 'provenance anchors' (compact signed fingerprints derived from model manifest + sample telemetry) and a 'version notary' service that issues short canonical version tokens and generates a succinct release blurb suitable for changelogs and automated release notes.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a provenance anchor generator (tools/anchor_generator.py) that canonicalizes manifest fields, computes a content-hash, and attaches sampled telemetry signatures to improve de-dup and drift detection. 2) Introduces a notary microservice (notary/service.py) that consumes anchors and returns an immutable version token (vtoken) together with a short humanized summary used by release automation. 3) Plumbs anchor metadata into the onboarding pipeline (ingest/worker.py changes) so every successful model intake stores anchor and vtoken in the model index. 4) Adds a changelog helper (scripts/brief_builder.py) that converts vtoken + anchor into a one-paragraph release note draft and a compact manifest excerpt for audits. 5) Tests for anchor stability and notary idempotency (tests/test_anchor.py, tests/test_notary_idempotency.py). 6) CI pipeline updates to run anchor stability matrix on a sample of previously onboarded models.

Design notes: - Anchors are intentionally compact (<= 256 bytes) and include: canonical manifest hash, sampled latency/quantile telemetry fingerprint, and a short provenance salt. Anchors are signed using the existing keystore integration so they can be verified offline. - The vtoken is a short base32 token (8-10 chars) derived from the signed anchor fingerprint; it is intended for human-friendly usage (UIs, changelogs) and is not a replacement for full model versioning semantics. - Notary enforces idempotency: repeated submissions with identical canonical manifest -> same vtoken. Different telemetry samples will be canonicalized into the anchor deterministically. - The changelog helper emits an opinionated short blurb: model alias, vtoken, delta hints (new/changed inputs), and a single-line cost/perf note if telemetry delta > threshold.

Checklist: - [x] Anchor generator implementation + unit tests
- [x] Notary service + integration tests
- [x] Pipeline integration (worker commit) + warmup hooks
- [x] Changelog helper + template
- [x] CI stability matrix job
- [x] Docs: docs/provenance_anchors.md + examples in redwood-examples repo (link added)

Testing & validation: ran anchor stability suite against 120 model manifests (2/14/2025 sample) and verified bit-stable anchors after canonicalization. Notary idempotency tested with 50 repeated uploads. CI job includes an expanded sample check that previously failed once (flaky serialization) and was fixed by normalizing timestamp fields.

Rollout plan: feature-gated by config flag model_registry.enable_provenance_anchors (default off). We'll rollout to staging for 48 hours, run a smoke ingestion of the nightly model-catalog and verify anchors and vtoken generation. After monitoring (console dashboard widget added), toggle on in production. Backout: disable flag and purge vtoken index writes (safe no-destructive path).

Security & compliance: Keystore usage relies on existing KMS integration; signing keys are rotated per current rotation policy. No sensitive telemetry is included — only aggregated sample hashes and quantiles. Compliance reviewed by Security (SUP-1282) and accepted with minor doc clarifications.

Related work: builds on prior intake normalization work (ENG-3780) and the changelog autobuilder prototype (ENG-4602).
Luca Romano (2025-02-15): Nice compact representation. Small request: can we avoid including raw quantile arrays in the anchor payload? Suggest storing a hash of the quantile vector instead so the anchor stays tightly bounded.
Author (Priya) (2025-02-15): Good catch — switched quantile vector to a SHA256 of the vector and updated tests. Anchors are still verifiable with the hash plus signature.
Maya Chen (2025-02-16): Security reviewed the keystore usage; confirm rotation semantics. Also please add a note about rate limits for the notary to avoid accidental floods during bulk backfills.
Author (Priya) (2025-02-16): Added keystore doc links and a circuit-breaker to notary/service.py; rate limit default is 500 reqs/min per api-key. Added to docs and config.
Diego Alvarez (2025-02-17): Integration test failed once due to nondeterministic JSON ordering in example manifests. Recommend adding a deterministic serializer — either canonical JSON or stable field ordering.
Author (Priya) (2025-02-17): Implemented deterministic serializer using sorted keys and explicit field whitelist. Re-ran stability matrix; all green.
Introduce provenance anchors: compact, signed fingerprints tying model manifest + sampled telemetry into a short verifiable anchor.
Add version notary that issues stable human-friendly vtokens for use in UI and changelogs.
Pipeline integration so newly onboarded models record anchor + vtoken in the model index (feature-gated).
New changelog brief builder that converts vtoken + anchor into a one-paragraph automated release note draft.
CI: anchor stability matrix job added to nightly checks.

title: SLO Lease Rebalancer for Soft Regional Handoffs
body:
SLO Lease Rebalancer for Soft Regional Handoffs

Background: Regional incidents and maintenance windows frequently force temporary redistribution of SLO responsibility across regions. Existing failover semantics are abrupt: either route fully to a fallback region or trigger a global throttle, which causes avoidable churn and user-visible latency spikes. This PR implements a SLO Lease Rebalancer that permits soft, capacity-aware handoffs: regions can donate or acquire SLO leases over a bounded window, with attenuated traffic shifts, circuit-aware backoff, and an emergency reclaim path for correctness. Design highlights: 1) Lease model: each region holds leases for tenant partitions with a lease_window_ms TTL and an associated capacity_score updated from per-route throughput and node health. 2) Rebalancer algorithm: periodic scoring pass computes donors and receivers and proposes chunked lease transfers sized by capacity_delta and handoff_threshold_pct. Transfers are staged over windows with exponential backoff on transient failures. 3) Soft resume: receivers apply an attenuated activation that gradually increases weight (0 -> target) so downstream caches and KV warmup reduce cold-start SLO violations. 4) Circuit interplay: when a receiving region has active circuits tripped for a tenant, the transfer is paused and marked for retry; donors maintain temporary sticky leases until a safe handoff can complete. 5) Observability: new lease_migration_success/failure, lease_transfer_duration_ms, and region_capacity_score metrics plus handoff traces. 6) Safety: emergency_force_reclaim shortcut (operator-triggered) for edge cases and a conservatively defaulted handoff_threshold_pct=0.25 to avoid aggressive churn. Changes made: - runtime/lease_manager.go: core rebalancer, scoring, transfer orchestration, retry/backoff. - runtime/lease_manager_test.go: unit tests covering scoring, chunking, backoff semantics. - routing/handshake.go: handshake extension for staged weight updates and compatibility checks. - observability/metrics/lease_metrics.prom: metric definitions and dashboard hints. - docs/operational/lease-rebalancer.md: runbook, default knobs, and troubleshooting. - deploy/k8s/upgrade-hooks.yaml: prestop hook to drain leases on node removal. - cli/ctl-handoff.sh: convenience operator script to trigger handoffs or force-reclaim. - ops/runbooks/slo-hand-offs.md: incident runbook additions. - examples/handshake-sim.json: simulation scenarios used in testing. Testing and validation: comprehensive unit coverage added; integration test in perf-canary simulated a cross-region outage and validated a staged handoff with 0.12% SLO breach delta (within target). Chaos testing included region-level partitioning and node terminations; rebalancer paused transfers and resumed once capacity stabilized. Performance: small CPU overhead (~3% p99 increase during active rebalances) observed in canary, within SLA. Rollout plan: canary at 5% traffic in us-west-2 for 2h, monitor lease_migration_success, slo_violation_rate, region_capacity_score and downstream error/latency. If stable, ramp to 25% for 4h then global. Auto rollback on >0.5% sustained increase in SLO breaches for 15m or >2s median token latency regression. Backwards compatibility: no changes to public APIs; all behavior behind runtime feature-flag runtime.slo_lease_rebalancer.enabled=false by default for safe staged rollout. Operator knobs: lease_window_ms (default 900000), handoff_threshold_pct (default 0.25), max_chunk_size (default 100 partitions), emergency_force_reclaim (manual). Migration and upgrade notes: ensure dedicated nodes have upgrade-hooks applied to allow graceful lease drain; upgrade order should follow cross-region canary then control plane. Known limitations and mitigations: in extreme multi-region partition churn the rebalancer defers transfers to avoid oscillation; we log deferred_transfer_* metrics to aid future tuning. Documentation added and internal runbooks updated. Checklist: [x] Implementation and tests, [x] Integration/perf canary, [x] Observability and runbooks, [x] Operator scripts, [x] Reviewed and approved. This description consolidates rationale, design, testing, and rollout guidance for operators and reviewers.
Introduce SLO Lease Rebalancer: enables controlled handoff of SLO responsibility between regions with time-boxed soft resume and capacity-aware lease migration. Config knobs: lease_window_ms, handoff_threshold_pct, emergency_force_reclaim. No user-facing API changes.
Ethan Patel: Can you explain how this avoids oscillation when two regions try to rebalance simultaneously? Reply: The scoring pass is leader-elected per-tenant-partition and uses monotonic timestamps plus a proposed-token based compare to avoid split decisions; we also add a jittered backoff on retries.
Riley Gonzales: Request: add metric for deferred_transfer_count and a debug flag to force single-step transfers. Reply: Added deferred_transfer_count and ctl-handoff now supports --force-single-step for operator testing.
Samira Noor: Question about SLA impact on hot path: why not warm cache before weight increase? Reply: soft resume increments weight in 10% steps with 30s spacing by default; this was tuned in canary to balance warmup vs failover speed.
Ethan Patel: Approve after addressing lint and adding runbook section on emergency_force_reclaim. Reply: Lint fixed and runbook extended.
Riley Gonzales: Approved on green CI.
Unit tests exercise scoring and backoff; integration tests simulate cross-region outage; perf-canary measured p50/p95/p99 token latency and CPU; chaos engineering (region partition) validated pause/resume semantics. Synthetic traffic sim harness included in examples/handshake-sim.json.
Canary 5% traffic in us-west-2 for 2 hours, monitor lease_migration_success and slo_violation_rate; if stable ramp to 25% for 4 hours then global. Auto rollback on >0.5% sustained SLO breach increase for 15m.
Feature-flag flip to disable runtime.slo_lease_rebalancer.enabled=false instantly disables rebalancer; operator script ctl-handoff.sh --reclaim can force donor sticky leases back. In case of systemic regressions, revert the commit on main and trigger emergency reclaim per runbook.

title: page-siloing-locality-preserving-evictor-and-spill-attenuation
body:
page-siloing-locality-preserving-evictor-and-spill-attenuation

Context: Our KV cache has increasing fragmentation and frequent small spill writes under mixed workloads (short chat traces + occasional long contexts). Motivation: reduce tail latency and spill I/O amplification by keeping hot keys co-located in contiguous page 'silos' and by making the evictor prefer locality-preserving demotions. This PR implements a page siloing allocator, a locality-preserving eviction policy, and a spill attenuation controller that defers and coalesces spill writes when under transient pressure. Changes are gated behind a runtime flag (kv.page_siloing_enabled) and incremental by default. Design summary: 1) Page siloing allocator groups allocations into silos by tenant and affinity score computed from recent access fingerprinting. Silos aim to keep related KV entries on contiguous page ranges to reduce fragmentation and sequentialize spill write patterns. 2) Locality-preserving evictor selects victims not only by recency/heat but also by silo contiguity score so evictions prefer reclaiming whole subranges that yield contiguous free segments. This substantially reduces micro-fragmentation. 3) Spill attenuation controller monitors spill sink bandwidth and in-flight spill latency; when spikes occur it switches from immediate per-page spill to deferred coalesced-write mode (batching multiple evicted pages into a single larger write, limited by a configurable max_coalesce_bytes). 4) Integration with scheduler: the evictor now exposes a hint to the continuous-batching scheduler so that inflight generation batches avoid pinning tokens to pages that are being reclaimed, reducing KV lookup latency spikes during concurrent eviction. 5) Telemetry and evaluation: new metrics (kv.silo_fill_ratio, kv.eviction_contiguity, kv.spill_coalesce_ratio) and an end-to-end perf test harness that simulates mixed short+long context traffic. Implementation notes: - New package/runtime files: kv/silo_allocator.{cc,hh}, kv/evictor_locality.cc, kv/spill_attenuator.cc, scheduler/evictor_hints.go - Conservative default config: silo max size = 8MB, coalesce window = 50ms, max_coalesce_bytes = 2MB - Backwards compatible: no public API changes, feature off by default. Migration path: customers can enable per-tenant via console or feature flags; rollout plan includes dark launches and Canary pool in Dedicated. Test plan: unit tests for silo placement, fuzz tests for contiguity heuristics, integration perf job in perf-canary (redwood/perf-canary) comparing tail latency and WAN spill traffic. CI: initial CI run failed on an intermittent scheduler race in continuous batching; fixed by adding a small handshake between evictor and scheduler (evictor_hints now uses a version token to ensure stale hints are ignored). Outcomes: synthetic perf runs show 18-28% reduction in spill IOPS for mixed workloads and 6-12% tail latency improvement (95th/99th) in our canary environment. Risk/Tradeoffs: - Coalescing spikes into larger writes increases latency of reclaim path under sustained pressure; attenuation controller uses conservative defaults to avoid unbounded backlog. - Siloing increases internal fragmentation risk for extremely small tenant workloads; mitigated by letting small tenants share silos until threshold. Related: follows patterns from ENG-2143 and borrows parts of earlier spill-backpressure work (SUP-4021).
Introduces page siloing and a locality-preserving evictor to reduce fragmentation and spill I/O; adds adaptive spill attenuation knobs and telemetry; no API changes.
Marco DeLuca: Nice work. Can you quantify memory overhead for silo metadata? Also please ensure the allocator path is hot-path optimized (avoid locks).
Priya Natarajan: Silo metadata is ~128 bytes per active silo; silos are sized to amortize metadata. Hot path uses a lock-free fastpath (see silo_allocator.h comment) and falling back to a per-thread slab under contention.
Lina Zhao: The contiguity score looks promising but I'm concerned about tenant fairness—could a noisy tenant hog contiguous pages?
Priya Natarajan: Added a tenant-share cap and a decay on affinity score; documented in configs/kv_default.yaml and added unit test 'tenant_share_cap_test'.
Owen Park: CI reported a flake in continuous-batcher when evictor hints were delayed. Did you add ordering guarantees?
Priya Natarajan: Yes — added a version token in evictor_hints; scheduler ignores hints with older tokens. This resolved the flake (see commit 9f8e7d6).
Marco DeLuca: Approving pending squash and a short perf run on the canary cluster.
Lina Zhao: Observability looks adequate; approve after addressing small doc nits.
Automation Bot: CLA and license checks passed.

title: Introduce intake quickcheck CLI and localized release-brief generator
body:
Introduce intake quickcheck CLI and localized release-brief generator

Motivation: Onboarding reviewers and downstream product owners often need concise, translated release briefs for model updates. Manual translation and privacy-aware redaction are causing delays in rollouts across EMEA/APAC. This PR adds a small intake quickcheck CLI that runs deterministic probe replays and emits a compact, privacy-aware release brief in one or more locales.

What this PR does: Adds 'rmd-intake-quickcheck' (CLI) that: runs a configurable set of probes against a candidate model bundle in a sandbox, extracts a compact performance summary, and synthesizes a release brief using templates per-locale. The generator supports: en, es, fr, de, ja by default and a pluggable translator adapter for additional locales. It also applies redaction rules for detected PII and sensitive sample text in briefs. The onboarding manifest schema gains an optional 'release_brief_locales' field to pin locales for automatic generation. A small migration script converts existing manifests with default locale sets.

Checklist: 
- [x] CLI implementation and documentation (quickstart) 
- [x] Release brief templates and locale mappings 
- [x] Privacy redaction rules + tests 
- [x] Translator adapter interface + fallback to English 
- [x] Integration test that runs a mocked probe replay and validates brief output 
- [x] Migration script for existing manifests 

Commits (high-level): 
- Add CLI entrypoint and probe-replay harness (5f3a1c)
- Locale templates and translation adapter with offline glossary (9b7d22)
- PII redaction rules and unit tests (c2a4be)

Files changed (high level): 
- cmd/rmd-intake-quickcheck/main.go (CLI and config parsing)
- internal/probereplay/runner.go (small harness for replaying probes)

PII redaction uses a conservative heuristic; we err on redacting ambiguous tokens and log redaction summaries for audit.

Related work: ENG-4762 (onboard telemetry improvements), ENG-5121 (release notes automation).

Notes for reviewers: Focus on the redaction rule coverage and fallback behaviour for missing locale translations. We should confirm legal/compliance signoff is OK with the conservative redaction strategy before enabling auto-generation for enterprise bundles.

title: introduce-invocation-compressor-and-slo-smartlink
body:
introduce-invocation-compressor-and-slo-smartlink

Context and motivation: customer incident SUP-881 showed long-tail token cost spikes correlated with repeated redundant context blocks across streaming and non-streaming invocations. This PR introduces an invocation compression middleware (server-side) that detects repeated prefix patterns at the invocation level and compresses the outgoing trace/metric payloads and token-cost annotations for storage and dashboarding. In parallel, we add a small SLO SmartLink feature that binds compressed invocation fingerprints to SLO incidents so on-call can quickly jump from an SLO violation to representative uncompressed traces for triage. Design notes: the compressor runs in the observability sidecar and performs a lightweight rolling hash to identify repeated prefix segments and a canonical token-map delta encoding to preserve cost attribution per token. Compression is lossless for cost attribution metadata and lossy for raw token text (we store a digest to rehydrate only for on-demand debug flows). The SLO SmartLink stores a compact fingerprint index in the observability metadata service and surfaces a deterministic link in the SLO UI that will trigger a gated rehydration flow and time-bound audit access. Migration and rollout: feature gated behind 'invocation_compressor' and 'slo_smartlink' feature flags; rollout strategy is staged by tenant percentage with a background backfill job to compress 7 days of recent invocations for opt-in tenants. Backfill is throttled and can be paused via the console. Observability impacts: compression reduces storage and query egress for invocation artifacts (estimated ~3x reduction for customers with high prefix reuse). We add new metrics invocation_compressor.compress_rate, invocation_compressor.rehydrate_latency, and slo_smartlink.link_resolution_time; dashboards included in this PR. Testing: unit tests for the rolling hash and delta encoding, integration tests exercising end-to-end compression and rehydration, plus a small replaybench scenario with synthetic repeated prompts. Performance: compressor introduces sub-millisecond overhead on p95 invocation path in production profile; profiling results included in commits. Rollout notes: start at 5% tenants, monitor compress_rate and rehydrate_latency, escalate abort on >100ms rehydrate p95 or if cost attribution divergence >0.1% on sample prompts. Related work: follows patterns in ENG-3421 (token-cost attribution) and complements the token-heatmap panels. Checklist: add feature flags, add metrics and dashboards, add backfill job, e2e tests, docs updates, console link wiring, add perf bench.
Diego Alvarez: Nice approach — can we avoid double-hashing when rehydration is requested? Also question on GC strategy for fingerprint index.
Author(Maya): We cache the last-10k fingerprints in-memory with LRU; added note and test to ensure GC doesn't evict active SLO links. Rehydration flow computes digest only if the fingerprint is missing (no double-hash).
Priya Nair: Need more clarity on security/audit when rehydrating compressed text for on-call — please add KMS/HSM and access audit in docs.
Author(Maya): Added a section in docs/observability/invocation-compression.md describing gated KMS usage and short-lived rehydration tokens; rehydration now requires audit log entry before full-text retrieval.
Samir Patel: Perf numbers look good; one nit on metrics cardinality — invocation_compressor.compress_rate should be tenant-scoped only, not prompt-shape labelled by full prompt.
Author(Maya): Adjusted metrics to tenant and prompt_shape labels only; removed full prompt label to protect PII and control cardinality.
Add invocation compression sidecar to reduce observability storage and speed up SLO triage via SmartLinks. Feature is behind feature flags and rolled out staged by tenant. Includes new metrics and dashboards; see docs/observability/invocation-compression.md for operational guidance.
If slo_smartlink shows >1% unresolved links in 10m window, pause backfill and set feature flag to false for affected tenants.
If rehydrate_latency p95 exceeds 100ms, set invocation_compressor to passive and open an incident runbook: observability/invocation-compressor-runbook.md.
Backfill throttle can be controlled from the console under Observability -> Backfill Jobs -> invocation-compress.

title: starvation-prober-soft-ejector: detect KV-heavy starvation and softly eject to preserve latency SLOs
body:
starvation-prober-soft-ejector: detect KV-heavy starvation and softly eject to preserve latency SLOs

Motivation: Continuous-batcher occasionally experiences prolonged tail latency during KV-heavy workloads where certain requests pin large KV regions and prevent fair progress for low-KV or stateless requests. Existing admission and fairshare heuristics alleviate this in steady state but do not react fast enough to transient starvation caused by sudden KV-window growth. This PR introduces a starvation prober plus a soft-ejector policy that detects likely starvation windows and gently evicts a small number of KV-hot requests to restore headroom and keep latency SLOs.

What this change does: 1) Adds a lightweight background "starvation prober" that samples queue windows and maintains a short-term KV-load histogram. The prober uses a rolling measurement (3s default) to detect when the effective KV-saturation exceeds a configured threshold relative to lane capacity. 2) Introduces a "soft-ejector" path in the continuous-batcher which, when the prober signals starvation, marks a minimal set of in-flight KV-heavy slots for soft-ejection: they are moved to an expedited eviction path that preserves KV cache warmup where possible (writes back partial KV pins) and optionally hedges to a lower-capacity model variant. 3) Adds a new scheduler hint (kv_evict_score) used by the allocator to prefer ejecting the smallest-effect requests first (by estimated KV pins and remaining tokens). 4) Tuning knobs exposed via config: prober_window_ms, kv_saturation_threshold, soft_eject_max_pct, eject_backoff_ms. 5) New unit and integration tests and an e2e perf benchmark harness that simulates sudden KV pressure spikes.

Why this is safe: soft-ejector does not forcibly kill requests — it moves them to a controlled eviction lane which tries graceful spillback or migration to compatible model variants. The feature is opt-in by default and guarded behind a config flag. Rollout plan is conservative: feature flag off, enable in Canary stage for dedicated pools with 1% traffic, then gradual ramp with telemetry checks for request success rate and KV cache warmth regressions.

Metrics & Observability: new metrics added: runtime.starvation_prober.saturation_ratio, runtime.soft_ejector.ejections_total, runtime.soft_ejector.avg_eject_latency, and tracing tags on ejected requests (eject_reason=starvation_prober). There is a dashboard tile and alert rule suggestion PERF-STARVE-01 (high sustained saturation_ratio >0.85 for >30s).

Related work: follows earlier KV-aware schedulers (ENG-3512) and complements the holdback/reserve features; differs by being transient-probe driven and prioritizing minimal disturbance to overall throughput.

title: unify-retry-profiles-and-lightweight-stream-helpers-across-sdks
body:
unify-retry-profiles-and-lightweight-stream-helpers-across-sdks

Motivation: SDKs historically contained duplicated retry/backoff and stream ergonomics code that diverged subtly between Python/TypeScript/Go. That made cross-SDK behavior inconsistent (different default jitter, different max_retry windows) and increased maintenance burden. This PR extracts a transport-agnostic RetryProfile and introduces a tiny, consistent set of lightweight stream helpers for each SDK so app code can be ported with fewer surface changes.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduce a core RetryProfile concept and backoff parameter mapping used by all SDKs (max_attempts, initial_backoff_ms, max_backoff_ms, jitter_mode, hedged_retries).
- Replace ad-hoc retry logic in each SDK with small adapters that map RetryProfile -> transport specific retry strategies.
- Add ergonomic streaming helpers: Python async generator wrapper (stream.iter_lines_safe), TS async iterable shim (stream.consumeSafe), Go StreamHandle interface + convenience ReadPump.
- Add cross-SDK unit/compat tests that assert parity on default retry timeline for common scenarios (auth 401 then refresh, transient 429, slow downstream).
- Documentation: migration guide and explicit examples for moving from the legacy per-SDK backoff flags to the unified RetryProfile.
- Version bumps: python sdk -> 0.12.0, typescript sdk -> 1.27.0, go sdk -> 1.8.0.

Why transport-agnostic RetryProfile: Teams run heterogeneous stacks (frontend TS, backend Python, microservice in Go). Previously, moving a workload between services required tuning three different knobs. The RetryProfile is a single well-documented primitive that can be serialized as JSON, stored in config, and applied consistently across languages.

Migration notes:
- If you set per-SDK backoff env flags (RETRY_INITIAL_MS, RETRY_MAX_MS, RETRY_ATTEMPTS), they will continue to be read but are deprecated — migrate to a RetryProfile config shipped to your service.
- Streaming helper names changed: start_stream -> open_stream is preserved at the transport level but helper names for safe iteration are new (see examples in docs/sdk/migration/retry-profile.md).

Scope and risk: The change is primarily additive (new adapters + helpers) but rewires retry decision points in each SDK. We validated with end-to-end test harness and Canary run against staging traffic for 48h.

Release notes (summary): Unify retry/backoff semantics across SDKs, add safe streaming helpers, improve cross-language portability, bump SDK versions.

Sofia Martinez: Added optional callback parameter (onBackpressure) with test; wired it to the consumeSafe shim as a noop by default.
Luca Bianchi: Go adapter looks good. One nit: prefer context-aware Close for StreamHandle to make cancellation explicit.
Sofia Martinez: Updated interface to CloseWithContext(ctx) and kept Close() for compatibility. Added deprecation comment for Close().

title: improve-streaming-backpressure-kernel-pacing-and-flush-cadence
body:
improve-streaming-backpressure-kernel-pacing-and-flush-cadence

Motivation: production streaming customers saw 95th/99th token latency spikes when model sequence interleaving and kernel dispatch jitter aligned under high concurrency. Root causes identified: the token emission loop was flushing per-request too aggressively, kernel selection introduced micro-scheduling stalls on heterogenous sequences, and continuous-batching queues lacked a backpressure signal tied to active KV cache memory pressure. This PR addresses these by (1) introducing an adaptive flush cadence that groups sub-token flushes into a short window to amortize syscalls and network writes while preserving low tail latency for first tokens, (2) adding a soft backpressure token to the continuous-batcher that temporarily reduces per-request batching depth when KV cache hit-rate drops or memory pressure rises, (3) pacing kernel dispatch for mixed sequence lengths via a simple cost-estimator in the kernel selector to avoid dispatching long-seq kernels immediately ahead of short-seq work, and (4) minor refactors to the token loop to separate emission, checkpointing, and stall-detection logic. Implementation summary: streamer.cpp now tracks per-stream last-flush timestamp and an adaptive_window_ms computed from recent per-token latency percentiles; a new flush_coalescer module consolidates writes within the window. continuous_batcher adds a backpressure_count that increments when kv_cache_manager reports degraded hit_rate or memory_watermark>0.8; when backpressure_count>threshold, the batcher lowers max_batch_size and exposes a diagnostics metric. kernel_selector computes a normalized cost metric (compute_tokens*cost_factor + io_penalty) and delays high-cost kernels by small randomized jitter to reduce head-of-line blocking. Observability: added metrics streaming.flush_coalesce_ratio, batcher.backpressure_level, kernel.pacing_delay and tagged spans for flush-window boundary events. Tests and benchmarks: synthetic microbenchmarks show 95th token latency reduction of 18-32% across r4 and a100 instances for mixed-long/short workloads, and overall token throughput maintained within 2% of baseline. Safety and rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.streaming.adaptive_flush=true and batcher backpressure disabled by default. Rollout plan: enable in canary for 10% of traffic for 48h, monitor streaming.flush_coalesce_ratio and tail-token SLOs and KV cache hit_rate; automatic rollback if 95th latency regresses >5%. Notes: this is performance-sensitive; code paths touched are hot and extra attention paid to allocations and atomic operations. See release_notes for user-facing changes and observability additions.
Alec Zhou: Please add a microbenchmark comparing fixed flush cadences vs adaptive_window_ms; we need a reproducible script. Author reply: added tests/benchmarks/streaming_latency.py with parameters and CI entry.
Priya Menon: Concerned about atomics in hot path; can we avoid extra CAS in streamer? Author reply: changed to read-mostly atomic with seqlock fallback for updates, moved cost computation off critical path.
Diego Ramirez: Suggest exposing the backpressure signal in the SDK / control-plane so ops can opt to drain queues; minor nit about metric labels. Author reply: exposed batcher.backpressure_level as numeric gauge and added tags runtime.instance_id and model.name per Diego's suggestion.
Alec Zhou: CI flake on macOS test harness unrelated; reran and all green. Approve after small logging cleanup.
Priya Menon: Approved. Diego Ramirez: Approved.
- Reduced streaming token 95th latency by 18-32% for mixed-sequence workloads via adaptive flush coalescing and kernel pacing. - Added runtime flags: runtime.streaming.adaptive_flush and runtime.batcher.enable_backpressure. - New observability metrics: streaming.flush_coalesce_ratio, batcher.backpressure_level, kernel.pacing_delay.

title: Streamlined credential fallback and multi-SDK pullstream ergonomics
body:
Streamlined credential fallback and multi-SDK pullstream ergonomics

Motivation: multiple SDK teams and downstream apps reported subtle mismatch in credential handoff semantics between Python/TS/Go pull-stream implementations and a confusing fallback surface that made token rotation fragile. This PR consolidates the credential fallback strategy into a small composable "CredFallbackChain" and rationalizes the pullstream iterator shape across SDKs so that caller ergonomics and retry semantics are consistent.

Summary of changes (single-pass continuous description): Implement CredFallbackChain abstraction with three pluggable providers (env -> cached refresh -> delegated callback). Add lightweight CredLease helper that exposes expires_at and refresh_if_needed hooks. Replace legacy token swap hooks in Python/TS/Go SDKs with a single adapter layer that translates chain outcomes into the language-specific session objects. Introduce PullStream.v2 ergonomics: a single async iterator pattern that yields chunk envelopes and exposes a .resume() hook for resumable streams; ensure backpressure is preserved for TS and Go via the same resume semantics. Unify retry profile defaults across SDKs: 3 fast-retries for handshake, exponential backoff for token refresh, idempotent request hints for streaming resumes. Add parity test harnesses that exercise cross-language replay of a recorded streaming session to validate token-rotation timing, resume correctness, and finalization semantics. Bump SDK versions: python 0.42.1 -> 0.43.0, typescript 2.1.0 -> 2.2.0, go 0.9.4 -> 0.10.0.

Files changed (high level): packages/sdk-python/redwood/credentials.py (new chain + lease), packages/sdk-python/redwood/streaming.py (pullstream v2), packages/sdk-typescript/src/credentials/chain.ts, packages/sdk-typescript/src/stream/pullstreamV2.ts, packages/sdk-go/session/cred_chain.go, packages/sdk-go/stream/pullstream_v2.go, shared/test/interop/recorded_replays/*, docs/sdk-migration/pullstream-v2.md, changelogs/CHANGELOG-0.43.0.md, package manifests for version bumps.

Testing & CI: added unit tests covering CredFallbackChain permutations, integration harness that replays a mocked region with token rotation, and cross-language parity tests that run sequentially in CI (Dockerized runner). CI initially failed on flaky TS stream backpressure test; fixed by delaying segment ack by 5ms in the harness and added deterministic timing harness. Final CI: all checks green.

Compatibility notes and upgrade path: PullStream.v2 is opt-in in this PR; existing PullStream.v1 adapters are provided in each SDK under legacy/compat to ease transition. CredFallbackChain defaults mirror the old behavior (env -> refresh token) but expose a simple register_callback() API for advanced environments (sidecar/hardware tokens). The version bumps are minor (no breaking API surface unless consumers explicitly adopt v2). Migration doc included at docs/sdk-migration/pullstream-v2.md.

title: soft fallback mapper for legacy tool envelopes and streaming stability
body:
soft fallback mapper for legacy tool envelopes and streaming stability

Summary: Adds a non-destructive backward-compatibility layer that maps legacy v1 'tool envelopes' and mixed-mode streaming events into the current structured tool-calling shape. This is a runtime-level, opt-out behavior controlled by a lightweight request header (X-RW-Compat: legacy=1) and a server-side fallback profile. Motivation: We continue to see client integrations that emit the older tool/function envelope format and interleave streaming 'event' fragments that do not align with the v2 structured tool-call and streaming framing. These cause either broken tool invocation or stream mangling for customers who cannot upgrade immediately. This PR provides a safety net so clients can continue to operate while we deprecate v1 on a scheduled timeline.

What this change does (single-line sections concatenated into this description): - Adds a LegacyEnvelopeMapper in the API gateway that coalesces fragmented streaming events into a canonical tool-call request object when the compat header is present. - Introduces X-RW-Compat header handling and a short-lived server-side flag for rollout (defaults disabled). - Adds unit and integration tests that simulate partial streaming frames, nested tool payloads, and mixed text-with-tool streams. - Exposes a per-tenant opt-in via Console feature flag and adds telemetry to track how often mappings are used and whether coercion dropped any fields. - Adds a best-effort deterministic fallback for ambiguous payloads: the mapper will prefer tool metadata in this order: explicit tool_name > envelope.tool > legacy_inferred_name.

Implementation notes and constraints: - The fallback is intentionally conservative: fields are not removed; ambiguous sub-fields are placed under a legacy_metadata map on the coerced payload so v2 handlers can log and surface them without losing data. - Mapper runs early in the request handling pipeline to preserve KV cache keys and batching behavior. - This PR does not change the public schema contract unless the compat header is supplied.

Tests and CI: - Commits include a new suite that replays recorded incident streams (replay fixtures) where older clients sent 3-part event envelopes; these fixtures were captured from a postmortem trace and scrubbed. - CI matrix covers gateway unit tests, end-to-end gateway->runtime smoke, and SDK regression checks. - Initial CI run failed on a flaky streaming test; flake fixed with a deterministic buffering tweak.

Commits (high-level): - feat(gateway): add legacy envelope mapper and header parsing - test(gateway): add replay fixtures and streaming integration tests - feat(console): tenant opt-in flag and telemetry hooks - fix(tests): deterministic buffer improvement to stabilize CI - docs: add compatibility guide and scheduled deprecation note

Files changed (high level): - gateway/compat/LegacyEnvelopeMapper.go (core mapping logic and heuristics) - gateway/handlers/stream_decoder.go (stream coalescing, small buffering change) - runtime/handler/tool_invoker.go (adds legacy_metadata passthrough) - console/flags/compat_flags.go (tenant opt-in surface) - telemetry/mappers/compat_telemetry.go (usage counters and histograms) - test/fixtures/legacy_stream_replays/ (three JSONL fixtures) - docs/compatibility/legacy-to-structured.md (how to opt in/opt out and examples)

Review conversation highlights (excerpted and paraphrased into a single string): - Oliver Park: "Nice conservative approach. Question: what happens to token-level billing attribution when we coalesce fragments?" Author reply: "We preserve token counts and annotate the coerced payload; billing code reads token totals from the annotated envelope unchanged." - Sana Iqbal: "Ensure mapper is O(1) memory for tiny fragments; we don't want it to buffer entire large streams." Author reply: "Mapper bounds to max 8KB aggregation window, then emits partial-coercion with legacy_metadata and a telemetry counter for truncated envelopes." - Diego Morales requested an additional integration test for tool-call failure paths; author added it in second commit. CI status and reruns: - First pipeline: failed (1 flaky streaming test) - Second pipeline: pass after deterministic buffer fix - All required checks (unit, integration, lint, go vet) passed before merge

Release notes / migration guidance (user-facing blurb): "Introduced a temporary compatibility mode for legacy tool envelopes. Customers still on older SDKs may opt into X-RW-Compat: legacy=1 to keep behavior stable during migration. This is planned for deprecation; watch Console announcements for timelines." Rollout and telemetry plan: - Feature flag gated per-tenant; rollout started on beta tenants 2025-02-18. - Telemetry collects mapping.count, mapping.truncated_count, mapping.ambiguous_count; SRE will monitor for error increase and latencies. - Plan to enable campus-wide read-only audit logs for 30 days before turning on auto-coercion by default.

Related work and follow-ups: - Follow-up task ENG-3381: adapt SDKs to emit the new structured tool payloads (Python and TS patches). - Deprecation RFC will be published and linked in Console and docs; schedule will be at least 90 days after default-on. Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2025-02-20 after approvals from Oliver Park and Sana Iqbal. No breaking changes introduced.
Temporary compat header X-RW-Compat: legacy=1 enables soft-mapping of legacy tool envelopes and fragmented streaming events into current structured tool-call requests. Opt-in via Console flag; telemetry added. Planned deprecation with 90+ day notice.

title: Migrate lint and release scripts to Go wrapper for hermetic presubmit

Migrate lint and release scripts to Go wrapper for hermetic presubmit

Context: Our long-running presubmit and release automation relied on a mix of bash wrapper scripts and ad-hoc node/python invocations which caused flaky toolchain differences across CI runners and local devs. This PR introduces a small Go-based presubmit wrapper that vendors deterministic toolchain invocation, unifies lint/release flows, and adds an opt-in dep-vetting phase to catch transitive upgrades before they reach main. title: introduce-resilient-dedicated-throttle-controller-and-percentile-throughput-reporter
body:
introduce-resilient-dedicated-throttle-controller-and-percentile-throughput-reporter

Adds a DedicatedThrottleController to smooth burst allocations and a PercentileThroughputReporter metric for SLA visibility. Backwards compatible; config defaults preserve existing behavior. Operators should review new helm values documented in the release notes.
Motivation: Dedicated capacity customers need predictable throughput guarantees even during fleet-wide transient surges and node churn. Existing burst allocation logic can over-commit short-lived warm pools and create noisy percentile signals in observability. This PR introduces a DedicatedThrottleController, a small control-plane component that enforces soft per-tenant token smoothing, speculative backfill limits, and a drift-correction heuristic that prevents slow leak/accumulate behaviors when telemetry is sparse. The controller is configurable by tenant-level policy and integrated with the existing fleet headroom allocator so it can provide graceful degradation rather than hard rejects. We also add a PercentileThroughputReporter that computes 50/90/99 throughput percentiles for each tenant over sliding windows and emits both summary and raw-sample metrics for downstream reporting and SLO evaluation. Design highlights: 1) Token smoothing: uses a leaky-bucket style accumulator with a two-timescale smoothing (fast window for immediate burst allowance, slow window for baseline throughput) and an adjustable recovery factor to support graceful reduction after sustained high load. 2) Speculative backfill limiter: allows short-lived allocation from ephemeral warmlets but caps effective concurrency headroom per-tenant so large tenants cannot monopolize burst slots during cluster-wide surges. 3) Drift-correction heuristic: when the reporter detects steady mismatch between requested capacity and observed completions, the controller applies conservative calibration to the smoothing parameters to avoid runaway optimistic allocations. 4) Telemetry: the PercentileThroughputReporter emits per-tenant throughput percentiles (p50/p90/p99 tokens/sec), a burst-utilization ratio, and a 'smoothed_headroom' gauge used by autoscaler advisors. 5) Compatibility: new helm values default to disabled for clusters with custom schedulers; enabling requires setting dedicated.throttleController.enabled=true. Implementation notes: changes span controller code (pkg/controllers/dedicated_throttle.go), allocator integrations (pkg/allocator/headroom_adapter.go), telemetry (pkg/telemetry/percentile_reporter.go), a small operator CRD addition (deploy/crds/dedicatedpolicy.yaml), unit and e2e tests (pkg/controllers/*_test.go, test/e2e/dedicated_throttle_test.go), and chart values (charts/dedicated/values.yaml). Tests: added deterministic unit tests for smoothing math, three e2e scenarios that simulate short microbursts, sustained high load, and telemetry sparsity, plus a load harness run that asserts no regressions in 95th percentile latency. Observability: dashboards updated (observability/dashboards/dedicated_throttle.json) and a short runbook entry included (docs/ops/dedicated_throttle_runbook.md). Rollout plan: staged rollout behind the helm flag with canary percentage by tenant label; operator tooling will surface the new percentile metrics and suggestion engine will recommend knob values based on historical load. Backwards compatibility: controllers default to no-op if DedicatedPolicy CRD not present and helm flag is off. Related work: builds on ENG-1427 (headroom allocator refactor), leverages some heuristics from ENG-1683 (burst bank smoothing). Checklist: - [x] controller logic implemented - [x] allocator integration hooks - [x] unit + e2e tests - [x] telemetry + dashboards - [x] helm values + docs - [x] perf benchmark and no-regression check - [x] runbook and rollout notes

title: Cohort-traceback fanout conductor with interruptible rollback and explainable recovery
body:
Cohort-traceback fanout conductor with interruptible rollback and explainable recovery

Summary: Introduces the 'Cohort Traceback Fanout Conductor' (CTFC), a rollout controller that prioritizes session-coherent cohorts for canary/A-B promotions, supports interruptible rollbacks mid-fanout, and exposes an explainable rollback oracle that surfaces the minimal contributing signals when a promote fails.

Motivation: Recent incidents showed large blast radii when promotions ignored session affinity and when rollbacks were binary and opaque. CTFC reduces user-visible regressions by ensuring fans are constrained to cohort boundaries, enabling on-the-fly interruption, and providing triageable telemetry to SREs and PMs.

Changes:
- New controller binary: controllers/ctfc with core reconcile loop, progress checkpointing, and interrupt logic.
- Exhaustive telemetry: telemetry/ctfc_metrics.go + new events for "fanout_step", "rollback_interrupt", and "counterfactual_smoke".
- Explainable rollback oracle: a modular evaluator that runs a compact counterfactual smoke replay on recent samples and returns ranked signal contributions.
- Safety budget integration: honor existing rollout budget tokens and expose a credit refund when early-interrupts avoid downstream degradation.
- Dry-run mode: a CLI flag and API path that runs validation without committing traffic.
- Tests: e2e smoke harness that replays recorded traffic and unit tests for oracle scorer.
